5.11 Stat Tiles

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

layout-stat-tiles · rule layout slides

✅ Normative

Each stat tile MUST be rendered as one printed label–value pair, in tile reading order, under the panel's heading where the panel prints one. Units and qualifiers MUST stay attached to their value.

A slide panel that prints a big number with a short label — Out-of-home +26.5%, Total -19.8% — usually two or three of them side by side under a heading.

┌─ 2025 volume growth¹ ──────────┐
│  Out-of-home        Total       │
│  ┌────────┐       ┌────────┐    │
│  │ +26.5% │       │ -19.8% │    │
└──────────────────────────────────┘

Read top to bottom, the labels come first and the values after, so a geometric reading separates each figure from its label — the failure to avoid.

Requirements

  • Each tile MUST be one key-value line, - label: value, with the label and the value as printed; bold only where the glyphs are heavier.
  • The tiles MUST follow tile reading order, each label next to its own value.
  • A printed panel heading MUST come before its tiles. A heading MUST NOT be invented where the panel prints none.
  • A unit, sign, footnote marker or qualifier (LFL, (+1.9%)) MUST stay with the value it qualifies; an icon that carries the direction MUST be kept — see Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4.
✅ Sample — a growth panel beside two photos

2025 volume growth¹ over two labelled figures, inside an orange box under four bullets. Each tile becomes one line, label then value, in left-to-right order. The rest of the slide — tabs, photos, footer — is rendered in Slide Furniture§5.10.

✅ Sample — a headline figure over a small table

Q1 2026 over €240m, with the qualifiers +2.2% and +6.7% LFL in pills beneath, then a four-column table in the same card. The headline figure is one tile: its label, its value and both qualifiers on one line. The right-hand card is rendered in Slide Furniture§5.10.

✅ Sample — tiles with an arrow icon

Two rounded tiles beside a stacked-bar chart: 1H FY25/26 over $9,675.2M, then YoY with a green up-arrow before $177.8M (+1.9%). The arrow carries the direction and is kept as a bracketed tag. The chart prints no value axis and no values; its rendering follows the Charts chapter and is elided here.

§6 Headings and page structure

6.1 Dot Leader Lines

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-dot-leader-lines · text rule layout

✅ Normative

Dot leaders MUST NOT appear in the output. The label and the value on either side of a leader MUST be kept exactly as printed; the dots themselves produce nothing.

A deliberate exception to verbatim transcription

Everywhere else printed ink survives — see Values Are Verbatim§10.3.3 and Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3. Dot leaders are the one carve-out: they exist only to guide the eye across a gutter and carry no information.

A dot leader is a run of dots filling horizontal space between a label and a value, most often in a table of contents, a directory or a price list.

Chapter 3 — Reserving  . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  47

Requirements

  • A run of leader dots MUST be removed wherever it is printed: in running text, in a directory line and in a table's stub cell.
  • The label and every value the leader connects MUST be kept, verbatim. The dots go; everything they connect stays.
  • Removing a leader MUST NOT split a label or a value, and a leader MUST NOT be absorbed into either side (no trailing dots on a label, no leading dots on a number).
  • Where a leader separates two values on one line, the values remain on that line, separated by a space.

A dot leader is typesetting, not content: it exists because a label and a number are far apart on the line, and it disappears the moment the text is reflowed. Transcribing it damages what is around it — a run of dots inside a label breaks any string match on that label.

✅ Sample — leader lines with two values at the end

A court directory: each person's line runs a dot leader to an e-mail address in grey and a phone number at the margin. Some lines have no e-mail, so the leader runs straight to the number. This is text, not a table: one line per person, leaders removed, the values separated by spaces. The grey of the e-mail addresses is decoration and is not carried. Heading depths are relative: the page does not show where CALDRIVANE COUNTY sits in the whole directory.

✅ Sample — leaders inside a financial table

Two goodwill tables whose stub labels run dot leaders to the first value column — Balances as of January 1, 2002 . . . . . . . — inside an otherwise ordinary $-gutter table. The leaders go; the columns stay. The (In millions) line is rendered as a second header row.

Related

  • Table of Contents§6.10 — the page type where leaders are most common
  • Line Separators and Breaks§6.3 — a printed rule between blocks, which is kept
  • Values Are Verbatim§10.3.3 — the verbatim rule this note is the exception to

6.2 Line Breaks Inside a Block

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-line-breaks-inside-a-block · text layout line-breaks

✅ Normative

One printed block set on several lines MUST stay one element, with a plain newline between its printed lines — no trailing spaces, no <br>. The same spelling MUST be used for every multi-line block in the document. Inside a table cell, where a newline cannot be written, the break is <br>.

One printed block that runs to more than one line because the page sets it that way: a stacked masthead, a postal address, a two-line banner, a title broken across a rule. The lines belong together; only the typesetting separates them.

MEREVALD                     ← one block, two printed lines
Merevald Retail Ltd

Settled: the block stays whole

  • One printed block MUST be one element, whatever break is written between its lines. Two stacked lines of a masthead MUST NOT become two headings, two paragraphs, or a heading with a subtitle. Splitting it is the never invent failure: the page printed one block, and a split claims it printed two.
  • Whether lines form one block is judged by the printing, not the wording: a single set, a single alignment and a single leading mean one block, even when the two lines read as separable phrases.

The break is a plain newline

The Markdown source keeps every printed line on its own source line. A renderer shows a single newline inside a paragraph as a space, so a rendered view runs the lines together; that is a display artefact, not a change to the output, which is judged on its source (see Numbered Section Headings§6.5 for the same principle). Two trailing spaces are invisible and are stripped by most whitespace normalisation; <br> puts markup on every line. Neither is used outside table cells.

  • The break MUST be a plain newline, and the same spelling MUST be used for every multi-line block in the document — paragraphs, addresses, headers and footers alike.
  • Inside a table cell a newline cannot be written, so a printed break there is <br> — see Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells§9.5.3.
  • A line that Markdown would parse as a list item or heading (- , 1. , # at its start) is escaped — see Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4.

Not this rule's case

  • A rule printed between blocks is a separator, not a break inside one — see Line Separators and Breaks§6.3.
  • A line that wraps because it ran out of column width is not a printed break at all: its lines MUST be joined with a space.
  • Text whose line breaks carry meaning, such as verse, is governed by Verse and Hard Line Breaks§7.2.13.

Related

  • Line Separators and Breaks§6.3 — a rule between blocks, which resolves differently
  • Verse and Hard Line Breaks§7.2.13 — text whose breaks are content
  • Stacked Headings§6.9 — a title wrapped over several lines, joined with spaces
  • Recurring Page Furniture§4.6 — header and footer bands, which take the same break

6.3 Line Separators and Breaks

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

layout-line-separators-and-breaks · rule layout model-divergence

✅ Normative

A printed section separator MUST be rendered as <hr/>, at its place in reading order. --- MUST NOT be used for it: --- is reserved for page boundaries. A rule MUST NOT be inserted where the page prints only whitespace.

A horizontal rule or separator printed between sections of a page. It is printed content: it tells a reader that one block has ended and another begun, so it survives into the output.

… end of the first section.
────────────────────────────        ← printed rule between sections  →  <hr/>
Start of the next section …

Requirements

  • Each printed separator between sections MUST produce one <hr/> line, placed between the elements it separates in reading order.
  • The separator MUST NOT be written as ---, ***, ___ or any other Markdown thematic break.
  • Vertical whitespace between sections, with no printed line, MUST NOT produce <hr/>.

Why never ---

--- is already load-bearing twice. It is the page-break marker of Markdown Rendering§3.2, and at the top of a file it opens frontmatter. A separator that renders identically to a page break makes page attribution ambiguous for anything splitting on it, and can silently truncate a document at the top of a file. <hr/> avoids both collisions and follows the general posture of falling back to HTML wherever a Markdown spelling is ambiguous — see Text Formatting Conventions§7.1.

Related

  • Markdown Rendering§3.2 — --- as the page boundary
  • Line Breaks Inside a Block§6.2 — a break within one block, which resolves differently
  • Dot Leader Lines§6.1 — the other printed line-filler, which is removed rather than kept
  • Text Formatting Conventions§7.1 — HTML where a Markdown spelling is ambiguous

6.4 Marginal Notes

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

layout-marginal-notes · layout rule structure legal

✅ Normative

Each printed marginal note MUST be rendered as a separate block placed immediately after the element it annotates. Where the element it belongs to cannot be established, the note MUST still be kept as a separate block and MUST NOT be merged into body text.

Statutes and some textbooks print short notes in the outer margin — a citation, a one-word gloss — aligned with the line they annotate. They are printed text, not handwriting, and they belong to a particular line.

SEC. 105. INVESTIGATIONS AND DISCIPLINARY PROCEEDINGS.        15 USC 7215.
   (a) IN GENERAL.—The Board shall establish, by rule, …      Establishment.

Requirements

  • A marginal note MUST be its own element, never part of the heading or paragraph it sits beside.
  • It MUST follow the element it annotates — the heading or paragraph level with it — in reading order, before the next element of the body.
  • A geometric reading that inserts 15 USC 7215. into the middle of the section heading, or splices a gloss into a line of the paragraph, does not conform.
✅ Sample — a public law with sidenotes


Source: Public Law 107-204 (Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002), 116 Stat. 759, §105 marginal notes (public domain)

15 USC 7215. and Establishment. in the right margin, level with SEC. 105. and (a) IN GENERAL.; the body is set in one narrower column. The small capitals of IN GENERAL are transcribed as capitals. The heading depth is relative: the page does not show the outline above the section.

Related

  • Reading Order§5.9 — notes go where a reader meets them
  • Run-In Headings§6.8 — the small-cap run-in heads on the same page
  • Handwritten Annotations§7.3.3 — the handwritten equivalent
  • Small Capitals§7.2.10 — how IN GENERAL is transcribed

6.5 Numbered Section Headings

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

headings-numbered-section-headings · structure headings lists

✅ Normative

A numbered line that stands alone as a title with body text beneath it MUST be rendered as a heading, one level deeper per level of numbering. A numbered line that is itself the content — including a bare number printed above its paragraph — MUST be rendered as a list item carrying that content. The printed number MUST be kept exactly as printed, on the same line as its text.

Legal and technical documents number their sections — 1., 1.1., 2.3. — and set each on its own line, often underlined or bold, with a paragraph beneath. On the page this is a heading; in the text layer it is indistinguishable from an ordered list.

1.    AFFIDAVIT

1.1.  COMPLETION AND SIGNATURE
      The Commissioner of Oaths must print his full name …
1.2.  SECURITY
      If security is claimed, then the amount …

Heading or list item

The page prints Rendering
A numbered title on its own line, with body text beneath (1. AFFIDAVIT) heading, depth from the numbering: ## 1. AFFIDAVIT, ### 1.1. COMPLETION AND SIGNATURE
A numbered line that is itself the content list item: 3. The Registrar will set the matter down …
A bare number on a line of its own, above its paragraph (29.) list item: the number joins its paragraph's line, 29. As a direct and proximate result …

The test is the one Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7 applies: a title organises the block beneath it; a numbered paragraph is an item of an enumeration. Heading depth follows the printed numbering, as Heading Depth Across Pages§4.5 requires.

A bare number is moved onto its paragraph's line because it labels that paragraph ("paragraph 29"). Left on a line of its own it would read as an empty list item followed by an unrelated paragraph. Only the centring is lost, and centring is layout.

Numbers are written verbatim

The printed number MUST be written as printed — 29., 1.1., (a), IV. — and MUST NOT be renumbered, normalised or escaped to prevent list parsing. A number that is a valid Markdown list marker (29.) then renders as a list item; one that is not (1.1., (a)) renders as a paragraph beginning with the number. Both carry the printed numbering exactly in the source, which is what the output is judged on; a renderer that shows skipped numbers (29, 31) as consecutive is a display artefact, not a change to the output.

The one exception is a line that Markdown would turn into a list although the page prints no list, such as a sentence that begins 1995. was a record year. Its marker MUST be escaped (1995\.) — see Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4.

✅ Sample — two-level numbered notes

"1. AFFIDAVIT" over "1.1. COMPLETION AND SIGNATURE", "1.2. SECURITY", each sub-heading underlined with a paragraph beneath it. Four top-level numbers on the page, sub-numbered under two of them. Each numbered line is a heading, one level deeper per level of numbering; the depths shown assume this page opens the document, under its title.

✅ Sample — a paragraph number on its own line

29. to 34. each centred on a line of their own, the paragraph beneath. The number is neither a heading with text nor a list marker on the paragraph's line. The numbered paragraph is the text, so each number opens a list item carrying its paragraph. The depth of DAMAGES is relative: the page does not show the outline above it.

Repeated item labels

“Question N”, “Interrogatory No. N” and “Request for Production N” are item labels, even when bold and alone on a line, and MUST NOT be rendered as headings. A standalone section title organises a block; a recurring label merely identifies the next item. See Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7 for the distinction in context.

Related

  • Bullets and Sub-Bullets§8.1 — ordered lists keep their printed numbering
  • Block Classes§5.3 — Section-header versus List-item
  • Table of Contents§6.10 — where the same numbers reappear as an index
  • Heading Depth Across Pages§4.5 — printed numbering sets the depth

6.6 Printed Page Numbers

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

layout-printed-page-numbers · rule layout

✅ Normative

A printed page number (the folio) MUST be kept in the header or footer band it is printed in, verbatim, and MUST NOT appear as a loose element in the body. When the printed page number is requested, it MUST also be recorded on its own for the page, as printed, and MUST NOT be inferred for a page that prints none.

The folio is the number a document prints on itself: 26, Page 6, Page 3 of 12, iv, A-3. It sits in the top or bottom margin, often beside a date, a form number or a URL.

FORM CMS-2567  Previous Versions Obsolete       If continuation sheet Page 3 of 12
                                                                      ↑ the folio

Two records

Record Requirement
In the band The folio is part of the header or footer it is printed in. The band MUST be kept together and verbatim — see Recurring Page Furniture§4.6.
On its own When the printed page number is requested (Output Options§3.5), the number MUST also be recorded alone for the page — the sidecar's printedPageNumber, see The Sidecar§3.4. The label MUST be stripped and the numbering kept as printed: 6, not Page 6; roman numerals stay roman; A-3 stays A-3.

The offset is the point

Front matter, covers and inserts mean printed page 1 is often not sheet 1. A magazine feature can open on sheet 1 and print 26; a report can run twelve sheets of front matter before printing 1. That mapping is a fact about the document, not the page, and it is the reason the number is worth recording separately — a reader citing "page 26" cannot otherwise be sent to the right sheet.

  • The recorded number MUST be the number the page prints. It MUST NOT be renumbered to match the sheet position.
  • A folio MUST NOT be inferred for a page that prints none.

Pages that print nothing

Covers, plates and continuation sheets frequently carry no folio; their printed page number is empty, which is not an error. A pre-printed blank, Page ___ of ___, is also no folio: the blank MUST be transcribed in the band (as [blank]) and no number recorded.

A folio never sits in the body

A number that ends up as a loose line among the page's content means the band was read wrongly. The folio MUST belong to its margin band whether or not the rest of that band was recognised — the same never invent failure as promoting furniture to a heading.

Related

  • Recurring Page Furniture§4.6 — the band the folio belongs to
  • Output Options§3.5 — the option that asks for the number on its own
  • The Sidecar§3.4 — where the number is recorded
  • Block Classes§5.3 — a page number alone qualifies as Page-footer

6.7 Recognising Ambiguous Headings

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

headings-recognising-ambiguous-headings · rule headings structure

✅ Normative

A standalone structural title that organises what follows MUST be rendered as a heading. Run-in labels, repeated item labels, captions and page furniture MUST keep their own roles and MUST NOT be rendered as headings. Font size alone MUST NOT decide whether a line is a heading.

What a line does decides its role; its depth is chosen afterwards. A short bold line can organise a section; a large banner can belong entirely to a form or a table.

Company name over a title    ← its own line, above the heading
Company name alone           ← furniture
Document title               ← heading
Standalone section title     ← heading
Bold label: value or sentence ← inline label
Table 1: ...                 ← caption

Heading depths in the samples below are relative wherever the crop does not show the outline above the heading: the rendering keeps the hierarchy the crop shows, and the absolute level comes from Heading Depth Across Pages§4.5.

Run-in labels

A label followed on the same line by a sentence, value or URL MUST stay inline, with its printed emphasis preserved. A line that wraps onto another line remains the same paragraph. See Run-In Headings§6.8.

✅ Sample — run-in labels 1


Source: Federal Rules of Evidence, Rule 410 (public domain)

“(a) PROHIBITED USES.” stays inline with its sentence; its small capitals are transcribed as capitals. The standalone “Rule 410. Pleas, Plea Discussions, and Related Statements” is a heading. The crop clips item (3), which is elided.

✅ Sample — run-in labels 2

“Consumer Banking and Lending” stays in its paragraph: the sentence continues immediately after the bold, underlined label. The line below the paragraph is outside this example and is elided.

✅ Sample — run-in labels 3

“Original Article:” stays with its URL as a label–value line. The red of the label is decoration and is not carried; the URL is raw text.

Standalone subheads

A standalone title that organises the paragraphs or bullets below it MUST be a heading, even at body-text size. Weight, colour and underlining support the reading; none decides it alone.

✅ Sample — standalone subheads 1

“Highlights:” and its subordinate “Summary” are headings; each introduces the bullet block below. “Summary” is one level deeper than “Highlights:”. The quotation above is elided.

✅ Sample — standalone subheads 2

“Risk weighted assets” is a heading: its own line introduces the following prose.

✅ Sample — standalone subheads 3

“Strong cash performance” is a heading. Colour does not prevent the line from organising its bullets. one-off breaks at its own hyphen and keeps it.

✅ Sample — standalone subheads 4

“Restatement of operating costs” is a heading; it introduces the paragraphs below it.

Numbered titles and numbered paragraphs

A printed number or letter MUST stay with the standalone section title it numbers. A number opening a body sentence is a list marker. A number on a line by itself does not turn its paragraph into a section. See Numbered Section Headings§6.5.

✅ Sample — numbered titles and numbered paragraphs 1

“d. Employees and Volunteers” is a heading, with the printed letter attached. A faint diagonal watermark, only partly legible in the crop, is left out of this excerpt.

✅ Sample — numbered titles and numbered paragraphs 2

“25.” stays with the sentence it numbers; the numbered paragraph is not promoted to a heading. The centred title below it, printed on two lines, is one heading (see Stacked Headings§6.9).

Repeated item labels

Repeated Question, Interrogatory and Request for Production labels MUST stay with their items, even when bold and on their own lines. Each label MUST NOT be made a document heading.

✅ Sample — repeated item labels 1

“INTERROGATORY NO. 8:” is the label of its question, like the next interrogatory label below it. It is printed bold, underlined and in small capitals, which are transcribed as capitals.

Document titles and company lines

A document title MUST be separated from its logo, company-name line and exhibit label. The surrounding words are transcribed as furniture; only the title takes a heading role. A company name MUST NOT be joined to a title merely because they are stacked.

✅ Sample — document titles and company lines 1

“Benefits Terms of Service” is the document title. The Zendra logo — a small icon over the wordmark — and “Exhibit D” stay separate; the logo becomes [logo: Zendra]. The title is shown at the top level of the exhibit.

✅ Sample — document titles and company lines 2

“BOARD OF DIRECTORS GOVERNANCE PRINCIPLES” is the title. “BORVIKA LLC” stays a separate company line. The printed rule under the title is a separator.

Principal statement and schedule titles

The principal title of a financial statement or numbered schedule is structural and MUST be a heading. The company line and the units or audit-status line MUST stay separate. This is a specific exception to the caption rule below: a statement or schedule can itself be a document section.

A numbered schedule title remains structural when printed inside a grid. Its text MUST appear once, in its printed table position; it keeps its heading role in the element classes and boxes (see Boxes and Granularity§3.3) and MUST NOT be duplicated as a Markdown heading outside the table. Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3 governs its cell placement.

✅ Sample — principal statement and schedule titles 1

“CONDENSED CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEETS” is the statement heading. The company name and the parenthesised units line stay separate. The table beneath is elided.

✅ Sample — principal statement and schedule titles 2

“Operating Income by Geographic Market” is the statement heading. “Marlowick Consulting plc”, the currency units and the audit status stay outside the heading. The table beneath is elided.

✅ Sample — principal statement and schedule titles 3

“11. SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT EXPENSES” is a structural schedule title in its printed grid position: a full-width row of the table, not a Markdown heading. The company line is separate furniture. The blue of the current-year figures is decoration. The crop ends after Staff welfare.

Table captions and bands

An ordinary table caption, coloured title band, repeated caption stack or column label MUST NOT enter the document outline. A Table N caption remains a caption even when its typography resembles a heading or it appears in a PDF outline. The principal-statement exception above applies only to an actual statement or schedule section.

Captions stay outside the table and title bands inside it, as Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3 requires. The same title MUST NOT be emitted both as a cell and as an outside heading.

✅ Sample — table captions and bands 1

“Free Cash Flow and Free Cash Flow Dividend Payout Ratio” is the table's title band, inside the table.

✅ Sample — table captions and bands 2

“Ondrea Group. Summarized income statement” is the local table caption, with its units line separate; a caption is not promoted merely because it names a statement. Change over % is one wrapped header label. The paragraph above the caption is elided.

✅ Sample — table captions and bands 3

The “Portfolio Detail Statistics” stack stays with its table as caption text; its lines do not become heading levels.

✅ Sample — table captions and bands 4

“Table 1: Milestones achieved since the prior results announcement” is a caption. “Results highlights” organises the section above it and is a heading. The crop clips the table after its second row.

✅ Sample — table captions and bands 5

“Turnover” is a column header. “Growth” is the standalone title above the table and is a heading.

Chart titles and text-column titles

A title naming a chart is part of that chart. A standalone title organising a text column or explanatory block below or beside the charts MUST be a heading.

✅ Sample — chart titles and text-column titles 1

“Fourth Quarter 2025” and “Full Year 2025” are headings, peers, for the text columns beneath the charts. The two charts and their legend are elided.

Slides and embedded forms

The principal slide title and a real subtitle are structural titles and MUST be headings. Navigation sidebars, tabs, warning banners and form section labels are furniture or form labels and MUST NOT be headings. Titles inside an embedded form screenshot MUST NOT enter the containing slide's outline; their printed text MUST be kept in the embedded content.

✅ Sample — slides and embedded forms 1

“Caldrivane submission schedule” is the slide title and “Supplementary indications for existing brands” its subtitle. “Content” stays in the navigation sidebar. The navigation tabs print no text. Depths assume the file is a deck, where each slide title is top level.

✅ Sample — slides and embedded forms 2

The form title, warning banner and subcontractor-section label stay inside the embedded form content, outside the containing slide's outline: none of them is a heading. The instructions box and the code list are elided.

Running headers and decorative marks

Whether a page-top label is a running header is a document decision, made in Recurring Page Furniture§4.6: the same words may have been a section heading where the section began, and repetition at a page boundary does not open it again. From one page alone, a margin label that carries no argument of its own is furniture. A purely decorative arrow before a heading MUST be omitted from the heading text; a printed section number MUST be kept.

✅ Sample — running headers and decorative marks 1

When “Consolidated Financial Statements” repeats at the page top, it is a running header: a band paragraph, not a heading. The repetition is established on the surrounding pages; this crop alone does not establish it. The Markdown shown assumes it does.

✅ Sample — running headers and decorative marks 2

“19. Personnel expenses” is the heading text. The decorative arrow to its left is excluded. The table beneath is cut by the crop.

Depth comes after role

Heading levels MUST be the document-absolute levels of Heading Depth Across Pages§4.5. When only one page is available, the relative hierarchy the page shows MUST be kept consistent. The first heading on a page MUST NOT be assumed to be the top level, and a level that is common elsewhere MUST NOT be assumed for this page. Whether the deck convention applies is decided once for the file in Document Type§4.4; a level MUST NOT be copied from another document.

  • Heading Depth Across Pages§4.5 — choose the level after deciding that a line is a heading
  • Recurring Page Furniture§4.6 — the document-wide call on repeated page-top labels
  • Run-In Headings§6.8 — a label kept within its paragraph
  • Numbered Section Headings§6.5 — numbered titles versus numbered content

6.8 Run-In Headings

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

headings-run-in-headings · rule structure headings

✅ Normative

A run-in label and the sentence, value or URL that follows it on the same line MUST be rendered as one paragraph, with the label's printed emphasis preserved. The label MUST NOT be rendered as a Markdown heading.

A run-in heading is set at the start of its own paragraph, in bold or colour, with the body text continuing on the same line. Contracts number their clauses this way; glossaries print the term this way.

Section 11.1.1 The Department requires that business enterprises so certified by …
AMBIGUOUS  Confusing question in that it is capable of being understood in more than one sense.
  ↑ bold label, text continues on the same line

Requirements

  • The label and its text MUST stay in one paragraph; a label that wraps onto a further line remains part of the same paragraph.
  • The label's printed bold, italic, underline or small capitals MUST be kept as inline marks (see Bold and Italics§7.2.1, Underlined Text§7.2.12, Small Capitals§7.2.10).
  • The label MUST NOT be split onto a line of its own or promoted to a heading: a lead-in rendered as a heading creates a false outline entry.
  • A numbered title set on its own line, with its text beneath, is not run-in; it is a heading — see Numbered Section Headings§6.5.
✅ Sample — numbered contract clauses

Section 11.1.1 through 11.1.4 open their paragraphs in bold; Section 11.1 and 11.2 are set on their own lines, underlined, and behave as ordinary headings. Both shapes on one page. The two-line ARTICLE 11 title is one heading (see Stacked Headings§6.9). Heading depths are relative: the page, sheet 41 of 96, does not show the outline above the article.

✅ Sample — a glossary of objections

Thirty-odd entries, each a red bold term followed on the same line by its definition and a rule citation. Two entries carry a bold Note: inside the definition. The red is decoration and is not carried; the italic citations are. The left column is read before the right.

✅ Sample — section numbers in the margin

32.5 and 32.6 sit in a left margin column beside their headings; 32.5.1 … 32.6.2 open their paragraphs in bold on the same line. The page also prints each paragraph number a second time, in plain type, in the margin column; both copies are printed, so both are kept, in reading order. Heading depths follow the numbering and assume chapters are top level; the running header is left out of this excerpt.

Labels followed by values

A label followed on the same line by a value or URL MUST be kept as a label–value pair in one paragraph. Small caps, colour or underlining do not make it a heading. See Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7.

Related

  • Numbered Section Headings§6.5 — the same numbers on their own line, which are headings
  • Stacked Headings§6.9 — the other way a heading fails to be one line
  • Bold and Italics§7.2.1 — the label's bold is printed, so it is kept
  • Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7 — run-in labels among the other heading look-alikes

6.9 Stacked Headings

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

headings-stacked-headings · rule structure headings

✅ Normative

The wrapped lines of one title MUST be joined with spaces into one heading. An article number MUST stay with its title. A company name printed above a statement or document title, exhibit labels, units lines and other furniture MUST be kept separate from the title; a title and subtitle MAY be split only where the document establishes distinct roles for them.

A stacked heading is printed over two or three centred lines: an article number over its title, a note number over a title that wraps. A company name printed over a statement name looks the same but is not part of the title.

                ARTICLE 11
     ECONOMIC INCLUSION REQUIREMENTS

21 Total equity
   reconciliation

The question is whether the break is a wrap or a hierarchy. 21 Total equity / reconciliation is a wrap. ARTICLE 11 / ECONOMIC INCLUSION REQUIREMENTS reads as a number and a title — and the number stays with the title.

Requirements

  • The lines of one title MUST be joined with a single space, in printed order, into one heading.
  • Its lines MUST NOT become two headings at the same level, nor a parent heading with a child.
  • An article or note number printed above its title MUST be the start of that title's heading.
  • A subtitle MAY be a separate element only where the document gives title and subtitle distinct roles; otherwise the lines are one heading.
✅ Sample — an article number over its title

ARTICLE 11 and ECONOMIC INCLUSION REQUIREMENTS are centred on two lines, both bold and underlined, at the same size. They form one heading. Its depth is relative: the page does not show the outline above the article.

✅ Sample — a note title that wraps

21 Total equity breaks to reconciliation on a second line in the same green face; the earlier 20 Reserves fits on one. Both note titles are printed inside the grid, under one shared header, so each is a full-width band row of a single table (see Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9); the wrapped title is joined with a space in its cell.

Company name over a statement title

A company or entity name set directly above a statement, report or agreement title is not part of the title. It MUST be rendered as its own paragraph above the heading, keeping its printed emphasis, and the heading is the title alone:

**CORVANE MEDIA CORPORATION**

# CONDENSED CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEETS

(unaudited; $ in millions)

The heading then names the document, so an outline reads "Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheets" rather than repeating the company in every statement title. The same holds for financial statements, agreements and reports alike. The units or date line beneath MUST also stay a separate paragraph. A company name with no title beneath it — only a grid, or a running stack repeated on every page — is furniture; the repetition is judged across the document, see Recurring Page Furniture§4.6.

Furniture is separated before a title is joined

Exhibit labels, units lines and other furniture MUST be separated from the title before its lines are joined; only the lines of the title itself are joined. See Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7 for the distinction between titles and furniture.

  • Numbered Section Headings§6.5 — the level a printed number implies
  • Header Wrap vs Real Tier§9.3.2 — the same wrap-or-tier question inside a table header
  • Line Breaks Inside a Block§6.2 — one block over several lines outside headings

6.10 Table of Contents

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

lists-table-of-contents · layout lists navigation

✅ Normative

A table of contents, table of authorities or index MUST be rendered as a list: one item per entry, nested as the page indents it, each item the label then its page number(s) exactly as printed, separated by a space. It MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

A contents page pairs each label with a page number, usually across a dot leader.

Chapter 3 — Reserving  . . . . . . . . . . . .  47
Chapter 4 — Pricing    . . . . . . . . . . . .  63

Rendering

Printed:   1  Introduction ....................  3
              1.1  Scope ......................  4
           2  Reserving .......................  47

- 1 Introduction 3
  - 1.1 Scope 4
- 2 Reserving 47
  • Every printed entry MUST survive, with its page number(s) attached to the right label.
  • The label and the number are separated by a single space. The dot leaders produce nothing — see Dot Leader Lines§6.1.
  • Nesting shown by indentation MUST be carried as list nesting, not flattened.
  • An entry with several page references keeps them all, as printed: HCR 2.603(A) 4-50, 4-57.
  • A contents page is navigation, not data: rendering it as a table would make it read as facts to anything that consumes the page. A list also holds a run of page references that a two-column table could only cram into one cell.

The exception is a contents page printed as a real ruled grid with column headers (Section | Title | Page). That is a table by the ordinary rules of Is This Even a Table§9.1.5, not a contents exception.

✅ Sample — a table of authorities with several pages per entry

HCR 2.603(D) 3-27, 4-49, 4-54, … — each rule followed by a run of page references in blue, no leaders, one to twelve references per line. A label paired with a list of numbers. The entries form a list, each rule followed by its references; the blue is decoration. The running header and footer bands open and close the page.

Related

  • Dot Leader Lines§6.1 — what the dots become
  • Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 — the test that applies to a contents page printed as a ruled grid
  • Bullets and Sub-Bullets§8.1 — how list nesting is written

6.11 Transcript Pages

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

layout-transcript-pages · layout structure legal line-numbers

✅ Normative

On a transcript page, each speaker turn MUST be rendered as one paragraph that begins with its printed marker (Q, A, THE COURT:), with its wrapped lines joined. Printed line numbers MUST NOT appear in the Markdown; when line numbers are requested they are carried in the page's line_numbers map, exactly as for Pleading Line Numbers§5.8.

A deposition or hearing transcript: numbered lines 1–25, a Q / A column, and text that wraps to the left margin on its continuation lines. The line numbers are cited ("page 47, line 12"), so the line structure is part of the content in a way ordinary prose is not.

 4    Q    Was ████████ paying that before?
 5    A    Yes, he was.
 6    Q    At the time of the temporary hearing, he was
 7  paying the car insurance?

Rendering

  • Each speaker turn — a Q, an A, or a colloquy line such as MR. HALE: or THE COURT: — MUST be its own paragraph, separated from the next by a blank line.
  • The turn MUST begin with its speaker marker exactly as printed (Q, not Q:), followed by its text.
  • A turn that wraps onto further printed lines MUST be joined into one paragraph: the continuation lines carry no marker on the page, and they carry none in the output.
  • The printed line numbers MUST NOT appear in the Markdown, and the page MUST NOT be rendered as a line | speaker | text table.

Citing a line

Transcripts are cited by page and line ("page 83, line 13"). The citation is carried by the line_numbers map defined in Pleading Line Numbers§5.8: when line numbers are requested, each printed number beside text gets an entry whose span covers that line's text inside its turn's paragraph. A wrapped turn therefore keeps both of its line numbers even though it is one paragraph.

✅ Sample — a deposition page

Twenty-five numbered lines in a ruled frame, Q and A in their own column, three turns wrapping to the left margin (lines 6–7, 12–13 and 24–25), each joined into one paragraph, a black redaction bar inside line 4, the folio 83 above the frame and the reporting firm's name and telephone number as a footer.

Related

  • Pleading Line Numbers§5.8 — the same margin numbers on a filing, and the line_numbers map
  • Redacted Text§7.3.8 — the bar in line 4
  • Verse and Hard Line Breaks§7.2.13 — text whose line breaks are content, unlike a transcript's

§7 Text

7.1 Text Formatting Conventions

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-text-formatting-conventions · text formatting inline

✅ Normative

Inline marks MUST be written with exactly the markup in the table below. Where Markdown has no syntax for a mark, the output MUST use the HTML element named here and MUST NOT use a notation of its own.

This is the inline-markup table for the whole protocol. Each row states its requirement; the linked rule holds the detail, the sub-cases and the examples.

Printed mark Requirement Rule
Maths, inline or displayed MUST be LaTeX inside $$ … $$; single $ delimiters MUST NOT be used Inline Equations§7.2.6, Displayed Equations§7.2.2
Hyperlink or email address MUST be raw text by default; link syntax MAY be used only when link extraction was requested Links§7.2.8
Bold / italic MUST be Markdown **bold** / *italic*, and only where the glyphs are heavier or slanted Bold and Italics§7.2.1
Underline MUST be <u>…</u> Underlined Text§7.2.12
Strikeout MUST be ~~…~~ over exactly the struck glyphs Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7
Superscript / subscript MUST be <sup>…</sup> / <sub>…</sub>, never a Unicode raised or lowered glyph Superscript and Subscript§7.2.11
Highlight MUST be <mark>…</mark> over exactly the highlighted run Highlighted Text§7.2.5
Highlight colour MUST be carried as style="background-color: HTML_COLOR_NAME" on the <mark>, using the nearest HTML colour name Highlighted Text§7.2.5, Text Colors§7.3.12
Text colour, when it is the only distinguisher MUST be <font color="HTML_COLOR_NAME">…</font> Text Colors§7.3.12
Signature MUST be [signature:{name}], or bare [signature] when the name is not legible Signatures§7.3.10
Logo MUST be [logo: printed words], or bare [logo] when it prints no text Logos§12.1.3
Watermark MUST be [watermark: printed words], first in its page's content Watermarks§7.3.13
Stamp MUST be [stamp: printed words], or bare [stamp] when illegible Stamps§7.3.11
A printed character that is also Markdown syntax MUST be escaped — \*\*, \_, \|, \` — and MUST NOT be dropped to avoid the collision Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4

Why HTML elements at all

Markdown has no syntax for underline, superscript, subscript or highlight. The HTML element passes through every downstream Markdown renderer unchanged, and it survives a round-trip: a reader can strip it, render it or read the base characters underneath. A Unicode substitute (², ₂) does not, which is why Superscript and Subscript§7.2.11 forbids it.

Related

  • Markdown Rendering§3.2 — the block-level constructs, of which this table is the inline half
  • Elements§3.1 — the Text class takes its inline marks from this table
  • Quick Reference§D.1 — every rule's requirement on one page

7.2 Inline formatting

7.2.1 Bold and Italics

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-bold-and-italics · text formatting inline

✅ Normative

Bold MUST be written **bold** and italic *italic*, in Markdown, except where the Markdown delimiter cannot close, where <strong> / <em> MUST be used. They MUST be applied only where the printed glyphs are heavier or slanted than their neighbours.

HTML elements are reserved for marks Markdown cannot express at all — see Underlined Text§7.2.12, Superscript and Subscript§7.2.11 and Highlighted Text§7.2.5. <b>, <i>, <strong> and <em> MUST NOT be used for ordinary emphasis in the Markdown text.

Where ** cannot close

CommonMark cannot close ** or * between a punctuation mark and a letter: **---**To be is not bold when rendered. In exactly that case — the emphasised run ends in punctuation and a letter or digit follows with no space — the run MUST be written with <strong> (bold) or <em> (italic) instead: <strong>---</strong>To be. Everywhere else the Markdown delimiters are used. (Inside HTML table cells, emphasis is always <strong> / <em> — see Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2.)

Styling comes from the glyphs, not from the role

The syntax is the easy half. The failure that costs fidelity is styling text because of what it is rather than what it looks like: bolding a heading because headings are usually bold, or bolding a whole column because one cell in it is heavy.

  • Styling MUST be decided from the glyphs on the page, one run of text at a time.
  • A run MUST NOT be styled because of its role (heading, label, total) when its glyphs are not heavier or slanted.
  • Where it cannot be established whether a run is heavier than its neighbours, the run SHOULD be left unstyled. An unmarked run loses a nuance; a wrongly marked one asserts something the page does not print — the never invent failure.

Tables are where this goes wrong most often, and they are judged cell by cell — see Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2.

Related
  • Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2 — the same rule applied cell by cell, where over-application is most common
  • Text Formatting Conventions§7.1 — the full inline-markup table
  • Drop Caps§7.2.3 — size is typography, not a style the output records

7.2.2 Displayed Equations

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-displayed-equations · text formatting math

✅ Normative

Displayed mathematics MUST be written as LaTeX inside $$ … $$. Its printed equation number MUST follow the closing delimiter as plain text in the same formula block: $$ … $$ (1).

A displayed equation is set on its own line, usually centred, often with a number at the right margin — (1), (2) — that the prose cites.

                 ΔE = ΔE⁰ − (RT / m·F) [ ln(θ / 1−θ) + fθ + gθ^(3/2) ]          (1)
Requirements
  • The delimiters are those of Inline Equations§7.2.6: $$ … $$, never single $.
  • The equation number MUST be kept. It is content — "as shown in (1)" appears in the prose — and dropping it is the one option that loses something (never drop).
  • The number MUST be written after the closing $$, as plain text, in the same block — not inside the LaTeX, and not as a separate paragraph. The Formula block includes its number; see Block Classes§5.3.
  • An unnumbered display MUST NOT be given a number.
✅ Sample — numbered equations in a two-column article

Two display equations, numbered (1) and (2) at the right margin, each cited in the surrounding text. Equation (2) spans the full column width and wraps after ⇒; the wrap is typesetting, so the LaTeX is one line. The symbol cited in the prose after (1) is itself maths and takes the inline form.

✅ Sample — a typewritten paper

Equation V = pu_y numbered (2) at the right margin, then an unnumbered display ½ mV², in a scanned typewritten proceedings page. Run-in underlined headings, also set in italic, open two paragraphs.

Formulas drawn as boxes

A formula laid out as boxes joined by operators is still an equation.

  • A boxed arithmetic formula MUST be written in $$ … $$, keeping every printed operand, operator and label; the box labels become the operands.
  • Where the boxes express a process rather than an equation, the region is a diagram and MUST be rendered as a diagram block instead — see Images and Figures§12.1.2.
✅ Sample — a formula drawn as boxes


Source: Defense Business Practice Implementation Board, Financial Indicators Task Group, Report FY03-1, "Capital Asset Growth Rate" (public domain)

A growth-rate calculation laid out as black boxes: two boxes joined by - over a rule, a third box beneath, each box holding a labelled sum in bold white type. It is a fraction with no LaTeX on the page. The grouping the boxes print becomes parentheses in the numerator.

Related
  • Inline Equations§7.2.6 — the delimiters
  • Block Classes§5.3 — the Formula block carries its number
  • Images and Figures§12.1.2 — where boxes describe a process, the region is a diagram
  • Drop Caps§7.2.3 — the article sample opens with one

7.2.3 Drop Caps

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-drop-caps · text formatting inline

✅ Normative

A drop cap MUST be joined directly to the rest of its word, with no space, line break or styling added. The output MUST NOT mark the letter as bold, enlarged or otherwise distinct.

A drop cap is an enlarged first letter, sunk two or more lines into the opening paragraph. The letter belongs to the first word; the text layer often separates it, and a line-by-line reading puts the rest of the word on a different line from its initial.

T  he modern Recreational Boating Safety (RBS)
   Program traces its inception to the Federal Boat
   Safety Act (FBSA) of 1971.
Requirements
  • The initial MUST be joined to its word. The page prints one word in two sizes, not two words.
  • The letter MUST NOT be bolded, enlarged or otherwise marked. Size here is typography, not emphasis — the same reasoning as Bold and Italics§7.2.1.
  • A decorated or ornamental initial is treated the same way: it is still the letter.
  • The letter MUST be read from the image, not the text layer — see Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3. A legible initial MUST NOT be dropped or replaced by the text layer's reading.
✅ Sample — a magazine opener


Source: U.S. Coast Guard, "The Value of the Recreational Boating Safety Program" by Verne Gifford, Chief, Boating Safety Division, Proceedings Vol. 83 No. 1, p.7 (public domain)

The article opens with a three-line "T"; the first word is "The". The text layer of the file splits it as T then he.

✅ Sample — a journal article

A four-line "D" opening "Deposition via surface limited redox replacement". The citation 2–4 is split across two lines by the column; it is one superscript. The same page carries numbered display equations — see Displayed Equations§7.2.2.

Related
  • Bold and Italics§7.2.1 — styling comes from the glyphs, and size is not a style the output records
  • Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3 — the image wins over the text layer
  • Line-End Hyphenation§7.2.7 — the other place the text layer splits a word

7.2.4 Escaping Printed Marks

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-escaping-printed-marks · text formatting inline

✅ Normative

A character the page prints is content, even when Markdown would read it as syntax. It MUST be escaped so that it cannot open a span — \*\*, \_, \| — and it MUST NOT be deleted to avoid the collision.

Some marks a document prints are also Markdown's own punctuation: a menu that flags allergens with **, a form that labels a field _____, a legal citation using |. The mark is transcribed, and kept from being read as markup.

Melt-in-the-Middle Fish Pie Fishcake**      ← ** is a printed allergen marker
Beer-Battered Haddock & Chips§**               pointing at a legend elsewhere

Written unescaped, that ** opens a bold span that never closes and swallows the rest of the block.

What to escape

| Printed | Output | Would otherwise | | --- | --- | --- | | * ** | \* \*\* | Open emphasis or bold | | _ __ | \_ \__ | Open emphasis, or vanish inside a word | | # at line start | \# | Become a heading | | | inside a table cell | \| | Split the cell | | ` | \` | Open a code span | | ~~ | \~\~ | Strike the text through | | --- at line start | \-\-\- | Become a horizontal rule, or collide with the page separator | | A literal bracketed number or word — [1], [date] | \[1\], \[date\] | Read as a marker ([x], [blank]) or a form id | | A literal angle-bracket placeholder — <NAME> | &lt;NAME&gt; | Be read as an HTML tag and vanish |

  • Escaping SHOULD be applied only where the collision is real. A * in the middle of a word, or a # mid-sentence, needs nothing.
  • A printed character MUST NOT be replaced by a different mark to avoid the collision: rewriting ** as <sup>2</sup> or as a word is the never invent failure, and dropping it is the never drop one. The marker is the only thing tying an item to its legend; a legend entry with nothing pointing at it is unusable.
A raised marker is still a superscript

Escaping decides how the character survives; it does not decide its position. A marker printed above the baseline MUST be written <sup>\*\*</sup> — both rules apply, and neither substitutes for the other. See Superscript and Subscript§7.2.11.

Dashes, literal brackets and angle brackets
✅ Sample — lines that open with three dashes

Every sub-point on the slide begins with --- as its marker, printed bold. Left as printed, each line becomes a horizontal rule and its text vanishes into the rule above. The --- in the middle of New Strategy---Fund is not at line start and needs no escape.

✅ Sample — bracketed numbers that are not form ids

[1], [2], [3] number the sub-items of a note; the value None sits at the right. The same page carries (1), (2), (3) for the items above them, which need no escape. The bold heading *Notes opens with a printed asterisk.

✅ Sample — bracketed template placeholders

[#say on oath #affirm], [date], [name], [specify language] printed on grey highlights inside the sentences of a court template. Every one would read as a form id or a checkbox, and the grey is a highlight — see Highlighted Text§7.2.5. The italic notice [on separate page] under the page number is bracketed too.

✅ Sample — angle-bracket placeholders

<LEGAL DESCRIPTION OF PROPERTY>, <AFFIANT SIGNATURE>, <TYPE NAME OF AFFIANT> on grey highlights. Left as printed, each is an HTML tag and vanishes from a rendered page. The first line is the tail of a placeholder that began on the previous page, so only its closing > is printed. The ruled lines are empty fields — see Blanks Inside Sentences§10.4.1.

Related
  • Superscript and Subscript§7.2.11 — a raised marker is tagged as well as escaped
  • Text Formatting Conventions§7.1 — the full inline-markup table
  • Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 — where a printed marker belongs inside a table

7.2.5 Highlighted Text

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-highlighted-text · text formatting color

✅ Normative

Highlighted text MUST be wrapped in <mark> carrying the highlighter colour as an attribute: <mark style="background-color: yellow">the highlighted phrase</mark>.

Text printed on a highlighter background is content, not decoration. The highlight MUST NOT be dropped, and MUST NOT be reduced to bold or italic.

<mark style="background-color: yellow">the highlighted phrase</mark>
Requirements
  • The colour MUST be named with the nearest HTML colour name — yellow, green, cyan, magenta, lightgray — not a hex value or an invented label. That keeps the vocabulary finite and matches the treatment of colour in Text Colors§7.3.12 and Color as the Value§9.6.4.
  • The <mark> MUST cover exactly the run of text that carries the background. If the highlight stops mid-sentence, so does the <mark>.
  • Inside a table, only the cells whose background is actually coloured are marked; a whole row or column MUST NOT be marked because part of it is highlighted — the same over-application problem as Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2.
Why keep the colour

In a reviewed document, different highlight colours usually mean different things — one reviewer per colour, or one category per colour. A bare <mark> collapses that distinction and there is no way to recover it afterwards.

Related
  • Text Colors§7.3.12 — the same colour vocabulary for coloured text
  • Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2 — highlighting inside tables inherits the over-application problem
  • Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4 — highlighted template placeholders, marked and escaped

7.2.6 Inline Equations

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-inline-equations · text formatting math

✅ Normative

Every equation MUST be written as LaTeX inside $$ … $$, inline ones included. Single-$ delimiters MUST NOT be used.

the coefficient $$\alpha$$ is fixed

The same delimiters apply whether the equation sits in the middle of a sentence or on a line of its own; there is no separate inline form. Displayed equations and their numbers are covered in Displayed Equations§7.2.2.

Why double delimiters

A lone $ is ambiguous. Notebook and Markdown renderers treat an unrelated currency sign further down the page as the closing delimiter, open an unterminated maths span and swallow everything after it. Doubling the delimiter removes the ambiguity. It is non-standard for inline maths, and that cost is accepted.

Related
  • Displayed Equations§7.2.2 — equations on their own line, with their printed number
  • Text Formatting Conventions§7.1 — the full inline-markup table
  • Chemical Molecules§13.1 — LaTeX packages for chemistry

7.2.7 Line-End Hyphenation

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-line-end-hyphenation · text formatting fidelity

✅ Normative

A word broken across a line end MUST be joined, and a hyphen that exists only for the break MUST be removed. A hyphen that belongs to the word MUST be kept. Where the two cannot be told apart, the visible hyphen MUST be kept.

Justified prose breaks words at line ends with a hyphen. The break is typesetting; the word is one word. But a compound that happens to break at its own hyphen looks identical.

… judges on the Court of Appeals for the District of Co-
lumbia Circuit concluded …                              ← join: Columbia

… And sales of air-
conditioning, industrial and other equipment …          ← keep: air-conditioning
The line ends with Output
A fragment of a word that has no hyphen of its own — Co- / lumbia Joined, hyphen removed — Columbia
A compound broken at its own hyphen — air- / conditioning Joined, hyphen kept — air-conditioning
A break that could be either Joined, hyphen kept — the visible glyph is not removed on a guess

Keeping the hyphen when unsure is the never drop side of the choice: a printed glyph survives, and nothing the page does not show is asserted.

✅ Sample — a Supreme Court slip opinion


Source: Supreme Court of the United States, Opinion of the Court, 609 U.S. ___ (2026), p.3 (public domain)

Justified text breaking Gov-ernment, human-itarian, Co-lumbia, prose-cutorial, [c]on-trol, Shaugh-nessy, en-trusted and Ho-tel at line ends, plus a footnote with Im-migration. None of these are compounds. A hyphenated compound elsewhere on the page, separation-of-powers, sits mid-line and keeps its hyphens.

✅ Sample — compounds broken at their own hyphen

e- / government, air- / conditioning and private- / sector all break exactly at a hyphen the word carries anyway. Joining without the hyphen would produce egovernment.

Related
  • Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3 — homoglyph hyphens, which are a different question
  • Drop Caps§7.2.3 — the other place the text layer splits a word
  • Header Wrap vs Real Tier§9.3.2 — a wrap inside a table header

7.2.8 Links

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-links · text formatting

✅ Normative

Hyperlinks and email addresses MUST be transcribed as raw text. Link syntax — <email>, [url](url) — MAY be used only when link extraction was explicitly requested.

Default
Contact support@example.com or see https://example.com/pricing
When link extraction is requested
Contact <support@example.com> or see [https://example.com/pricing](https://example.com/pricing)
Why raw text

The output is read mostly by a model or an extraction step. Link punctuation adds noise to every chunk for a payload most readers never use. Raw text keeps the default output clean and still leaves the address recoverable.

Anchor text that differs from its target

When the printed words differ from the target — click here pointing at a long URL — the output MUST keep the printed words as they appear. Under the raw-text default the target is not represented, and it MUST NOT be added in place of, or beside, the printed words: the page does not print it (never invent).

Related
  • Text Formatting Conventions§7.1 — the full inline-markup table
  • QR Codes and Bar Codes§7.3.7 — a URL carried by a code rather than printed text
  • Output Options§3.5 — other outputs that depend on what the producer was asked for

7.2.9 Quote Blocks

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-quote-blocks · text formatting

✅ Normative

A quoted or inset region MUST be flattened: its content is rendered as ordinary text, headings and tables included. The output MUST NOT add > block-quote markers.

A boxed or inset region on the page renders as:

## here we go
Yeah

not:

>
> ## here we go
> Yeah
Why flatten

Block-quote markers interact badly with headings and tables that sit inside the quoted region. Most inset regions in real documents are not quotations at all — they are callouts, pull quotes or sidebars that happen to be visually offset. Flattening keeps the content addressable. The cost is losing the "this was inset" signal, and that cost is accepted.

A real quotation

In prose documents an inset block sometimes does mean someone else said this. It is flattened all the same: the words survive, and every printed character of them — quotation marks, attribution line — MUST be kept.

Related
  • Text Formatting Conventions§7.1 — the full inline-markup table
  • Reading Order§5.9 — where an inset region's content falls in the page's sequence
  • Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4 — printed characters that are also Markdown syntax

7.2.10 Small Capitals

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-small-capitals · text formatting inline

✅ Normative

Text set in small capitals MUST be transcribed as uppercase letters. The output MUST NOT add small-caps styling, and MUST NOT substitute the text layer's mixed case for the capitals the page shows.

Running heads, bylines and firm names are often set in small capitals: capital letterforms at lowercase height, usually with a full-size initial. The text layer may hold Jackson while the page shows JACKSON; Markdown has no small-caps mark.

JACKSON, J., dissenting          ← small caps on the page
WASSON & ASSOCIATES, CHARTERED   ← the same face, full name
Requirements
  • Every letter printed as a capital letterform — full-size or small — MUST be an uppercase letter in the output.
  • The rendered letterforms take precedence over the text layer's casing — see Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3.
  • Small caps are not emphasis: they MUST NOT be turned into bold, italic or an HTML style. Bold or italic set in small caps is still marked, from the glyph weight and slant — see Bold and Italics§7.2.1.
  • Letter-spacing is typography, not content: the letters of a spaced word MUST be written as one word.
✅ Sample — a running head


Source: Supreme Court of the United States, Jackson, J., dissenting, 600 U.S. ___ (2023), p.15 (public domain)

JACKSON, J., dissenting centred under the citation line, in small capitals; the citation line itself carries a printed ____, and the page number 15 sits at its right.

✅ Sample — a letter-spaced footer

HALVORNE & VOSS, CHARTERED in bold small caps with wide letter-spacing, over an address line. The masthead's Trial Law TIPS, in bold italic, is also letter-spaced, which the text layer renders as Tria l La w; the page shows the words Trial Law.

✅ Sample — run-in small-cap headings in a statute


Source: Public Law 114-255 (21st Century Cures Act), 130 Stat. 1278, §13001 (public domain)

(2) NO PARTICULAR OR UNIFORM ELECTRONIC VISIT VERIFICATION SYSTEM REQUIRED.—Nothing in the amendment …: the heading in small capitals, an em dash, then the paragraph on the same line. See Run-In Headings§6.8. Heading (4) and the body text break words at line ends (REQUIRE-MENTS, selec-tion, elec-tronic), which are joined — see Line-End Hyphenation§7.2.7.

Related

  • Bold and Italics§7.2.1 — styling comes from the glyphs
  • Run-In Headings§6.8 — the statute's small-cap headings run into their paragraphs

7.2.11 Superscript and Subscript

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-superscript-and-subscript · text formatting inline

✅ Normative

Raised and lowered text outside maths MUST be written with <sup> and <sub>. A Unicode superscript or subscript character MUST NOT be substituted for the tag.

H<sub>2</sub>O        ← conforming
H₂O                   ← non-conforming

The same applies to superscripts: x<sup>2</sup>, not x². Inside an equation, raised and lowered terms are LaTeX ^{…} and _{…} within $$ … $$ — see Inline Equations§7.2.6.

Why the tag

A tag round-trips: a reader can strip it, render it, or read the base character underneath. A Unicode glyph is lossy in the other direction — ₂ does not compare equal to 2, so a downstream numeric parse or string match silently fails. Unicode also has no raised or lowered form for most characters, so substitution cannot be applied consistently.

Inside table cells

A footnote superscript attached to a value — 48,210³ — MUST be tagged as 48,210<sup>3</sup>. Whether the marker stays in the cell is a separate question, answered by Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6.

A raised marker that is itself Markdown punctuation is tagged and escaped: <sup>\*\*</sup> — see Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4.

Related
  • Text Formatting Conventions§7.1 — the full inline-markup table
  • Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 — where a footnote marker inside a cell belongs
  • Chemical Molecules§13.1 — formulas with subscripts
  • Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4 — when the raised marker is itself Markdown punctuation, it is escaped as well as tagged

7.2.12 Underlined Text

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-underlined-text · text formatting inline

✅ Normative

Underlined text MUST be wrapped in <u>…</u>. The output MUST NOT use <ins>, and MUST NOT use _ text _.

subject to the <u>prior written consent</u> of the lessor

Markdown has no underline of its own, so the HTML element is used.

Why not the alternatives

<ins> means inserted text — an edit-history claim that a plain underline on a page does not make. _ text _ collides with Markdown emphasis and renders as italics.

Underline in a redline

An underline-only replacement in a redlined table — a new figure underlined in place of a struck one — is still written <u>1.335</u>, next to the struck value. See Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7 for how the pair is encoded.

Related
  • Text Formatting Conventions§7.1 — the full inline-markup table
  • Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7 — the redline pair of a struck value and its underlined replacement
  • Bold and Italics§7.2.1 — the other inline styles, which do use Markdown syntax

7.2.13 Verse and Hard Line Breaks

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-verse-and-hard-line-breaks · text formatting line-breaks

✅ Normative

Text whose line breaks carry meaning — verse, song text, deliberately broken lines — MUST be written one printed line per source line, separated by a plain newline, and MUST NOT be reflowed into running prose. No trailing spaces, no <br>, no fenced block: the same spelling as Line Breaks Inside a Block§6.2.

Poetry, song text, addresses and deliberately broken lines carry meaning in their line breaks. Markdown joins single newlines into one paragraph when it renders, so the breaks vanish on screen unless they are marked.

your honor
since i've been convicted of murder
and have taken time to digest
just what that means

A plain newline keeps every printed line in the Markdown source, which is what the output is judged on; a rendered view that joins the lines is a display artefact. Trailing spaces are invisible and fragile, <br> puts markup on every line, and a fenced block turns the verse into code and loses its bold and italics. Inline marks stay per line: a bold line is **line**.

Prose has the opposite rule: a line break inside a paragraph is typesetting, and the sentence is joined. The question is only how to mark the lines when the break is the content. A verse line that is too long for its column and wraps is still one line: the wrap is joined like prose.

✅ Sample — a poem beside a biography

The left column is verse, set in bold: short lines, no punctuation at most line ends, each break intentional. Three lines are too long for the column and wrap (… through every / weather!, … on your lowest / stones, … that never / wavers — I think); each is one verse line. The right column is ordinary prose that wraps, then a QR code with its URL printed across two lines beneath it.

7.3 Marks on the page

7.3.1 Clipped Text

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-clipped-text · text fidelity layout

✅ Normative

Text cut off at the page edge MUST be rendered as the characters actually visible. A clipped word MUST NOT be completed, and an ellipsis or marker that the page does not print MUST NOT be appended to it.

A page whose content runs past the printable edge: the last letters of a label, the end of a sentence, the right-hand column of a table are simply absent. Nothing is overprinted or redacted; the ink was never there.

Research and developmen        49,294     ← the final t is off the page
Selling, general, and administrative     41,515
Note: … These measures ar
not in compliance with … different from po
forma measures …
Requirements
  • The visible fragment MUST be kept, verbatim — see Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3. Dropping it loses printed content; completing it adds content that is not printed. See Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2.
  • The clipping itself MUST NOT be marked inside the text. A producer MAY record that a page is clipped outside the Markdown.
  • A clipped line inside a paragraph is joined to the next line like any other wrapped line; the fragment stays as printed.
✅ Sample — a statement cut at the right margin

Research and developmen in the stub, measures ar and from po in the note: the stub label and the note lines that reach the right edge lose their last characters.

Related
  • Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3 — the image, not the text layer, decides what a value is
  • Overlapping Text§7.3.6 — the other way a string becomes hard to read
  • Ignoring and Rejecting§5.6 — a badly cropped page can be rejected; this page is not
  • Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2 — the two failures a clipped word invites

7.3.2 E-Signature Tags

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-e-signature-tags · text marks forms

✅ Normative

A field that carries only an e-signature tag is unsigned and MUST be rendered as a blank, [blank]. A tag that prints a word — SIGN, INITIAL — MUST be rendered as that word, separately beside the field, and MUST NOT be rendered as a signature or as the field's value.

Electronic signing tools print a small coloured tab beside each field the signer must complete — "SIGN", "INITIAL", an arrow. The tab is not a signature and not part of the form; it is an instruction to a future signer, often left in the exported file.

QUALIFYING DISABLED VETERAN'S   │ QUALIFYING DISABLED VETERAN'S   │ DATE
SIGNATURE                       │ PRINTED NAME                    │
▸SIGN                           │                                 │
Requirements
  • The field MUST be rendered as unsigned: [blank], as for any blank field — see Fill-Ins§10.4.4.
  • A tag's printed word MUST be kept, verbatim, beside the field and outside the field's value. The samples below place it on its own line directly after the field.
  • A tag that prints no word adds nothing to the text.
  • A page on which the signature fields carry only tags is unsigned. [signature] MUST NOT appear for such a field — see Signatures§7.3.10.
✅ Sample — signature cells with signing tabs

Two signature blocks, each a three-cell row. A small red tab reading SIGN▸ sits under "SIGNATURE" in the first cell of each; every cell is otherwise empty.

✅ Sample — a tag beside a name line

A small red tab sits at the start of the Name**: line in the signature block, ahead of an otherwise blank ruled line. The tab prints no word, so nothing is added for it; every field in the block is blank.

Related
  • Signatures§7.3.10 — the real thing
  • Fill-Ins§10.4.4 — an unsigned field is a blank field
  • Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4 — a mark that carries a meaning

7.3.3 Handwritten Annotations

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-handwritten-annotations · text marks handwriting

✅ Normative

A handwritten note on a printed page MUST be rendered as [handwritten: legible words], in a block of its own next to the content it annotates. Its legible words MUST be kept; words that cannot be read MUST NOT be reconstructed.

A note written on a printed page: an exhibit reference in the margin, a circled item, an arrow with a word, a reviewer's initials. Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5 settles handwriting that replaces a printed value inside a table; a note in the margin of prose replaces nothing.

    … to confirm the absence of cyclonic flow.

                                      2                     Attach. B   ← red pen
                                                       SAQB 193        ← Bates stamp
Requirements
  • The note adds information to the printed page, so it MUST be kept, and MUST be kept apart from the body text: it MUST NOT be spliced into the sentence beside it.
  • The block MUST sit next to the content the note annotates in reading order.
  • Legible fragments MUST be kept verbatim. Characters that cannot be read are left out, never guessed.
✅ Sample — an exhibit reference in red pen

Attach. B handwritten in red at the bottom right of a scanned protocol page, beside a printed Bates number SAQB 193. The page's own number, 2, is centred above.

Related
  • Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5 — handwriting over a printed grid
  • Signatures§7.3.10 — initials and paraphs
  • Margin Banners§7.3.5 — printed text in the same place

7.3.4 Iconography and Symbols

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-iconography-and-symbols · text images marks

✅ Normative

An icon that carries meaning MUST NOT be dropped. It MUST be rendered as a bracketed semantic tag in the icon's position: one lower-case word naming what the icon means — [yes], [no], [locked] — with : degree where the icons are graded ([water: 3], [sun: partial]), and [icon: shape] naming the shape where the meaning is unclear ([icon: sun]). The vocabulary is open: the word is whatever names the meaning on this page.

Small symbols and images that stand in for a value rather than decorate — a tick in a feature-comparison column, a padlock, a sun or water icon used as the cell content itself.

Rendering

The icon is read the way the page intends it, and that reading is written in brackets:

| Feature | Basic     | Pro   |
| SSO     | [locked]  | [yes] |
  • Each icon MUST produce one tag, in the position the icon occupies.
  • Where an icon has no clear meaning in context, the tag MUST describe what is drawn — [icon: sun] — rather than guess a value.
  • Where the icons are graded, the tag MUST carry the degree, not just the presence: [sun: full] / [sun: partial], [water: 3] / [water: 1]. A tag that distinguishes the values beats a prettier glyph that does not.
Why a tag, and an open vocabulary

A tag reads back unambiguously and does not depend on a glyph existing, where the nearest Unicode character or emoji may not exist or may carry a different meaning. Its word is not drawn from a fixed list: no list would cover every icon, so the word is whatever names the meaning on this page, in lower case, used the same way throughout the document.

Why it matters

When the icon is the value, dropping it empties the table. A feature matrix or a scorecard whose marks are gone says nothing at all. This is the same failure as Color as the Value§9.6.4, where a coloured fill with no text becomes an empty cell and the table stops meaning anything.

❌ Counter-sample — graded icons flattened to one glyph

A plant-list table with two icon-valued columns — Sun and H₂O. The printed page on the left uses graded symbols: a filled, a half-filled or an empty sun, and one, two or three water droplets. The parse preview on the right renders both columns as a single ☀️ and a single 💧.

That is the failure this rule exists to prevent. The icons were not dropped — they were flattened. A plant needing three droplets and one needing a single droplet come out identical, so the column still looks populated while the information it carried is gone. The columns are the whole point of the table: Sun and H₂O are the two facts a reader consults it for. The expected Markdown reads the empty sun as [sun: none]; the red outlines around the two columns are highlighting added to the figure, not part of the page.

Icons standing in for labels

An icon that clearly supplies a field's label — a pin before an address, a handset before a phone number — MUST be rendered as a bracketed semantic label beside its value: [address], [phone], [web]. The nearest word (Address:) MUST NOT be substituted: it is not printed. An icon whose function is unclear is described by its shape instead of guessed.

✅ Sample — icons standing in for labels

The footer prints a pin, a handset and a globe before the address, the phone number and the website — no words. The pictorial labels become [address], [phone] and [web] beside their values.

  • Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 — printed marks inside a table cell
  • Color as the Value§9.6.4 — the same failure when a fill is the value
  • E-Signature Tags§7.3.2 — a small printed mark that is an instruction, not a value

7.3.5 Margin Banners

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-margin-banners · text marks layout

✅ Normative

Rotated text printed along a side margin MUST be rendered once, as a furniture block of its own outside the body flow, with its words kept — branding included. It MUST NOT be tagged as a watermark unless it actually overlays the content.

Text printed rotated along the page margin, outside the content area: an archive stamp, a brand line, a firm mark. Unlike a watermark§7.3.13 it does not overlap the content, and unlike a page header it is not in the top or bottom margin.

 U │                                         │
 S │  Overview of Risk Ranking Symbols       │
   │                                         │
 E │  One way to rank environmental impacts  │
 P │  …                                      │
 A │                                         │
Requirements
  • The words MUST be kept. Some banners are document metadata — "US EPA ARCHIVE DOCUMENT" tells the reader the document is superseded, the same kind of fact "DRAFT" carries. Branding is printed text too, and MUST NOT be dropped as decoration.
  • The banner MUST be one block of its own, rendered once on the page, and MUST NOT be spliced into a body sentence, table or list.
  • The [watermark: …] marker MUST NOT be used for text that does not cross the content.
  • The rotation MUST NOT be described. The words are the content.
  • The samples place the banner at the start of its page's content.
✅ Sample — an archive stamp down the left margin


Source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Specialty-Batch Chemical Manufacturing Industry — EMS Implementation Guide (Appendix D) (public domain)

"US EPA ARCHIVE DOCUMENT" printed vertically in a red band, full page height, beside an ordinary text-and-table page. The banner carries a fact about the document that appears nowhere else on it.

✅ Sample — a brand line on a slide

"PRECISION & MOTION" runs down a decorative band on the left of the slide. This is branding, but it is still printed text.

✅ Sample — a firm mark on pleading paper

A small rotated wordmark, ARCLIGHT LEGAL COPY SERVICES, in the left margin of a court filing, beside the line numbers.

✅ Sample — a download stamp on a journal article

Downloaded via VARENBROOK UNIV on February 22, 2021 … See https://pubs.velmora.example/sharingguidelines rotated up the left margin of a first page, in two lines. Metadata about this copy, printed nowhere else.

  • Pleading Line Numbers§5.8 — the other margin furniture on the third sample
  • Block Classes§5.3 — page-header and page-footer cover the top and bottom margins only
