7.3.6 Overlapping Text

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-overlapping-text · text marks legal

✅ Normative

Where two printed strings overlap, each legible string MUST be rendered whole, in a block of its own, with the stamp first. Legible fragments MUST be kept; characters hidden by the overlap MUST NOT be reconstructed.

Two printed strings occupy the same space. The common case is a court e-filing stamp — Case 1:19-cv-00892 Document 36 Filed 04/04/19 Page 2 of 2 — laid across a header the page already had, so the two texts interleave character by character.

4/4/2019   PresCase 1:19-cv-00892-KSC Document 36 Filed 04/04/19 Page 2 of 2ates | The White House
           ↑ browser print header             ↑ filing stamp, printed over it

The stamp is the more important string — it identifies the exhibit — but the underlying header is still printed content.

Requirements
  • Every legible string MUST be kept: the stamp and the text beneath it are both printed. Keeping only the more legible one drops content.
  • The strings MUST NOT be interleaved into one line. Each is rendered whole, in its own block.
  • At the overlap, the stamp MUST come first, as its [stamp: …] marker (see Stamps§7.3.11), followed by the string it is printed over.
  • Characters that the overlap hides MUST be left out rather than guessed; the legible part of the string is kept — see Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2.
✅ Sample — a filing stamp over a print header


Source: Executive Office of the President, Presidential Proclamation Declaring a National Emergency Concerning the Southern Border, Feb. 15, 2019; filed as court exhibit (public domain)

A web page printed to PDF, then filed: the blue filing stamp sits directly on the grey browser header line, and the two are unreadable as one string. Read apart, both are legible. The footer URL and 2/2 are untouched.

✅ Sample — two filing stamps over a print header

An exhibit divider page — EXHIBIT D alone — whose header carries the clerk's boxed FILED stamp over the header's own FILED:, and Index # over INDEX NO., both overprinted. Everything but the page count at the foot is set in bold.

✅ Sample — three headers on one line

A browser print header, an e-filing stamp and the article's own Page 22 of 37 all printed at the top of a nearly empty page, on top of each other. The browser timestamp is legible up to 09; the characters after it lie under the stamp's opening Ca and are left out.

  • Watermarks§7.3.13 — text that crosses the body rather than a header
  • Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5 — a stamp over a grid

7.3.7 QR Codes and Bar Codes

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-qr-codes-and-bar-codes · text images marks

✅ Normative

A QR code or bar code MUST be rendered as an image reference whose alt text holds the decoded content and whose target holds the literal label: ![decoded content](QR Code), ![decoded content](Bar code). The code MUST also be an element of its own, carrying the decoded value and a box around the code.

The rendering
![content of qr code](QR Code)
![content of Bar code](Bar code)

So a code that decodes to a tracking URL becomes ![https://example.com/t/9F2K](QR Code).

The alt-text and target slots are used in the reverse of the usual Markdown convention: the content goes in the alt slot, the literal label in the target slot. That is deliberate.

Why this form

It is the only encoding where the Markdown alone is useful. A reader gets the decoded payload — usually a URL or a tracking number — without following an element reference. The code's own element still carries the scan value, and its box locates the code for anyone who needs the image.

When the code does not decode

A payload MUST NOT be invented. A code that does not decode MUST be rendered with the label alone and an empty alt text, and is still its own element with its box:

![](QR Code)
Example
✅ Sample — a QR code closing a product page

A QR code printed at the foot of a product page, beside the line "Pour découvrir d'autres exemples, c'est ici :" — the prose leads directly into it, so dropping the code leaves a sentence pointing at nothing. The code on this page does not decode, so the alt text stays empty; had it decoded, its payload would fill the alt slot. The code is its own element, with a box around the code alone.

Related
  • Images§12.1.1 — what other printed images become
  • Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4 — small marks that carry a value
  • Redacted Text§7.3.8 — another bracketed stand-in for a non-text region

7.3.8 Redacted Text

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-redacted-text · text marks

✅ Normative

Each contiguous redacted span MUST be rendered as one [REDACTED] marker, in the position the suppressed text occupied. Visible text and any printed exemption code MUST be kept; the hidden characters and their count MUST NOT be inferred.

Text blacked out or boxed over in the source document.

The rendering

The marker sits where the suppressed text was, so the surrounding line still reads correctly:

Account holder: [REDACTED]

Where only part of a value is covered, the marker MUST replace only the covered part, and the visible characters MUST be kept verbatim — not normalised, padded or reconstructed. Printed masking characters are visible characters, escaped where they are Markdown syntax (see Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4):

Account number: \*\*\*\*-\*\*\*\*-\*\*\*\*-4471

When boxes are requested, a redacted span has a box like any other printed region — see Boxes and Granularity§3.3.

Why a positive marker beats silence

A redaction is an assertion: something was here and was deliberately removed. If the output emits nothing, a reader cannot tell "the field was blank" from "the field was suppressed" — a meaningful difference in a legal or regulatory document.

[REDACTED] is the same bracketed-placeholder shape used for Signatures§7.3.10 ([signature]) and for QR Codes and Bar Codes§7.3.7 (![](QR Code)).

✅ Sample — a redaction bar inside a sentence

One black bar where the appellant's name was, between filed by and , against the response of the. The bold case number and council name on either side are printed and kept.

✅ Sample — a redaction bar inside a transcript line

Line 4: Was ████ paying that before? — one black bar in the middle of a question, the rest of the page untouched. The transcript lines follow Transcript Pages§6.11.

Exemption codes

A redacted region that prints an exemption code MUST be rendered as [REDACTED: code] — [REDACTED: (b)(5)] — with the code copied exactly, once. Unrelated text near the region MUST stay outside the marker.

✅ Sample — a redaction that prints its exemption code


Source: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), FOIA production document (public domain)

Under Cybercrime, a dashed box the height of eight bullets prints only (b)(5); the eight bullet glyphs remain in the margin, their text gone. The code and the surviving bullets are both content the page prints: the eight bullets stay as eight list items, and the code appears once, inside the marker, at the start of the redacted span.

Related
  • Signatures§7.3.10 — the same bracketed-placeholder shape
  • Transcript Pages§6.11 — the page shape of the second sample
  • Watermarks§7.3.13 — another mark laid over printed content

7.3.9 Seals and Round Stamps

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-seals-and-round-stamps · text marks

✅ Normative

A seal or round stamp MUST be rendered as [seal: printed text], holding all of its legible rim and centre text in reading order, in a block separate from body prose. The bare [seal] MUST be used only when none of its text is legible.

A round or oval impression — an auditor's firm seal, a notary seal, a court seal — printed or inked on the page, usually beside a signature. Its text runs around the rim.

   ╭────────────╮        For, Caldrivane & Rao LLP
  ( CALDRIVANE &    )       Chartered Accountants
  (  RAO LLP     )       [signature]
   ╰────────────╯        A. N. Bhatt
Requirements
  • The seal MUST NOT be dropped. It is the page's proof of authority, the same kind of fact as a signature, and its text is often the only place the firm's name is printed.
  • Its text MUST be kept verbatim and in a readable order — in the samples, upper rim, then centre, then lower rim — including a word the rim cuts short. Illegible characters are left out, never guessed.
  • The seal MUST be its own block, never part of a sentence beside it.
  • A stamp that lands on a table is kept out of the grid — see Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5.
  • A signature written across the seal is a separate mark — see Signatures§7.3.10.
✅ Sample — an auditor's seal beside a signature

A blue circular seal: CALDRIVANE & RAO LLP along the upper rim, H&R over LLP in the centre, and CHARTERED ACCOUNTAN along the lower rim — the rim runs out before the word ends. Beside it, a handwritten signature over a printed name, designation and registration numbers. Also the sample for a signature whose name is printed beneath it — see Signatures§7.3.10.

✅ Sample — a firm stamp with a signature inside it

A purple round stamp at the foot of a scanned letter: KESSLER & VANE on the upper rim, CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS in the centre, FRN-408217E • ASTILBE on the lower rim, and a handwritten mark through its centre. The letterhead prints a logo on the left and two address blocks on the right.

Related
  • Signatures§7.3.10 — the mark it usually accompanies
  • Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5 — a stamp that lands on a table
  • Watermarks§7.3.13 — the other page-level mark with its own placement

7.3.10 Signatures

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-signatures · text marks

✅ Normative

A handwritten signature MUST be rendered as a bracketed placeholder: [signature:{name}] when its glyphs are genuinely legible, the bare [signature] otherwise. A name MUST NOT be guessed.

A handwritten signature over a signature line.

The rendering

A signature whose name can be read from its glyphs:

[signature:Mariana Augusta de Figueiredo Lacerda e Souza]

A signature whose name cannot:

[signature]

A half-readable signature MUST get the bare [signature] form.

Why

A signature is semantically meaningful — the document is signed — but it is not text. The placeholder records the fact without asserting a transcription that could be wrong, and the name-carrying form preserves the value when the glyphs really are readable.

This is the same shape as [REDACTED] in Redacted Text§7.3.8: a bracketed tag standing in for a non-text region.

Edge cases
  • Two signatures on one line MUST get two placeholders, one each, in reading order — even when both are illegible.
  • A signature that is also a stamp, or that overlaps a printed grid, follows Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5.
On a form

A signature field follows the same shapes, with one addition: an unsigned field is a blank fill-in, [blank], not a missing signature.

- **Your signature**: [signature:John Doe]
- **Spouse's signature. If a joint return, both must sign.**: [blank]
- **Date**: [blank]
- **Your occupation**: Accountant

A signature line's date and occupation companions are ordinary fill-ins — see Fill-Ins§10.4.4.

A signature with its name printed beside it

The name in [signature:{name}] is read off the signature's own glyphs. Many documents print the signer's name directly under the signature line.

A name printed under or beside an illegible signature MUST NOT fill [signature:{name}]: the signature is the bare [signature], and the printed name is rendered as the text it is. The tag records only what the strokes show — the printed name is not always the signer, as when someone signs on another's behalf — and the name is kept as text beside it, so nothing is lost.

✅ Sample — an auditor's signature over a printed name

A handwritten signature whose glyphs cannot be read, with A. N. Bhatt, Partner, a membership number and a UDIN printed beneath it, and the firm's round seal to the left — see Seals and Round Stamps§7.3.9.

Initials on every page

Handwritten approval initials MUST be rendered as [signature] on every page that carries them, with the initials inside the placeholder only when their glyphs support it. The placeholder MUST be kept outside body sentences.

✅ Sample — a scanned decision with a paraph

A handwritten mark at the bottom right of a scanned court decision page, below the footnotes, with no printed line or caption. No letters can be read in it.

Typed names on signature lines

A name typed in a plain face on a signature line, or a conformed /s/ signature, is not a signature: it is printed text. It MUST be rendered as that text, verbatim — /s/ included — and MUST NOT be given a [signature] placeholder, which would assert handwriting the page does not show.

✅ Sample — typed names on signature lines

Marcus Feldkirk, Renata Solis, Owen Tarrant typed in a plain face on the three signature lines of an approval box, with typed dates. No handwriting anywhere.

✅ Sample — a conformed /s/ signature

By: /s/ Dana R. Whitfield in underlined italics on the signature line, the typed name beneath. The /s/ convention stands for a signature that was never inked.

  • E-Signature Tags§7.3.2 — a signing tab is not a signature
  • Seals and Round Stamps§7.3.9 — the mark that often sits beside a signature

7.3.11 Stamps

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-stamps · text marks legal

✅ Normative

Ink applied over or beside the printed page — overprinted, boxed or rotated, or in a different ink — MUST be rendered as [stamp: its words], exactly as printed, at its place in reading order. A stamp with no legible words MUST be rendered as [stamp]. The page's own printed text is never a stamp, however official it looks.

A stamp records an act on this page: FILED, RECEIVED, PAID, APPROVED, a court e-filing line laid across the header, a clerk's dated box. It was added after the page was printed, and it is recognised by that: it overprints the page's text, sits in a box or at an angle the page's layout does not use, or is in a different ink.

Requirements
  • A stamp is written with the protocol's bracket marker, [stamp: …], carrying its words exactly as printed; a stamp on several lines is one marker, its lines joined with a space.
  • It keeps its place in reading order. Where it overprints other text, the marker comes first, then the text beneath it — see Overlapping Text§7.3.6. Over a table it stays outside the table — see Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5.
  • A stamp whose words cannot be read is the bare [stamp].
  • A round seal is [seal: …] — see Seals and Round Stamps§7.3.9. A watermark, background text that describes the whole document, is [watermark: …] — see Watermarks§7.3.13. The three share one bracket shape because each is ink laid on the page; they keep separate names because a watermark describes the document while a stamp or seal records an act on this page.
  • Header text that the page prints itself — a filing header, an official form number — is ordinary text, not a stamp.
✅ Sample — a clerk's stamps over a filing header

The boxed FILED is stamped over the header's own FILED:, and Index #: E2026004417 over the header's INDEX NO. E2026004417. The two stamps become markers, each first at its overlap; the header's own lines stay text.

  • Watermarks§7.3.13 — background text that describes the whole document
  • Overlapping Text§7.3.6 — a stamp printed over other text
  • Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5 — a stamp over a table

7.3.12 Text Colors

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-text-colors · text formatting color

✅ Normative

Text colour MUST be carried only when it is the only thing distinguishing some text from the rest, written as <font color="NAME">…</font> around exactly the coloured words, with the nearest HTML colour name. Colour that is decoration MUST NOT be rendered.

Coloured text in the source document.

Decoration or meaning

Most coloured text is styling: a blue heading, a brand-coloured lead paragraph, a page printed in one colour. The words are kept and the colour is not rendered.

Colour becomes content when it is the only thing distinguishing some text from the rest — an insertion printed in red with no underline, a figure in red meaning negative, a status word whose colour is the status. There the colour MUST be carried:

… will testify. <font color="red">Before or promptly after the notice or subpoena is served …</font> A subpoena …
  • The element wraps exactly the coloured words, so the output says which text carries the colour.
  • The colour MUST be the nearest HTML colour name — not a hex value and not an invented label.
  • Text whose colour is doubled by another mark — red and underlined, red and bold — is already distinguished; the colour is decoration there and is not carried.
The extreme case

A cell that is a coloured fill with no text at all — a risk-matrix square, a heat-map grid — becomes an empty cell if the colour is dropped, and the whole table stops meaning anything. See Color as the Value§9.6.4 for that situation specifically.

Staying consistent

Highlighting already has a settled encoding built on the same vocabulary:

<mark style="background-color: HTML_COLOR_NAME">…</mark>

Text colour uses the nearest HTML colour name too, so there is one colour vocabulary for both: <mark style="background-color: NAME"> for a highlight, <font color="NAME"> for coloured text.

✅ Sample — a whole page in one colour

Every word on the page, headings included, is set in dark red. Nothing is distinguished from anything else by the colour, so it is decoration and the output carries none of it.

Related
  • Highlighted Text§7.2.5 — the settled encoding that shares the colour vocabulary
  • Color as the Value§9.6.4 — a fill with no text that is the value

7.3.13 Watermarks

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

text-watermarks · text marks layout

✅ Normative

A watermark MUST NOT be deleted and MUST NOT be left inside the body text. It MUST be rendered once per page that prints it, as its own element at the top of that page's content: [watermark: DRAFT].

Diagonal or background text stamped across the page — "DRAFT", "Redline Version", "CONFIDENTIAL", "VOID".

Requirements
  • The watermark is its own element, not a phrase inside the text it happens to cross.
  • It is written as the protocol's bracket marker, [watermark: …], carrying its words exactly as printed, and placed first in the page's content — not in the middle of the paragraph or table row it physically overlaps.
  • A watermark printed on several lines is one marker, its lines joined with a space.
  • It is recorded on every page that prints it, and not carried onto a page that does not.
[watermark: Redline Version]
Why not simply drop it

A watermark says something about the whole document, and it is often the single most important fact on the page. "Redline Version" says that every figure in Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7 is in play; "VOID" invalidates everything underneath it. Removing it silently loses real information.

Why not leave it inline

The watermark overlaps body text physically. Rendered in place, it injects a stray phrase into the middle of a sentence or splits a table row — corrupting content that was otherwise clean.

Keeping it as a separate element gets both: the fact is recorded and the text stream stays intact. The bracket marker is the same shape as the protocol's other marks laid on a page — [seal: …], [logo: …], [signature] — see Markdown Rendering§3.2.

✅ Sample — a diagonal stamp across a pay stub

THIS IS NOT A CHECK printed diagonally across the cheque-shaped lower half of an earnings statement, with NON–NEGOTIABLE beneath it. Both cross printed text; neither enters the lines they cross.

✅ Sample — a watermark across a form grid

Sample in large grey letters diagonally across a mostly empty project grid, crossing cells that hold checkbox lists. Same placement: once, out of the grid, at the top of the page.

Related
  • Margin Banners§7.3.5 — rotated text in the margin that does not cross the body
  • Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5 — the stamp equivalent, over a grid
  • Overlapping Text§7.3.6 — a stamp laid over a header rather than across the body

§8 Lists

8.1 Bullets and Sub-Bullets

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

lists-bullets-and-sub-bullets · lists

✅ Normative

A top-level bulleted item MUST be rendered with the * marker and a sub-item with the - marker. The two markers carry the nesting and MUST NOT be interchanged.

A printed list: items led by a bullet glyph or a number, sometimes with indented sub-items beneath them.

• Top-level item
   – Sub-item beneath it
   – Another sub-item
• Next top-level item

* Top-level item
  - Sub-item beneath it
  - Another sub-item
* Next top-level item

Ordered lists

  • A printed numbering MUST be kept verbatim, including its style: 1. 2. 3., a. b. c., (i) (ii) and 1) 2) differ on the page and MUST differ in the output. The numbering is often cited elsewhere in the document.

Deeper nesting

  • Where the page shows more than two levels, each further level MUST be carried by indentation.
  • The relative structure MUST be preserved: a three-level list MUST NOT be flattened into two.

Lists inside table cells

A cell holding a vertical list is governed by Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells§9.5.3: <ul><li> and <br>• both conform inside a cell, and parallel lists across several columns of one row MUST NOT be collapsed — they become one row per printed line.

Bridge text between lists

An unbulleted line printed between two runs of bullets, such as partially offset by, MUST be rendered as a paragraph between the two lists. It MAY be rendered as indented continuation text only when it belongs to one specific list item.

✅ Sample — a line between bullets that is not a bullet

Four bulleted increases, then partially offset by on its own unbulleted line, then one more bullet. The interjection is a paragraph between two lists.

Bullet glyphs that carry meaning

  • A printed bullet glyph that carries meaning — a tick for acceptable, a cross for unacceptable — MUST be kept as the first content token after the Markdown marker: * ✓ Bank statement.
  • A decorative bullet shape (•, ◦, ▪, ➢) MUST be normalised to the Markdown marker and MUST NOT be transcribed.
✅ Sample — bullet glyphs that carry meaning

Acceptable Financial Documents bulleted with ✓, Unacceptable Financial Documents bulleted with ⊗, side by side. Each meaningful glyph is kept after the Markdown bullet; see Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4. The two captions are standalone subheads over their lists.

Related

  • Checkboxes§10.4.2 — a box before an item is a form control, not a bullet
  • Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells§9.5.3 — lists printed inside table cells
  • Row-Label Hierarchy§9.5.5 — indentation that nests table rows rather than list items
  • Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4 — glyphs that stand for a value

§9 Tables

9.1 What counts as a table

9.1.1 Borderless Whitespace Tables

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-borderless-whitespace-tables · tables detection ocr borderless whitespace

✅ Normative

A whitespace-aligned block with columns MUST be rendered as a table. Its column tracks MUST be read off the widest row, every value MUST be placed in the track it sits in, and the block MUST NOT be rendered as preformatted text.

Typewriter and fixed-width reports where the columns exist only as alignment — no column rules, no fills, no shading. Nothing on the page shows where one column ends and the next begins except the whitespace.

DURATION    LAPSE     EXPENSE
   1        12.0%       48.00
   2         8.5%       22.50     ← columns are pure whitespace
✅ Sample — wat

A long zip-code territory table with no rules or fills anywhere — columns exist purely as alignment. The two-line headers are wrapped labels and join into one header cell each.

Reading the tracks
  1. The column tracks are taken from the widest, most populated row.
  2. Every remaining row is checked: each value MUST start inside one track.
  3. Where they all do, the block is a table with those columns.
  4. Where a value drifts toward a neighbouring track, or straddles two, it MUST be placed in the track its left edge is closest to. The block is still a table.

A printed header line (a row of labels, often underlined) is strong evidence that columns are intended, and a reason to look harder for consistent tracks. It is not on its own a licence to create columns that the body rows do not support (never invent).

✅ Sample — aa

A Medicare-supplement premium table with thin rules between the rows but none between the columns: the columns are held together by underlined headers and whitespace alone.

✅ Sample — xl

Two tax-rate calculation blocks with no rules, embedded in a memo. Each two-line column header is one wrapped label over one column, so it is one header cell, and the page underlines every header line and the last figure before each sum.

✅ Sample — ppy

Three loss-triangle blocks aligned purely by column position, with underlined headers.

✅ Sample — 2cc

A fictional automaker's subsidiaries list with a single header underline and nothing else. The second header is one label wrapped over two lines.

Why the alignment test, and not a guess

Columns guessed wrong produce silently misaligned data — a lapse rate filed under expense. The alignment test is how the columns are read, not a reason to give up on them: the widest row fixes the tracks, and every other value is placed by where it starts. A preformatted block would keep the characters but lose every number to anything that consumes structure, which is the worse loss — so it is never the conforming output.

A purely visual "it must have printed rules" reading of Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 would exclude this entire class by construction. It does not: these are tables when the alignment holds.

✅ Sample — a four-line key-value panel on a slide

Under the chart, the Working Capital panel prints four labels and four amounts on two whitespace tracks and nothing else. Every row is the same kind of record — a component and its amount — so it is a table even with no header row and no grid (see Is This Even a Table§9.1.5). The neighbouring panels are bullet lists. The panel title sits above the table as text.

✅ Sample — an exhibit with no rules and empty cells

Four headers over fourteen rows, every value right-aligned in its track, several cells empty, and a Total: row after a two-line gap. The alignment holds all the way down. The gap is rendered here by leaving it out, one of the two conforming forms of Blank and Spacer Rows§9.5.1.

✅ Sample — a headerless results list with band rows

Rank, name, company and points on four whitespace tracks with no header row anywhere; event names — Fairmont & Voss Tennis Singles Men 30-39 — printed flush left between the groups as bands. The alignment holds for the whole page. Each band is one full-width row, as Bands Inside the Grid§9.2.1 requires.

Related
  • Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 — the relation test this class passes without printed rules
  • Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3 — values placed in their track are still transcribed verbatim
  • Gutter Columns§9.4.1 — whitespace gaps that are not columns
  • Blank and Spacer Rows§9.5.1 — what to do with the vertical gaps between groups

9.1.2 Chart With a Printed Data Grid

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-chart-with-a-printed-data-grid · tables charts orientation

✅ Normative

When a chart prints its data grid beside or beneath the canvas, the output MUST render that grid exactly as printed — same orientation, same headers, same row order — and MUST NOT render any other table for the chart.

Some charts print their numbers as a small grid next to the canvas: a bar chart with bucket-columns × metric-rows underneath, for example. That printed grid is often transposed relative to the [Category, Value] shape a chart is usually reasoned about in.

Printed under the bar chart:            Transposed reconstruction — non-conforming:
| Metric   | $0–1k | $1k–5k | $5k+ |    | Bucket | Avg Premium |
| Avg Prem | 412   | 388    | 351  |    | $0–1k  | 412         |
                                        | $1k–5k | 388         |
Requirements
  • The table representing the chart MUST open with <table data-source="chart">, including when its values come from the printed grid.
  • The grid MUST be transcribed in its printed orientation. Metrics that run across the top stay across the top.
  • The grid MUST NOT be transposed, and its rows and columns MUST NOT be reordered into a more natural shape.
  • The output MUST NOT add a second, reconstructed version alongside it. One grid is printed; one grid is rendered.
  • Values MUST NOT be re-keyed off the chart canvas — bars, points and axis ticks are not the source. Only what is printed as text in the grid counts.

A transposed version is non-conforming even when it reads better, in the same way that rewriting a cell's text is non-conforming.

Why as printed

This is the verbatim posture the whole protocol takes: transcribe what is on the page, do not improve it (see Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3, Accounting Number Formats§9.6.1). A second reconstructed copy also creates the duplication described in Duplicated Tables§9.2.4 and Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3 — two tables where the page printed one (never invent).

✅ Sample — two charts with their grids beneath

Each chart prints a four-row grid under its bars — one row per series, one column per quarter, with the year as a spanning row between the quarters and the values. The grid is the rendering; the bars are not re-keyed.

Related
  • Rotated and Diagonal Content§9.8.1 — orientation is preserved there too
  • Duplicated Tables§9.2.4 — a reconstructed copy is a duplicate the page did not print
  • Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1 — the chart table used when a chart prints no grid

9.1.3 Empty Pre-Printed Grids

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-empty-pre-printed-grids · tables forms degenerate

✅ Normative

A printed grid with no values entered MUST be rendered as a table, with its headers and every printed empty row as a row of empty cells. It MUST NOT be skipped, and MUST NOT be reduced to its headers alone.

A blank form table — full ruled structure, headers printed, no values entered anywhere.

| Name | Date | Amount | Signature |
|      |      |        |           |
|      |      |        |           |
Requirements
  • The grid MUST be rendered as a table. The headers are the content: they are what the form asks for.
  • Every printed empty row MUST be rendered, as empty cells. An empty cell is a cell.
  • The headers MUST NOT be emitted on their own. A headers-only output is the degenerate shape ruled out in Header-Only Tables§9.1.4; here the printed empty rows are the body, so keeping them avoids that shape.
  • The table MUST NOT be skipped because it has no data. A page with a printed form on it is not blank.
  • A long run of identical empty rows — dozens of them — MUST be rendered in full, never trimmed to a representative few.
✅ Sample — xx

An NAIC rate-filing exhibit where every row after the first is a blank template row awaiting entry — the structure is the content. Each blank row still prints XX and the computed 0.00% / 0.00 subtotals, and all nine are kept. Each column header is one label wrapped over many lines, so its lines are joined into one cell, including the words broken mid-word by the narrow columns.

Why

A reader of a blank form is asking "what fields does this form ask for?", and the structure answers that question completely. Returning nothing gives nothing for a page that is manifestly not blank.

The row count is the awkward part: reproducing forty empty rows is faithful and repetitive, reproducing one is compact and unfaithful. Faithful wins — trimming cannot be undone downstream, while ignoring extra empty rows can be (never drop).

✅ Sample — a court scheduling order

SCHEDULING AND CUTOFF DATES: three columns, nine rows, every row's description printed and its two date cells empty. The banner above the header row is a title band inside the frame.

Related
  • Header-Only Tables§9.1.4 — the degenerate shape an empty grid must not collapse into
  • Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1 — the form content around such a grid
  • Blank and Spacer Rows§9.5.1 — blank rows inside a filled table, a different case
  • Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 — why a ruled grid with headers is a table even when empty

9.1.4 Header-Only Tables

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-header-only-tables · tables degenerate failure-mode

✅ Normative

The output MUST NOT contain a table that is a header with no body. A header row MUST either be rendered together with its body or, where no body can be joined to it, rendered as ordinary text — never as an orphan header row standing as a table.

The failure: a header row becomes a table of its own while the rows it describes end up in a neighbouring region as plain text. The result claims there is a table with no data in it, and separately claims there is a run of loose numbers with no meaning.

Emitted:   | Duration | Factor |     ← header-only table…

           1   0.94                  ← …its body rendered as plain text
           2   0.91                    from the neighbouring region
Joining a header to its body

A header row with no rows under it belongs to the body immediately below or beside it. The header and body MUST be rendered as one table only when all three hold:

  • the body is immediately adjacent — the next thing on the page, not across a gap of other content;
  • the column bounds match — the body's columns line up under the header's;
  • nothing sits in between — no paragraph, no other table, no unrelated band.

If any condition fails, the merge MUST NOT be made (never invent): the stray header line MUST be rendered as text rather than as a one-row table.

How large a gap is too large is not fixed. A gap large enough to put the adjacency in doubt counts as a failed condition, and the header is not merged.

The related shape

A single row of labels on its own is not a table. Neither is a small table folded into the middle of another table's body — see Side-by-Side Mini Tables§9.2.8 for that one.

The one exception

A blank pre-printed form is headers plus empty rows, and there the structure genuinely is the content: it MUST be rendered, rows included — see Empty Pre-Printed Grids§9.1.3. That case has a body of printed empty rows. It is not a header standing alone.

Related
  • Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9 — when a header legitimately covers fragments with a gap
  • Empty Pre-Printed Grids§9.1.3 — the one case where headers plus empty rows are the whole content
  • Side-by-Side Mini Tables§9.2.8 — a small table inside another's body
  • Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 — a lone label row fails the relation test

9.1.5 Is This Even a Table

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-is-this-even-a-table · tables detection boundaries

✅ Normative

A region MUST be rendered as a table when, and only when, its rows and columns encode a relation — when the position of a value in the grid is what gives the value its meaning. A region that encodes no relation MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

This is the first decision about a region, and every other table rule depends on it. A single page often shows the whole spectrum at once: real grids, gridded legends, ungridded label: value spec stacks, address blocks, and two-column prose that looks like a grid but is not.

Same page, three regions:

┌─────────────┬───────────────┐      Motor: 1/2 HP, 115V      ← ungridded spec
│ (1) Premium │ Base rate …   │      Speed: 3-speed              stack: table? text?
│ (2) Losses  │ Incurred …    │
└─────────────┴───────────────┘      Acme Corp
  ↑ gridded legend: table?           123 Main St    ← address block: never a table
The test

The question is: would this be a <table> in well-written HTML, or a <div> positioned with CSS?

A border alone does not make a region a table, and alignment alone is not always enough either. The relation decides.

Strong evidence it is a table Strong evidence it is not
explicit row and column headers running prose, however neatly it is set in columns
repeated records under a shared schema address blocks
a printed grid, or consistent column tracks running down the block text sitting beside a logo
a legend printed as label/definition records inside a grid decorative alignment with no record schema behind it
❌ Counter-sample — 4x

The page starts straight into data rows with no header row. Column meaning has to be inferred from the values, which is the edge of the relation test: repeated records under one schema still make it a table, and the output MUST NOT invent the missing header row.

Legends and static key-value references are tables

The "Column | Description" box under a rate grid, explaining what (1)–(11) mean, MUST be rendered as a table.

| Column | Description     |
| (1)    | Earned premium  |
| (2)    | Incurred claims |

It looks decorative, but it maps one thing to another, and a mapping is a relation. Omitting it drops real content off the page.

Prose and address blocks are never tables

Two-column running prose only looks like a grid — its columns carry no meaning, they are a typesetting choice. The same holds for an address block, or a caption stacked beside an image. These MUST NOT be rendered as tables.

❌ Counter-sample — 10k

A 10-K cover: Yes ✓ No check-mark lines and an address block, both column-shaped, neither tabular. The genuine table is the small Title of each class / Trading Symbols / Exchange grid.

❌ Counter-sample — xl

Two real calculation tables surrounded by narrative paragraphs. The prose is not a table however neatly it sits between them. Each column header is one label wrapped over two lines, so each is a single header cell, not a two-row tier (see Header Wrap vs Real Tier§9.3.2).

Label / value blocks without a grid

Two columns of labels and values with no ruled grid are a table or key-value content depending on the data, not the layout. The same two whitespace tracks can hold either.

The rows are… Rendering Examples
Records of one kind — every label is paired with the same kind of value (an amount per component, a factor per year) a table, even with no header row and no ruled grid a Working Capital panel (see Borderless Whitespace Tables§9.1.1); the Trend Factors block of wwa below
Different kinds of fact — each label names its own field (a filing number, a state, a date) key-value content — see Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1 filing metadata, a spec sheet, a biography's Name: / Affiliation: lines
Headline figures — labelled KPIs set as tiles or a highlight panel stat tiles — see Stat Tiles§5.11 Out-of-home +26.5%

A bold label with its value flowing after it — blower spec sheets and similar — is the second kind.

**Motor**: 1/2 HP, 115V      ← no ruled grid, value flows after the label
**Airflow**: 1,200 CFM

A stack whose labels name different kinds of fact MUST NOT be rendered as a table unless a ruled grid is printed around it; it is key-value content, and every line of it MUST still appear in the output. A stack whose rows are records of one kind MUST be rendered as a table.

❌ Counter-sample — ratefiling

The SERFF filing metadata is a label:value stack — SERFF Tracking #, State at the top, a separate Disposition block below. Both read as two columns; neither is a table. The two ruled grids further down the same page are.

✅ Sample — wwa

The bottom Trend Factors block (6th Prior Year … Most Recent Year) has no grid and no header, but every row is the same kind of record — a year and its trend factor — so it is a table, with its bold label as text above it. The large premium-trend grid above it and the ruled Rolling 4-Qtr box are tables too.

Form intertwined with a grid

Rate-filing pages that are half form, half table.

Insurer: [blank]   NAIC #: [blank]     ← form fields…
| Year | Rate change |
| 2024 | +4.2%       |               ← …and a genuine grid, same page

The ruled grid region MUST be rendered as a table and the form fields as key-value content, so that nothing printed is lost. The table MUST NOT be stretched to swallow the form fields, and the grid MUST NOT be dropped because the page as a whole reads like a form.

Cases the relation test does not settle on its own

The relation test alone MUST NOT decide these cases; each is governed by its own rule:

  • forms and ungridded key-value (Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1)
  • trailing totals outside a frame (Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1)
  • a printed data grid under a chart (Chart With a Printed Data Grid§9.1.2)
  • detached aligned cells
Why the cost runs both ways

A missed legend makes a real relation vanish from the output (never drop). A decorative box rendered as a table asserts structure the page never claimed (never invent). Neither error is recoverable downstream, which is why the relation test — not the border, not the alignment — decides.

❌ Counter-sample — two-column author biographies

Two columns, each with bold labels — Name:, Affiliation:, Address:, Main Works: — and values beneath them, separated by horizontal rules top and bottom. Every visual cue says table: aligned label column, ruled boundaries, repeated schema across the two halves.

It is not one. The two columns are independent biographies, not two records of one relation, and the rule lines are section dividers rather than a grid. Reading it as a table would pair Marcus Ainsley with Priya Delacroix as though they shared a row.

The label/value blocks inside each column are ungridded key-value content — see Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1 — and the bulleted publication lists are ordinary lists. The columns are unrolled in reading order, left biography first.

Related
  • Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1 — where ungridded label:value content goes instead
  • Borderless Whitespace Tables§9.1.1 — the "no rules at all" end of the spectrum
  • Table of Contents§6.10 — a column-shaped region with its own rendering
  • Header-Only Tables§9.1.4 — degenerate outputs that follow from getting this decision wrong

9.2 Boundaries

9.2.1 Bands Inside the Grid

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-bands-inside-the-grid · tables boundaries headers

✅ Normative

A full-width band inside a grid — a date line, a section line, a change of shading — MUST NOT end the table. The rows above and below it MUST stay in one table, and the band MUST be rendered as one row whose single cell spans every column.

The signal is the column headers. If the headers are not re-declared under the band, the table never closed: the band is an internal divider, not a boundary.

| Product   | Premium | Losses |
| As of December 2024 (bold band, headers NOT repeated) |
| Term Life | 1,204   | 887    |
| As of December 2023                                   |
| Term Life | 1,150   | 902    |

→ one table, with the two "As of…" lines as full-width band rows
Date and section bands

A bold "As of December 2024" line inside a grid whose column headers are not repeated is a band row spanning all columns, not a boundary. The rows above and below it MUST stay in the same table.

Splitting here is the most expensive boundary error. On a dense financial page, splitting per year turns two tables into four and throws away most of the page's value — every resulting fragment is wrong even though every cell in it is right.

The band's single cell MAY be a header cell (<th colspan=N>) or a body cell (<td colspan=N>); both conform, and a document MUST use one form throughout — see Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2. An in-frame title band is a spanning header cell (see Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3), so the header cell is the default where nothing else decides.

✅ Sample — warn

ASSETS and LIABILITIES AND EQUITY as full-width band rows inside one balance sheet, headers not repeated after either. The stub header is italic, the labels under Current assets: and Current liabilities: are indented one step, and the bold rows are totals.

✅ Sample — earn

Calculation of free cash flow: — a shaded band row that introduces a derived block mid-table, with the column headers not repeated under it.

✅ Sample — dtu

Three full-width bands (Pay TV digital subscribers, Free-to-view digital households, Additional homes receiving analogue multi-channel services) with no repeated column headers. The asterisks are printed on the baseline, attached to the words, and point at the notes below.

✅ Sample — P200509160137_0137_6519

Bilingual band rows — 服務行業 Service Industry, 服務界別 Service Domain — inside a business-receipts index. The stacked header lines are wrapped labels, joined without a space inside the Chinese phrase and with one between the Chinese and English parts.

✅ Sample — vap

Precision, in bold italic, heads Repeatability and Interm. Precision. Ambiguous by design: it reads both as a full-width band and as a parent row label — the band-versus-hierarchy boundary in one cell. It spans the full width, so it is a band.

❌ Counter-sample — 2012_tushin_nittei

清掃の時間 is centred and reads like a full-width band, but it sits inside the track column with the other columns' rules running through its row. It is an ordinary entry in that one cell, not a spanning band row. The letter-spaced headers are written as normal words.

Shading, zebra striping, colour changes

Shading MUST NOT be treated as a table boundary.

| A | 1.10 |   ← white rows
| B | 1.25 |
| C | 1.31 |   ← gray rows start here: still the same table

Shading is a readability aid applied by the typesetter. It makes no claim about what the rows mean, so it cannot start a new table.

What does justify a split

Only a semantic signal justifies a split:

  • a new subject
  • a new schema
  • a key that stops continuing

Appearance alone MUST NOT split a table.

Cohort bands with no column headers anywhere
FEMALE                 ← band; no column headers anywhere
| 25 | 1.02 | 1.10 |
MALE
| 25 | 1.08 | 1.15 |

This one resolves the other way: one table per cohort, with the band as that table's header row. The band is the only thing naming what the rows below it are. See Group and Cohort Bands§9.2.5.

Group bands over one shared row spine
|        | Loss of Income | Other         |  ← two boxed bands
| (1)    | (2)   | (3)    | (4)   | (5)   |  ← full-width numbered tier
| 2019   | 1,204 | 887    | 310   | 95    |  ← one shared row spine

One table. A full-width numbered tier running across the whole width shows that all those columns describe one row — splitting there destroys the row identity that crosses the groups. See Group and Cohort Bands§9.2.5.

Related
  • Repeated Headers and Title Bands§9.2.7 — a band with the headers printed again does open a new table
  • Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3 — in-frame title bands use the same spanning header cell
  • Group and Cohort Bands§9.2.5 — bands that head a table rather than divide one
  • Row-Label Hierarchy§9.5.5 — a parent label inside one column, the other reading of Precision

9.2.2 Column Continuation

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-column-continuation · tables boundaries continuation

✅ Normative

One long series printed as side-by-side blocks SHOULD be rendered as one table per printed block, each carrying its own copy of the headers, including repeated blocks inside one frame. A checker MUST accept source-supported joined equivalents without losing or reassigning records.

A long series — states A–Z, durations 1–36 — printed as two or three blocks beside each other under one title, with the headers repeated over each block and the key continuing from one block to the next.

Printed:   | State | Rate |   | State | Rate |
           | AL    | 1.10 |   | MT    | 0.95 |

Rendered:  one table for the left block, one table for the right block,
           each with its own | State | Rate | header.
Requirements
  • Each printed block SHOULD be its own table, in reading order, with its own copy of the headers exactly as printed above it.
  • Stacking the blocks into one table — the second block's rows appended under the first block's header — carries the same rows and is an accepted equivalent (see Accepted Alternatives§A.1); a document MUST use one form consistently throughout.
  • Do not invent a wide grid. For separately framed blocks, zipping row i of each block into one wide row MUST NOT be done: it pairs AL with MT and asserts a relationship between two unrelated records. A row reading STATE | AVAILABILITY | WITHDRAWAL | STATE | AVAILABILITY | WITHDRAWAL built from separate blocks is non-conforming unless that wide grid is itself printed inside one enclosing frame.
  • Repeated copies of the same schema inside one enclosing frame SHOULD also be split into one table per printed block. The outer frame and continuous horizontal rules do not make records with different keys belong to the same row. Keeping that source-printed wide grid is an accepted equivalent; splitting is preferred because each series can be traversed directly.
  • A shared title MUST remain attached to the whole group. It MAY appear once outside the group; a title band MAY instead be repeated over each block with its span reduced to the block width. Actual shared row keys, non-repeating column groups, and cells carrying relationships across blocks MUST NOT be split by this rule.
  • A shared key column MUST NOT be duplicated into both halves' output. It adds nothing and breaks the link between cells and their position on the page.
✅ Sample — 4tables

Kansas county codes as four side-by-side County | Code blocks. Header repeated, key continuing Allen…Ellsworth │ Finney…Lincoln │ Linn…Republic │ Rice…Wyandotte. The textbook case.

✅ Sample — 4t

A single quarterly return series split across four blocks, quarters running 1999 Q2 → 2019 Q2. Each two-line header is one wrapped label.

✅ Sample — ert

One ascending class-code series printed as four identical side-by-side blocks, so four tables. A printed blank row separates the 00xx codes from the 01xx codes in every block. Zipping the four blocks into one twelve-column table, as below, is the widening this rule forbids.

✅ Sample — 535

The SL Tier | Factor pair repeats three times inside one frame, with tiers 0–30, 31–61, 62–92. These are three consecutive ranges of one series. Three tables are preferred even though horizontal rules cross the entire frame. The source-printed six-column grid and a single vertically stacked series remain equivalent when every tier/factor association is preserved.

The case that looks the same but is not

Blocks with different super-headers over the same rows are one genuinely wide table, not a continuation. They MUST be rendered as a single table with each super-header spanning its columns.

| Non-Tobacco | Tobacco |     ← different super-headers over the same
| Age | M | F | M | F   |       ages: ONE genuinely wide table

The discriminator: in a continuation the blocks are the same columns with the key continuing onward; here the blocks are different columns describing the same rows.

❌ Counter-sample — 3tables

Same visual shape, different meaning: Solaris / Halcyon / Total are three independent series, not one series split by key range, so they are three tables, each with its boxed title as a spanning header row. Distinguishing this from the samples above is the whole difficulty.

❌ Counter-sample — 2tab

The contrast case sharpened: two differently titled panels that share one Region row spine are one wide table, each panel title a spanning super-header. The left title is bold and underlined, the right one bold, italic and underlined; the Total row prints values in the left panel only.

  • Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9 — the inverse: header printed once, not repeated
  • Repeated Headers and Title Bands§9.2.7 — a header repeated below, rather than beside, data rows
  • Side-by-Side Mini Tables§9.2.8 — independent schemas, including grids with no repeated continuation schema

9.2.3 Continued in the Title

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-continued-in-the-title · tables continuation captions

✅ Normative

A continuation marker — (cont'd), (continued), Table 5 — … (cont.) — is printed text and MUST be kept verbatim in the title. The fragment on this page MUST be rendered as a table in its own right.

Table 5 — Lapse Rates (cont'd)     ← explicit continuation marker
| Duration | Rate |
Requirements
  • The title MUST be transcribed exactly as printed, marker included. The marker MUST NOT be stripped to tidy the title, nor rewritten into a fuller form.
  • The table on this page MUST be rendered as a table in its own right. Its rows MUST NOT be fused with a fragment on a previous page (unless the join option of Output Options§3.5 was requested).
  • The kept marker is what records that the fragment continues an earlier table. It is the strongest continuation evidence a page can give — far stronger than the indirect signals other fragments offer.
Why this is the easy end of a hard problem

Everywhere else in Cross-Page Tables§4.3, continuation has to be inferred from weak signals: a missing header, a first row that starts mid-key, rows running right to the page edge. Here the document says it outright, so there is nothing to infer — only a statement not to throw away.

Keeping the marker settles the fidelity half of the question however the fragments are eventually joined: the words are printed on the page, so they survive (never drop). The fragment stays on its own page and is flagged as continued — see Cross-Page Tables§4.3.

✅ Sample — a band that says Cont'd

SELF-INSURED / $1 MILLION TO $3 MILLION CATEGORY – Cont'd as a band under the heading of a scanned schedule. It is boxed on its own, apart from the table frame, so it is a title above the table, kept with its marker. Each fund spans several printed lines, one benefit per line, with X marks in the INSURED, SELF-INSURED and three COVERAGE columns; the fund-name cell is one merged cell beside its benefit rows.

✅ Sample — —Continued in a table title


Source: U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), Table 7 (public domain)

Table 7. Graduation rates … cohort years 2004 and 2007—Continued over the last four rows of a table, with the full header stack repeated and a — Not available legend below. Every column header is one label wrapped over several lines; Public and the two private rows are indented under the first row.

  • Cross-Page Tables§4.3 — continuation without a printed marker
  • Repeated Headers and Title Bands§9.2.7 — a header repeated on the same page is a boundary
  • Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3 — where a title sits relative to its table
  • Output Options§3.5 — the same fragment joins into one table under a wider setting

9.2.4 Duplicated Tables

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-duplicated-tables · tables fidelity

✅ Normative

Every printed occurrence of a table MUST be rendered, in reading order, each as its own table — including a table the page prints twice. Transcription is not summarisation: page content MUST NOT be deduplicated.

Page prints:                    Non-conforming:
[Table X]  …  [Table X again]   [Table X]     ← second copy silently dropped
Requirements
  • Identical repeats MUST NOT be collapsed into one, and the second copy MUST NOT be replaced with a note that it repeats the first (never drop).
  • Duplication MUST be judged from the rendered page. A table seen once on the page is there once, whatever the underlying text layer says (never invent).
The trap

A PDF's text layer can carry a phantom second copy of a run — from a shadow effect, an overprint, or a quirk of whatever generated the file — that never appears on screen. Judged from extracted text rather than from the page as rendered, a duplicate can be "found" that does not exist, or two visually identical blocks can be missed as both printed.

The rule that resolves it is the one in Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3 and The Page Is the Ground Truth§2.1: the image is the authority, the text layer is a hint.

Repeated template is not duplication

Blocks with an identical header schema but different numbers are separate tables with real, distinct content — not copies. Three panels of the same shape showing 89%/11%, 100%/0% and so on are three tables, and none of them is a duplicate of another. The data, not the layout, decides.

❌ Counter-sample — about-disclosures-order-routing-2005q2

Three NYSE/AMEX/NASDAQ tables with an identical header schema — but distinct data (89%/11% vs 100%/0%). A repeated template, not a duplicate: all three are rendered. The Total Customer Orders rows are bold.

Related
  • Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3 — the image wins over the text layer
  • Chart With a Printed Data Grid§9.1.2 — the reverse error: a reconstructed copy the page never printed
  • Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2 — the two failures this rule guards against

9.2.5 Group and Cohort Bands

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-group-and-cohort-bands · tables boundaries headers

✅ Normative

Bands over stacked grids resolve on one question: is there a shared row spine? Grids sharing one spine MUST be rendered as one table. Grids with no shared spine and no column headers MUST be rendered as one table per band, with the band as that table's header row.

Shared spine No shared spine
Row spine one continuous spine, shared label column repeated, independent per band
Column headers present, often with a numbered tier absent entirely
Rendering one table one table per cohort, band becomes its header row

The row spine is checked first, then the column headers. Those two signals decide it; the bands themselves look identical in both cases.

Group bands over a shared spine — one table

Two boxed group headers sitting over one continuous row grid that shares a left label column MUST be rendered as a single table.

|        | Loss of Income | Other         |  ← two boxed bands
| (1)    | (2)   | (3)    | (4)   | (5)   |  ← full-width numbered tier
| 2019   | 1,204 | 887    | 310   | 95    |  ← one shared row spine
The decisive signal

A full-width numbered tier is proof of single-table semantics.

If (1)…(13) runs across the whole width, the page is asserting that all those columns describe one row. Splitting there loses the row identity that spans the groups — the fact that 2019's Loss-of-Income figures and its Other figures belong to the same year.

  • The group bands MUST be rendered as spanning cells over their column ranges.
  • The numbered tier MUST be kept as a header row, not dropped as decoration. See Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 — dropping the numbered tier as noise also destroys the evidence that the table is one table.
✅ Sample — yef

Full-width Year Ended… bands sharing one header and column spine across three fiscal years. The currency sign is printed with a space before the figure, and that space is kept.

✅ Sample — 10k1

Revenues, Earnings from operations, Operating margin bands over one shared segment spine — MerevaldCare, Vantage Health, Vantage Insight, Vantage Rx. The three Vantage lines and the eliminations line under MerevaldCare are indented one step; the consolidated rows are bold totals.

✅ Sample — 3samehead

Bold Issue Year / Issue Age / Attained Age bands over one shared column spine — one table, three cohorts. Each band is a full-width row. The last Issue Year row prints 32031.9% in the last column, and that is the value recorded.

Cohort bands with no column headers — one table per cohort

Same-shape grids stacked under cohort bands, with no column headers anywhere:

FEMALE
| 25 | 1.02 | 1.10 |
MALE
| 25 | 1.08 | 1.15 |

One table per cohort. The band becomes that table's header row.

Fusing these into a single table loses the row headers: with the bands demoted to ordinary rows, nothing says which block is female and which is male.

The band is a header here precisely because nothing else is — it is the only thing naming what the rows below it are.

✅ Sample — 5t

Five title bands (2/3/4/5/6 Year Benefit Period), each over its own block repeating the same Issue Age spine: five tables, each band as its table's first header row.

✅ Sample — 3tables2

Each rating class (0034 / 0035 / 0036) is its own titled cohort block, stacked; the class number and name form the first header row of each class table, and a separate credibility grid follows each. CLASS and its number are printed on two lines in a cell wide enough for one, and the industry and hazard groups are two separate lines.

Keeping the two apart

The two shapes look alike from a distance and resolve in opposite directions, so both checks are run deliberately:

  • Does the left label column run continuously through both bands, unrepeated? → one table.
  • Does each band restart the same labels under it, with no column headers printed anywhere? → one table per band.

Date bands and shading changes inside a single grid are a different question again — see Bands Inside the Grid§9.2.1.

Related
  • Bands Inside the Grid§9.2.1 — bands that divide one grid rather than head a new one
  • Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 — the numbered tier that proves the shared spine
  • Repeated Headers and Title Bands§9.2.7 — blocks that each re-declare their headers are separate tables

9.2.6 Horizontal Slicing

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-horizontal-slicing · tables continuation boundaries

✅ Normative

A table too wide for the page, printed as stacked column blocks, MUST be rendered as one table per printed block, each keeping its repeated row-label column. The blocks MUST NOT be re-widened into a single wide table.

A table too wide for the page is printed as column blocks stacked vertically, with the row-label column repeated in each block.

| State | Jan | Feb | Mar |
| AL    | 1.1 | 1.2 | 1.2 |

| State | Apr | May | Jun |   ← same rows, next columns
| AL    | 1.3 | 1.3 | 1.4 |
✅ Sample — 5line heaer

Columns (1)–(5) and (6)–(10) of one logical table stacked vertically, the Industry Group stub repeated in each block over the same six rows. Each column header is one label wrapped over many lines and is joined into one cell.

✅ Sample — busbands

A bus timetable too wide for the page, printed as stacked AM/PM/PM blocks with the stop-name column repeated in every block. The stop names are bold.

Requirements
  • Each printed block MUST be rendered as its own table, top to bottom.
  • The repeated row-label column MUST be kept in every block. It is printed in each one, and it is what makes the blocks joinable later.
  • The blocks MUST NOT be re-widened into a single State | Jan…Jun table, even though the repeated key makes the join look obvious.
How to recognise it

The blocks share their rows and differ in their columns — the same keys reappear down each block, with new column headers over them. That is the opposite of Column Continuation§9.2.2, where the blocks share their columns and the key runs onward from one block to the next.

If the row keys do not line up across the blocks, it is not a slice of one wide table at all: the blocks are separate tables, with no join to look for.

The asymmetry worth noticing

In Column Continuation§9.2.2, widening is the one shape that is always wrong: it pairs unrelated records with each other. Here it is the appealing option, because the repeated key column gives a reliable join and no record gets paired with a stranger. The rendering nevertheless stays one table per printed block: the page printed blocks, and the join is left to whoever consumes the output.

Related
  • Column Continuation§9.2.2 — the transpose: blocks side by side, key running onward
  • Cross-Page Tables§4.3 — blocks split by a page break instead of by width
  • Repeated Headers and Title Bands§9.2.7 — a header printed again below data rows opens a new table

9.2.7 Repeated Headers and Title Bands

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-repeated-headers-and-title-bands · tables boundaries headers

✅ Normative

Within one page, a column-header row printed again after data rows MUST close the table and open a new one at the repeat. Header repetition is the table-boundary signal.

| State | Rate |
| AL    | 1.10 |
| State | Rate |   ← header printed again after data rows:
| MT    | 0.95 |     the first table ends, a second starts here
Requirements
  • A re-declared header row MUST start a new table. The rows under it belong to that new table, not to the one above.
  • An entity or geography band that reappears as a title bar before each block likewise MUST open a new table each time it appears.
  • The repeated header MUST be kept: it is printed, so it is the new table's header row.
  • Two tables separated by a repeated header MUST NOT be fused, even where they read as one series broken up for layout.
✅ Sample — busbands

The Monday to Friday band with its AM/PM label reappears as a title bar before each stacked block, so each block is its own table.

❌ Counter-sample — 2021-q3-consensus-poll-calculation

Four period blocks that look like one table whose headers reappear after each data group. Each block has its own Period title and participant count above its header, so each is a wholly separate table — the title and count form its opening <caption> rather than data rows.

Read it against the mirror case

If two fragments share a header that is not repeated, they are one table — see Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9. Together, the two rules make header repetition the single boundary signal, decidable from what is printed without judging what the rows mean. An exception for a case that "obviously" continues weakens both rules and MUST NOT be made.

Across a page break

Across a page break, a repeated header is routine and says nothing about whether the table ended. That case is governed by Cross-Page Tables§4.3, not by this rule; within one page, a repeat is a boundary.

Related
  • Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9 — the mirror case: an unrepeated shared header joins fragments
  • Cross-Page Tables§4.3 — a header repeated after a page break is not a boundary
  • Column Continuation§9.2.2 — side-by-side blocks, each with its own header copy

9.2.8 Side-by-Side Mini Tables

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-side-by-side-mini-tables · tables boundaries failure-mode

✅ Normative

Boxes sitting side by side with their own titles and their own schemas MUST be rendered as separate tables — even when their rows line up perfectly. Neighbouring tables MUST NOT be woven together, and a small side table MUST NOT be folded into the middle of another table's body.

Printed:  [Box A]      [Box B]        Woven output (non-conforming):
          | a1 | a2 |  | b1 | b2 |    | a1 | a2 | b1 | b2 |
          | a3 | a4 |  | b3 | b4 |    | a3 | a4 | b3 | b4 |
                                        ↑ rows from unrelated boxes glued together

Weaving is not merely mis-structured. It asserts that a1 and b1 belong to the same record, which the page never said (never invent).

Requirements
  • Each box MUST be rendered as its own table, with its own title and its own header stack.
  • Row alignment MUST NOT be used as a grouping signal. Boxes are top-aligned for looks, so their rows land at the same heights by accident.
  • The title and the schema decide: its own title and its own columns means its own table.
  • A small side table MUST NOT be absorbed into another table's body. A "12pt / 3 Year" side panel is not three extra rows in the claims grid beside it.
✅ Sample — 3tables

Three separately bordered and titled card-count tables, identical schema, distinct data. Each boxed title is the first header row of its own table.

✅ Sample — 3tt

Three badged panels — DIABETES, OBESITY, RARE DISEASE — same schema, different products. The footnote numbers are printed raised.

✅ Sample — 2tt

Two independently framed pet-insurance worksheets (Cat, Dog), rendered as two tables. The blank gap after Coverage of Exam Fees is left out, and the bold Premium line closes each worksheet.

✅ Sample — waw

Five boxed ACA panels laid out in two rows, each with its own title band and its own full header stack. The dark band across the top of each panel shares its frame, so it is the first row of that panel's table. Carrier Cata- / strophic is one wrapped label; the lower panels print Cata-strophic with the hyphen mid-line, so the hyphen is part of the printed word and is kept.

✅ Sample — strike

Current Rates and Proposed Rates as independently titled boxed pairs: all four blocks are separate tables. Every current rate is struck through.

❌ Counter-sample — figure-cards-p6

The Figure 5 boxed panels look like side-by-side mini-tables but are image-plus-caption cards, not tabular data: they are rendered as the figure's content in reading order. The only table on the page is Table 3, whose bold Total row closes it.

Header attribution is per column, not per table

A header owns the columns printed under it, not everything to its right. A title like "Reported Claims" sitting over the claim-count columns does not also claim the year labels beside them. A spanning header MUST span exactly the columns it sits above.

Contrast with the cases that DO merge

The neighbouring cases pull the other way, which is why the title and schema are checked rather than a blanket "boxes are always separate":

  • Column Continuation§9.2.2 — side-by-side blocks that are one series: same schema, headers repeated, key continuing onward
  • Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9 — fragments that must merge: one header, printed once

The discriminator is own title / own schema. If each box declares what it is and how its columns are named, it stands alone.

✅ Sample — a two-sided balance sheet in one frame

Assets down the left, liabilities and equity down the middle, an income statement on the right, all inside one ruled box under two title bands. These are different schemas, not consecutive ranges of a repeated schema. Repeated-schema continuations follow Column Continuation§9.2.2 even inside one enclosing frame. Row n on the left has nothing to do with row n in the middle, and yet this is one table, row n across all blocks — the frame is one grid and is transcribed as the grid it prints. The side-by-side rule above is for boxes with their own frames.

Related
  • Column Continuation§9.2.2 — side-by-side blocks that continue one series
  • Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9 — fragments that share one printed header and merge
  • Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 — boxed panels that are not tables at all

9.2.9 Split Tables Sharing a Header

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-split-tables-sharing-a-header · tables boundaries headers proposed-rule

✅ Normative

Fragments that share a header row or a label column printed only once MUST be rendered as one table. The missing header is the proof that the second fragment was never meant to stand alone.

A grid is sometimes printed as two or more visually separated fragments — a gap, a page-design break, a divider — with the header row or the label column printed once and not repeated in the second fragment. Read on its own, the second fragment is unreadable without the header above it, so it is not a separate table. Emitting it as a separate headerless table, or dropping it, loses the meaning of every value in it (never drop).

Printed:   | Age | Rate M | Rate F |     ← header printed once
           | 25  | 1.10   | 1.05   |

              (visual gap / band)

           | 45  | 1.42   | 1.31   |     ← no header repeated: same table
           | 55  | 1.80   | 1.66   |

This is the mirror of the repeated-header test in Repeated Headers and Title Bands§9.2.7: a repeated header starts a new table, an unrepeated one continues the current one. Between them, header repetition is the single boundary signal on a page, read before gaps, rules or bands.

✅ Sample — 3samehead

The Count / % of Count / Premium / % of Premium header row is printed once and shared by three consecutive cohort blocks below it. None of the blocks below can be read on its own, so the page is one table with each cohort label as a band row.

✅ Sample — dt1

A company-relocation list whose header row is printed once here…

✅ Sample — dt2

…and continues onto the next page with no header row at all: the fragment depends on the header printed on the page before. Across a page break the fragments stay on their own pages — see Cross-Page Tables§4.3 — so this page's fragment is rendered headerless and carries the continuation flags instead of a copied header.

Two cases that need judgement

Something sits in the gap. A band row, a caption or a paragraph between the fragments does not automatically break the table. The fragments MUST be merged as long as the second one still depends on the header above it; a heading printed in the gap becomes a band row inside the one table.

The shared piece is the label column. Side-by-side fragments with the row labels printed once on the left and value blocks separated by a gutter follow the same test: the value blocks cannot be read without those labels, so they MUST be rendered as one table. Every printed value MUST be kept, with the blocks placed as further columns of the labelled table.

✅ Sample — one label column, two value blocks

A quarterly summary printed as one row-label column on the left — Revenue, Gross profit, Selling, general and administrative expenses, EBIT, Non-controlling interests, Net income — feeding two separately boxed value blocks: C$ millions and (% of revenue), each with its own Q2 2025 / Q2 2024 header pair.

The right-hand block has no row labels of its own. Read on its own it is ten unnamed values, which is the proof that the two fragments were never meant to stand apart. The same structure is printed again below for the year-to-date figures, with its header rows repeated, so that block is a second table.

The blocks do not share a header row: each has its own. It is the label column that is printed once — the mirror sub-case. The em-dashes in the Non-controlling interests rows are values, not blanks (Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6), and (% of revenue) is a units line in the header (Units Row§9.3.5). The empty gutter between the blocks is not a column (Gutter Columns§9.4.1).

✅ Sample — a numbered note heading in the gap

The four-column header (Consolidated / Merevald Retail Ltd, two dates each) is printed once at the top. Note 20 Reserves and note 21 Total equity reconciliation both sit under it, separated by the second note's heading. Neither fragment repeats the header, so it is one table, and each note heading is a band row inside it.

  • Column Continuation§9.2.2 — side-by-side blocks that each carry their own header copy
  • Header-Only Tables§9.1.4 — the failure this rule prevents
