9.3 Headers

9.3.1 Barely-Existing Columns and Headers

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-barely-existing-columns-and-headers · tables columns headers drops

✅ Normative

The output MUST transcribe what is printed and add nothing. A column or a header MUST NOT be dropped because it is empty, plainly styled or easy to miss, and a label MUST NOT be invented for a cell that has none.

|        | Current | New Program² |
| Rate A | 1.10    |              |    ← all-blank column, proven only by its
| Rate B | 1.25    |              |      header: it exists, keep it
  ↑ blank corner: leave it blank, do not invent "Category"

Four situations look like nothing and are routinely lost. All four are the same failure in one of two directions — a drop or an invention (Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2).

An all-blank body column proven only by its header

A column whose body is entirely empty still exists. It MUST be kept as an empty column, and any marker on its label MUST be kept — a superscript such as New Program² is part of the header text, not decoration.

✅ Sample — sln

The Bidder's Response column is entirely blank — proven to exist only by its header. Dropping it is the classic error. The merged item cells and the two-line specification values are printed that way.

✅ Sample — xx

Column 3 carries no header text at all, only XX filler values: its header cell stays empty and the column stays.

✅ Sample — en

Total Weightage Assigned stays blank across five rows, proven only by its header; the page prints that blank as one merged box, so it is one cell with a rowspan. The bold TOTAL row closes the table.

A blank corner cell over the stub

If the corner above the row labels is blank on the page, it MUST be rendered blank. "Category", "Item" or any other reasonable-sounding word MUST NOT be supplied. An unlabelled cell is data too.

✅ Sample — 3lineperorw

A blank top-left corner cell, ruled off from the Territory label below it.

❌ Counter-sample — 3lineperrowhili

The same table revised: no rule divides the corner from the Territory label, so the label fills a genuinely merged two-row cell — the mirror of the blank corner above. The green row fill is shading and is not rendered.

A numbered tier (1) (2) (3)… across the columns
| State | Premium | Losses |
| (1)   | (2)     | (3)    |   ← a header row: render it

A numbered tier running across the columns is a header row, not decoration, and MUST be rendered.

Dropping it costs twice. The tier also runs the full width of the grid, which is the evidence that every column below belongs to one row — the proof Group and Cohort Bands§9.2.5 and Bands Inside the Grid§9.2.1 rely on to show that banded blocks are a single table. Without the tier, both the header and the boundary signal are lost.

✅ Sample — xlt

A numbered tier (1)–(12) sitting above the real headers with no group meaning. Under (5) and (10) a formula is printed on its own line, so that break is kept.

Header bands that are not bold

A band naming a section is a header row even when it is set in plain type. "Lending" over a block of lending figures, or a CA|PPO line above its rates, are headers; demoting them to body rows is non-conforming.

| Lending    |       |   ← plain-styled band naming a section: still a header
| Commercial | 120.5 |

Boldness MUST NOT decide what is a header. Headers are recognised from position, span and what the line does for the rows beneath it — Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2 shows styling is applied unreliably in both directions and cannot carry this judgement.

Blank space beside or below a header label
| 34 | S |          | [rowspan=3]34     | S |
|    | M |    vs    | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE | M |
|    | L |          | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE | L |

A region that is visually blank beside or below a labelled cell MUST be rendered as separate empty cells. The label's rowspan or colspan MUST NOT be extended over it unless the cell is genuinely merged — when the print says so, not when it is inferred.

Telling a real merge from adjacent blankness
Genuine merge — extend Adjacent blankness — separate empty cells
No ruling divides the region: it is printed as one box Ruled cell borders continue through the blank region
The label is centred across the whole span The label sits in the first cell, blank cells follow
A stub label spanning the header tiers (<th rowspan="2">UW Category</th>) A header label that simply has nothing under it

The stopped-divider test. A ruling line that stops is as informative as one that continues. On a bundle-credit rate table the divider beneath Number of Additional Policies stops before the Factor column: that stopped rule is positive evidence that the group covers Car and Other only, and that Factor is a genuinely merged cell spanning both header tiers. What looks like "blank space above Factor" is in fact inside a visibly merged two-row header cell. Where a divider stops, the cell beside it spans.

Most blank-adjacency cases have no such geometry. Absent a stopped divider or an equivalent printed signal, nothing proves a merge — which is why the default is do not extend.

Carve-out. A stub label that spans the header tiers (Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3) still takes a rowspan across those header rows. That is a logical merge and this rule does not touch it.

Why this way. A span mirrors what is printed, never what is inferred. A blank cell asserts nothing; a span asserts "this label owns that region", which needs printed evidence. Making merge the default would teach the reflex when in doubt, rowspan — exactly the habit Repeated Identical Values§9.5.4 exists to suppress. It is also the simpler question: "is this cell's printed content empty?" rather than a semantic judgement, the same test Blank and Spacer Rows§9.5.1 uses in the table body.

The through-line

Every case here is a drop or an invention. One principle covers all of them, the one also stated in Repeated Identical Values§9.5.4: never emit less data than went in, and never invent what was not printed.

Related
  • Repeated Identical Values§9.5.4 — the same never-drop, never-invent discipline in the body
  • Header Body Column Count Mismatch§9.4.2 — columns that seem to disappear between header and body
  • Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3 — the stub rowspan carve-out
  • Blank and Spacer Rows§9.5.1 — the empty-content test applied to rows

9.3.2 Header Wrap vs Real Tier

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-header-wrap-vs-real-tier · tables headers heuristic

✅ Normative

A header line with a rule beneath it, standing over two or more self-standing leaf labels, is a real tier and MUST be rendered as its own header row. Fragments that simply stack with no border and read as one phrase are a wrapped label and MUST be joined with a space into a single header cell.

As printed:

As parsed — the failure:

Only "Common Stock" is a real tier here: it has a rule beneath it and spans two self-standing leaves, Shares and Amount. The other three are single wrapped labels — "Capital in Excess of Par Value" is one column heading broken across two lines to fit. Treating all four the same way splits every wrapped label into a phantom two-row tier, which is the error this rule prevents (never invent).

Wrapped header text looks exactly like a two-row tier, so the test is run deliberately rather than by eye.

Wrap (one header, join with a space):     Real tier (parent phrase over leaves):
| Published    |                          | (Paid as of 12-31-2020) |
| Availability |                          |   2018    |    2019     |
  ↑ fragments concatenate, no border        ↑ spans two sub-columns
The test
  1. A rule beneath the upper line. A printed border under a label, with columns continuing below it, points to a tier.
  2. The lower labels on their own. If each stands as a complete column heading — Shares, Amount, 2018, 2019 — the line above is a tier over them. If the lines only make sense concatenated, they are one wrapped label.
  3. The span. A tier covers two or more leaf columns. A label that sits over exactly one column is a wrap, whatever its line count.
✅ Sample — wqa

1 YEAR TO / LESS THAN / 2 YEARS wraps across three printed lines and is one header label. The month labels and the Total row are bold.

✅ Sample — ed

Committee Membership Until 2025 Meeting — one label wrapped over four lines, not a colspan tier. The checkmarks are rendered as [yes] (see Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6).

✅ Sample — wat

Water - Weather and Water - Non-Weather each wrap two lines; both are single labels.

✅ Sample — 5line heaer

Every header is one label wrapped over many lines, e.g. (1) Latest Year Current Expected Losses…; each is joined with spaces into one cell.

✅ Sample — 2linebug

MAINTAIN CURRENT COVERAGE: No Action Required wrapped across five lines in one cell. The bracketed field numbers are printed text, the empty boxes are unchecked checkboxes, and the header rows are padded where the payment column has no header. The call-out box covers the first two columns of its row.

The case that catches people out

A parent phrase can be wrapped and be a tier. "(Paid as of 12-31-2020)" is broken across lines and spans its sub-columns — so "it wrapped" never settles the question on its own. The span does: a phrase that covers more than one leaf column MUST be kept as a tier with its exact colspan, however many lines it takes. A phrase that covers one column is joined into that column's label.

❌ Counter-sample — 3t

POOLED RETURN (%) wraps across stacked lines in a narrow column and is one header — the contrast against a real tier. The coloured title band spans the whole block, and the bold 1997-2017 row closes it.

A label broken inside a word

A space join assumes the break falls between words. When a narrow column breaks inside a word — Distributio / n, Appointe / d — the fragments MUST be joined with nothing: Distribution, Appointed. A wrap with a printed hyphen inside a word (per- / form- / ance) is joined the same way, dropping the hyphens. A hyphen that belongs to the word, as in a compound, stays — see Line-End Hyphenation§7.2.7. Only a break between words gets a space.

✅ Sample — a header wrapped mid-word

Under each scenario the first sub-column is headed Distributio over n; the tier above it (Liquidation - Low, Liquidation - High, Recovery Per Plan) has a rule beneath and spans the sub-columns, so the tier test still holds. The $ printed in its own track joins its value.

✅ Sample — a wrap with printed hyphens

Trading / per- / form- / ance wraps over four lines with the hyphens printed. Joining with a space would give per- form- ance; the page means performance. See Line-End Hyphenation§7.2.7.

✅ Sample — a wrap that breaks inside a word, twice

Appointe / d / business over the first column of each year group, and Non- / appointed / business beside it. One wrap breaks a word with no hyphen and joins to Appointed; the other breaks at the hyphen of the compound Non-appointed, which is kept. The £'m line is a units row, and the empty gutter between the year groups is not a column.

9.3.3 Multi-Row Header Tiers

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-multi-row-header-tiers · tables headers encoding

✅ Normative

Every printed header tier MUST be rendered as its own header row, with exact colspans. A group header MUST span only its data columns; the row-label stub takes a rowspan across the header rows instead.

Printed:  |            BI          |            PD          |
          | Indicated  | Proposed  | Indicated  | Proposed  |
Every real tier is kept

Both rows are rendered with their spans — [colspan=2]BI over Indicated | Proposed, and so on.

The stack MUST NOT be flattened into one row of concatenated labels: "BI Indicated", "BI Proposed" is non-conforming, not a stylistic choice. It destroys the grouping that the page printed and makes the number of header rows depend on the producer rather than the page.

A wrapped parent phrase is still a tier. "(Paid as of 12-31-2020)" broken across two lines and spanning its sub-columns is a genuine tier — "it wrapped" does not demote it. The span, not the line count, decides; Header Wrap vs Real Tier§9.3.2 has the full test.

✅ Sample — 5lineperrow

Four stacked header rows: benefit period › inflation › Incurred Age Band › <75 / 75-84 / 85+ repeated four times. The stub label spans all four header rows; the month numbers are bold.

✅ Sample — 3tables2

CONVERTED LOSSES band over INDEMNITY LIKELY / NOT-LIKELY sub-bands, with rowspan leaves beneath.

❌ Counter-sample — 3in1

The Loss Ratio Summaries block prints no header row at all; supplying a tier of Premium/Claims/Ratio labels over its columns fabricates headers the page never printed. The block is rendered headerless, and the Projected Loss Ratio block below it keeps its own single header row.

❌ Counter-sample — w

The page prints one header row, each label wrapped over several lines. Splitting it into a rowspan="2" tier with an empty second row, as below, invents a tier. Trans- / ferred is one word broken at a line-end hyphen.

The group header stops at the first data column

A group super-header spans its data columns and never the row-label stub. The stub takes a rowspan across the header rows:

<th rowspan="2">UW Category</th><th colspan="3">Inception to Date</th>
<!-- then: -->  Earned Premium | Incurred Claims | Loss Ratio

The group's colspan MUST equal its leaf count, exactly.

The printed rule under the group starts at the first data column. The stub is not part of "Inception to Date" — the stub says which row, the group says which measure. Different axes, so they do not share a span. Spanning the stub as well is the most common way this goes wrong.

✅ Sample — star

Three genuine tiers: APPLICABILITY CHART (colspan 5) over TERRORISM OPTIONS – INCLUDING PRICING (colspan 4) over four leaves, with STATE taking rowspan 2 — a clean instance of the stub rule. The printed asterisks are escaped.

Reconciling the tracks

The leaf-column tracks N of the table are counted. For each header row, the expanded colspans, occupied plus explicit blank tracks, MUST add up to N.

A mismatch shows which kind of error was made, before anything else is inspected:

  1. a missed column
  2. a wrong span
  3. two tables fused into one
  4. a header line read as the wrong kind of thing
Period stacks in financial statements
| $ in millions |       Average for the        |  ← corner note; apex tier
|               | Three Months Ended | Year …  |
|               | December | December | Dec…   |  ← stacked "December"/"2024"
|               | 2024     | 2023     | 2024   |    is ONE leaf label

Period headers follow the same rules, with a few fixed calls of their own — apex qualifiers, stacked month-over-year labels and the "$ in millions" corner note. They are set out in SEC Period Tiers§9.3.4, which governs 10-K and 10-Q header stacks.

✅ Sample — wdb

Three Months Ended / Nine Months Ended bands split into year and Reported/Ex-FX sub-columns. A rule runs under the year row across the whole table, so the cells under 2024 and 2023 in the third header row are separate empty cells, not a rowspan. Ex-FX breaks at its own hyphen and keeps it.

✅ Sample — sssa

2023 (colspan 5) and 2024 (colspan 3) over Q1–Q4/FY leaves.

9.3.4 SEC Period Tiers

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-sec-period-tiers · tables headers sec

✅ Normative

A financial period stack MUST be rendered as its printed tiers: period groups over their own date leaves, an apex qualifier above them, a stacked month and year joined into one leaf label, and the units note kept verbatim as the corner header cell.

This is the header stack of every 10-K and 10-Q. It looks ambiguous, but every part of it has a fixed answer.

| $ in millions |       Average for the        |  ← apex qualifier
|               | Three Months Ended | Year …  |  ← sibling period groups
|               | December | December | Dec…   |  ← stacked month/year =
|               | 2024     | 2023     | 2024   |    ONE leaf, joined
The page shows Requirement
"Three/Six Months Ended…", "Year(s) Ended…" MUST be sibling group tiers over their own date leaves
An apex qualifier like "Average for the" MUST be a tier above them, spanning the period groups
Stacked "December" / "2024" MUST be one leaf label, the lines joined
Bold on the current-period column styling, not structure: the header structure MUST NOT change; the bold is marked per cell as printed
"$ in millions" in the stub corner MUST be the corner header cell, kept verbatim
✅ Sample — wdb

Three Months Ended / Nine Months Ended bands with the $ in millions corner note in the stub.

✅ Sample — 10k1

For the Years Ended December 31, spanning 2030/2029/2028 plus a Change tier, with an (in millions, except percentages) corner note.

✅ Sample — 2q

Three / Six Months Ended September 30, over 2004/2003 leaves, with an (in thousands) lead-in. Each period label wraps over two lines inside its own group cell and is joined. The currency sign is printed with a space before the figure; Nova Studio Net Product Revenue is indented one step.

Why the stacked month and year join

"December" and "2024" are not two levels of anything — no other column shares a "December" parent. The typesetter broke one label across two lines to fit a narrow column, so it is a wrap. A tier is kept only for a label that genuinely spans more than one leaf column, as Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3 requires.

  • Header Wrap vs Real Tier§9.3.2 — why a stacked month and year is a wrap
  • Units Row§9.3.5 — units printed as a line under the header rather than in the corner

9.3.5 Units Row

⚖️ Equivalent forms · 📄 page rule

tables-units-row · tables headers

⚖️ Equivalent forms

A units line under the header MAY be rendered as a second header row, or folded into the header label above it ("Premium ($000)"). Both forms conform, and a document MUST use one of them throughout (see Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2). A units line MUST NOT become the first body row.

| Premium | Losses | Ratio |
| ($000)  | ($000) | (%)   |   ← units line: a header tier, or folded into
| 1,204   | 887    | 73.6  |     the labels as "Premium ($000)"
Recognising it

A units line sits directly beneath the header, carries no values, and repeats the same kind of token across the columns — ($000), (%), (millions), (points). Every entry describes how to read the column below it rather than reporting a measurement.

✅ Sample — P200509160137_0137_6519

A （點） (Points) / （百分率） (%) row under the main header states units, not data; here it is kept as a second header row.

The two conforming forms

Second header row. The line is kept as its own header row, aligned to the columns it describes, and the values below stay bare. This is closest to what is printed.

Folded into the label. The unit is appended to the header text — "Premium ($000)". This is the most useful for downstream extraction, because the unit travels with the field. It does edit the header string, which sits awkwardly beside the verbatim posture of Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3, so the second header row SHOULD be preferred when a document uses units lines heavily.

The outcome to avoid

A units line MUST NOT be rendered as a body row. It is not merely inelegant: a reader of the first body row then gets ($000) as a premium value. Where the choice between the two conforming forms is unclear, the second header row is the default.

✅ Sample — a units row in the middle of the body

S$'m under the header, then a second units line — S$ in every column — printed mid-table before the Per share block. A units line between two blocks of body is a band row: every cell a <th>, the S$ cells included, never a body row and never a table split. Both units lines are italic.

  • Header Wrap vs Real Tier§9.3.2 — a units token stacked inside one label is part of a wrap
  • Accounting Number Formats§9.6.1 — the values the units describe stay verbatim

9.4 Columns

9.4.1 Gutter Columns

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-gutter-columns · tables columns currency

✅ Normative

A currency glyph or a separator typeset in a column track of its own SHOULD be rendered in the same cell as the value it belongs to — $ 277.09, $1,200 — $1,800. A marker numeral such as (i) or (ii) SHOULD be rendered in a column of its own.

Financial PDFs frequently typeset $ in its own column track, and print ranges as value — value with the dash in a track of its own. Those tracks are real in the typesetting, but they are layout, not data.

Printed tracks:  $ | 1,200 | — | $ | 1,800
Rendered as:     $1,200 — $1,800   (one cell)
Currency and separators: merged into the value
  • A currency glyph printed in its own track SHOULD be rendered in the cell of the number it belongs to. The glyph MUST NOT be dropped: where the page prints $ only on some rows, only those rows' values carry it.
  • A separator between the two ends of a range (a dash, +/-, to) SHOULD be rendered in one cell with both ends.
  • A $ kept in a cell of its own beside its value, as a pair of cells, also conforms; the single cell is the preferred form.
✅ Sample — warn

$ typeset in its own column track, separate from the digits, throughout the balance sheet. It is printed only on the first row of each block and on the grand total, so only those values carry it. The stub header is italic. The row labels are printed flush left, without indentation, so every label is level 0.

✅ Sample — earn

The same $-gutter pattern in Halyard Genomics' cash-flow statement.

✅ Sample — earnin

And again in Sablecrest Dynamics' statement of operations — this typesetting is the norm, not an oddity. Gross profit, Gross margin and Operating income (loss) are indented one step.

❌ Counter-sample — some

The $ sits in its own boxed column track in the image, which looks like a column of its own. It is not: the glyph belongs to the value, so the first value cell reads $274. The Second Quarter and January - June spanners printed above the header are part of the table.

Marker gutters: kept as a column
| (i)  | Base salary … |     ← one column for the numeral, one for the text
| (ii) | Bonus …       |

A marker numeral such as (i) / (ii) SHOULD be rendered in a column of its own. A merged (i) Base salary … cell also conforms, but the separate numeral column is the preferred form.

Why the two resolve opposite ways

A currency symbol is part of the value. A marker numeral is a reference label: it is cited elsewhere on the page ("see (ii)"), so it has an identity of its own and earns a column.

A gutter this rule does not name is decided by the column-count test: a track gets its own column only if a competent person modelling this data in a spreadsheet would give it one. That is the same appeal to how a person would model the content that decides Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 — judge by the data, not by what is inked.

✅ Sample — an operator in its own track

The Outlook table prints $5.70 Billion | +/- | $300 Million as three ruled cells, and 1.26 Billion spanning all three on the last row. The +/- track is the range dash of this rule in another costume: one value, one cell. Merged, the GAAP and Non-GAAP ranges each become one column and the reconciling amount sits between them; the row labels are bold.

✅ Sample — a line-number column in the middle

LINE # runs 1 to 22 in a column between the labels and the first year, not at the left edge. A marker gutter keeps its column wherever the page puts it. The column headers are italic except FOR THE PERIOD ENDED; the empty spacer track between 2023 and 2024 prints nothing and is not a column.

✅ Sample — v. in its own track

A court daily list: time, case number and party, v., the other party, hearing type. The v. column carries the same token on every row that has two parties and nothing on the rows that do not — a separator track, like the range dash, so it joins the two parties in one cell. Rows with a single In the matter of… line then take the same shape.

9.4.2 Header Body Column Count Mismatch

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-header-body-column-count-mismatch · tables columns repair

✅ Normative

Every row of a table MUST carry the full column count. Where the header and the body disagree, the short side MUST be padded with empty cells, one per missing position, and MUST NOT be padded with a duplicated or invented value.

Header:  | Duration | Factor | Trend |     ← 3 columns
Body:    | 1        | 0.94   |             ← Trend all-blank → body reads as 2
         | 2        | 0.91   |
Header wider than the body

The usual cause is a column whose body is uniform or empty — all 1.000, all blank, all —. The column MUST be restored as cells, empty where the page prints nothing, and its header label MUST be kept: a column proven only by its header still exists (Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1).

Header narrower than the body

The usual cause is a missed span in the header: a group label that carries a colspan, or a stub that takes a rowspan. The header's spans SHOULD be re-read against the page before the body is treated as the side that is short.

Padding
  • Padding MUST be individual empty cells, one per missing position — not a span across the gap. A span claims the page merged those cells; it did not, they were simply not printed. The same reasoning pads a jagged half cell by cell in Triangles and Matrix Tables§9.8.2.
  • Body cells MUST NOT be fabricated or duplicated to reach a count. An empty cell asserts nothing; a copied value asserts something false about the page. Where it cannot be decided which side is wrong, the output renders the cells that are printed and pads with empty cells rather than guess at content.
✅ Sample — 702

The header declares four price columns ($2,000–$5,000). Rows like Corporal Punishment print one merged note — "Medical Payments Not Available" — spanning all four instead of per-column values, and parent rows such as 612. Owned Watercraft Liability Coverage print no values at all: their four value positions are empty cells. The coverage labels are indented up to three steps.

9.5 Rows and cells

9.5.1 Blank and Spacer Rows

⚖️ Equivalent forms · 📄 page rule

tables-blank-and-spacer-rows · tables either rows disputed

⚖️ Equivalent forms

A genuinely printed blank row inside a table MAY be rendered as an empty row or left out; both forms conform, and a document MUST use one of them throughout. A blank row that is the only thing separating two groups of rows SHOULD be rendered as an empty row.

| ROU assets total   | 10,234 |
|                    |        |   ← printed blank row: on this page it is the
| Lease liabilities: |        |     only section boundary — rendered as an empty row
When the blank row is load-bearing

On a page with no rules, no bands and no repeated headers, the whitespace is the structure. Dropping a blank row there merges two sections the page deliberately kept apart — as in a lease note where a single blank line is all that separates the right-of-use totals from "Lease liabilities:".

  • A blank row whose removal would change how a reader groups the rows around it SHOULD be rendered as a row of empty cells, in its printed position.
  • A purely decorative blank line — even spacing between every row, padding at the foot of a block — carries no such meaning and MAY be left out.
  • An empty row MUST NOT be rendered where the page prints none: the row is kept because it is printed, never added to make groups easier to read.
✅ Sample — ert

A genuinely printed blank row separates the 00xx class codes from the 01xx codes, in every block; it is kept as a row of empty cells. The four side-by-side CLASS CODE | ELR | D RATIO blocks continue one class-code series, so each block is its own table (see Column Continuation§9.2.2); the first is shown.

✅ Sample — lakecruise

In the long-cruise timetable, a fully empty row is printed between the outbound run ending at Seeblick ○ and the return run starting at Seeblick; it is the only boundary between the two direction segments and is kept. Stop rows printed in heavier type are bold cell by cell. The header symbol under each service number is ⊛.

✅ Sample — 2012_tushin_nittei

A thin printed empty row sits between the 12:05–35 block and the 13:00 block, the only thing separating the morning heats from the afternoon semi-finals; it is kept.

❌ Counter-sample — e22

Blank rows are the only separation between the Experience Period, Annual … Trend and Projected groups; they are kept. A rendering that drops them runs the three groups together; it still conforms, but draws a warning. The red ($8.75) already carries its sign in the parentheses, so the colour is decoration and is not rendered.

❌ Counter-sample — 3samehead

Printed blank lines separate the cohort blocks and set off the Average Issue Age line. The bold cohort bands already separate the blocks, so these spacers MAY be dropped; they are kept here. The rendering below drops them, and it also records 10.9% for the 2004+ share of premium where the page prints 32031.9%, and splits the Issue Year band into a label cell and empty cells although the page prints one full-width band. Each ruled Total row is a total, so its label cell is a <th> and the stub carries levels (all 0: nothing is indented).

❌ Counter-sample — 3cell

Printed gaps sit under the BUILDINGS / OCCUPIED BY OWNER band, around the BUS. PERS. PROP. band and between Group 5 and Group 6; the last is the only thing splitting the rate groups in two, so it is kept, and the others are kept with it. The BUS. PERS. PROP. band prints its label in its own ruled cell with one empty cell across the rest of the row, so it is not a full-width span. The trailing gap under Group 10 is padding and is not shown.

Encoding an empty region

The encoding of an empty region is free. Its existence is not.

  • An empty region inside a table body MAY be encoded as individual empty <td> cells or as one blank cell spanning it (colspan / rowspan): three leading empty <td>s per row and one colspan="3" rowspan="8" blank block render identically, and both conform. Where the page draws no separation inside the empty region, neither encoding is preferred.
  • Carve-out: in a loss triangle or similar matrix, every empty position MUST be its own empty cell, never part of a span — each is a distinct, meaningful absence. See Triangles and Matrix Tables§9.8.2.
  • The half that is not free: the cells and columns MUST exist. A column proven only by its header still exists (Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1), and every value in it MUST stay reachable. Encoding is a choice; deletion is an error.
  • Blank space beside a header label is not free: it MUST be rendered as separate empty cells, not as an extended span, unless the page prints a genuinely merged cell. See Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1.

9.5.2 Nested Tables

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-nested-tables · tables encoding rare

✅ Normative

A small grid printed inside one cell of a table MUST be rendered by subdividing that cell into the outer table's own grid: the inner grid's cells become rows and columns of the outer table, and the neighbouring cells span them. The output MUST NOT contain a nested <table> element, and MUST NOT flatten the inner grid into text.

A cell that itself contains a small grid: a fee schedule inside a plan-comparison cell, a mini-table of components inside one row of a summary.

| Plan | Fees                          |
| A    | ┌ admin │ 0.25% ┐            |
|      | └ fund  │ 0.10% ┘   ← a table inside the cell
Recognising a nested table

The inner grid has its own alignment: two or more columns of its own, sometimes its own header row, and its own row boundaries that do not line up with the outer table's rows. That is what separates it from a cell that merely holds several lines of text, which is governed by Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells§9.5.3.

Rendering

The inner grid's cells MUST become real cells of the outer table, and every cell alongside it MUST span the rows it now occupies:

<tr>
  <td rowspan="2">A</td>
  <td>admin</td><td>0.25%</td>
</tr>
<tr>
  <td>fund</td><td>0.10%</td>
</tr>

A is printed once and genuinely covers both fee rows, so rowspan="2" is a true statement about the page — the same test Repeated Identical Values§9.5.4 applies everywhere else.

  • No nested <table>. A nested table makes the inner grid invisible to anything that walks the outer one: cell counts, column arithmetic and per-cell boxes all stop at the <td> boundary. Subdividing keeps every value addressable at the same level as the rest of the table, and the outer grid still reconciles — see the leaf-track check in Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3.
  • Pairs MUST survive. The pairing inside the inner grid is the data: admin goes with 0.25% and fund with 0.10%. An encoding that lists all the labels and then all the values has destroyed the table; so has flattening the cell to <br/>-separated text.

This is one of several cases that need HTML tables rather than pipe tables, which cannot express the spans this rule depends on (see Markdown Rendering§3.2). The others are spans in Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3, full-width band rows in Bands Inside the Grid§9.2.1, and level markers on the stub in Row-Label Hierarchy§9.5.5.

✅ Sample — en

The left two columns form an embedded Section / Marks mini-table, with its own Summative Assessment II / 30% heading row, while a single ruled cell on the right spans all five of its rows and prints nothing. The TOTAL row is bold.

✅ Sample — korean-curriculum

A rowspan-6 단 원 별 교 육 내 용 stub encloses its own mini-grid — complete with a shaded header row 단원(제목) / 시수 / 교육내용 — inside the outer table. The shaded label cells on the left are bold; the two bulleted cells print • bullets.

Related
  • Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells§9.5.3 — a cell holding several lines of text, not a grid
  • Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3 — the leaf-track check that a subdivided grid still passes
  • Repeated Identical Values§9.5.4 — the same "printed once, spans several rows" test

9.5.3 Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-record-groups-and-multi-line-cells · tables encoding rowspan

✅ Normative

Independently printed records MUST each be rendered as their own row, with rowspan only on cells the page genuinely merged. One prose cell MUST stay one cell, with <br/> between its title and its paragraph. In a boxed row holding lists in several columns, lines that pair up one-to-one MUST be separate rows, and a list whose neighbours print a single value for the whole list MUST stay in one cell, <br/>-joined, beside that value.

Printed boxed row:        Rendered:
| Products   | States |   | MoneyGuard | AL         |
| MoneyGuard | AL     |   | MG II      | AK<br/>AZ  |
| MG II      | AK     |
|            | AZ     |
A record spanning several printed lines

Each printed line of the record MUST be its own row, and the cells genuinely shared across those lines MUST carry a rowspan.

  • The record's lines MUST NOT be <br/>-joined into one row.
  • A blank continuation cell MUST NOT stand where a rowspan belongs.
  • The lines MUST NOT be rewritten — Owner: and Extended printed on two lines do not become Owner: Extended. The verbatim line structure is part of the output.
✅ Sample — sln

SL Nos 6, 7, 10 and 11 each print one number and one item name against several separately ruled Material / Diameter / Thickness sub-rows, so those two cells take a rowspan; every sub-row has its own empty Bidder's Response box.

✅ Sample — yep

The category and score cells are printed once against four activity rows, so they take a rowspan across them.

Parallel lists across several columns of one boxed row

When one boxed row holds several columns, each with its own vertical list, what decides the rendering is how the lines pair up across the columns:

  • Lines that pair up one-to-one — line i of one column beside line i of the next, each line a record of its own (English Language Paper 1 · 0815 – 0925 h · 1 h 10 min) — MUST each be their own <tr>. <br/>-joining them destroys which value belongs to which line.
  • A list whose neighbours print a single value for the whole list — eight papers beside one time and one duration; two states beside one product — is one record: the list MUST stay in one cell, <br/>-joined, beside that single value. Splitting it into rows would attach the value to the first line only.
  • A boxed row may hold both: MoneyGuard pairs with AL one-to-one, while MG II is printed once beside the list AK, AZ.

This is not the same as a line break inside a single cell, which follows.

In-cell lists and line wraps

These are inside one cell, and here more than one rendering conforms:

Printed Rendering
Bullet list in a cell <ul><li>…</li></ul> or <br/>• before each item; both conform
Two deliberate printed lines in a label kept as <br/>
Incidental word-wrap in a label flattened to one string, joined with a space
Break the page does not settle either rendering conforms
A label and its value packed into one cell, where the page does not settle whether they are two columns (N =, Z =) one cell or two existing columns; both conform

None of this licenses collapsing lines that pair up one-to-one across columns: <br/>-joining that case is an error.

✅ Sample — we

An exam timetable: each date is printed once against its boxed sub-rows and takes a rowspan. Where papers, times and durations pair up line by line (Thursday, Friday, Tuesday), each line is a record and gets its own row. Where a list of papers shares one printed time and duration (Monday, Wednesday), the list stays in one cell, <br/>-joined, beside that time.

✅ Sample — 2012_tushin_tyuui

練習 cells hold two stacked numbers joined by <br/>, and the 男子/女子 stubs span three and two rows.

✅ Sample — detector-computing

Bulleted sub-items stacked inside single cells, each item on its own printed line after a • bullet. The row labels in the shaded first column are bold.

When rowspan is right and when it is wrong

Rowspan is the required rendering here and the error in Repeated Identical Values§9.5.4. The discriminator is whether the page actually merged the cell: a value printed once against several lines takes a rowspan; a value printed separately on each line is that many cells.

A row label that wraps

The one-row-per-printed-line requirement is about records. A stub label that merely wraps — Increase (Decrease) in Accounts Payable / and Accrued Liabilities, value on the second line — MUST be one row, its label joined with a space. The tell is that the wrapped lines read as one phrase and only one of them carries values.

✅ Sample — wrapped stub labels in a cash-flow statement

Three labels wrap: the bold RECONCILIATION OF OPERATING INCOME (LOSS) TO / NET CASH FROM OPERATING ACTIVITIES band, Adjustments to Reconcile Operating Income (Loss) to Net / Cash Used in Operating Activities (no value), and Increase (Decrease) in Accounts Payable / and Accrued Liabilities (values beside the second line). Each is one row. - stands for zero throughout; the column headers are bold and underlined, and the $ gutter joins its value.

A cell holding a title and a paragraph

A single ruled prose cell MUST stay one cell in one row. Its title keeps its printed emphasis and MUST be separated from its paragraph by <br/>; values stacked in the adjacent cell are kept in that cell, joined with <br/>. Only independently printed records are split into rows.

✅ Sample — a cell holding a title and a paragraph

Each Description cell prints a bold underlined title, then two or three lines of plain explanation; the City Personnel cell beside it stacks two values, (3)P over (2)NP. One <tr> per printed line would split the title from its text and the two personnel figures from each other. The Total Agency Program row is bold.

✅ Sample — paragraphs inside one cell

The Model cell for the data acquisition system holds three paragraphs separated by blank lines; the Description cells print [must be on approved list] in brackets.

  • Nested Tables§9.5.2 — a grid inside a cell, not lines of text

9.5.4 Repeated Identical Values

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-repeated-identical-values · tables rowspan failure-mode

✅ Normative

A rowspan MUST be used only where the page genuinely merged the cell. A value printed k times at k distinct vertical positions MUST be rendered as k cells; repeated content MUST NOT be merged.

"82.13%" printed nine separate times, "Data Page" repeated down a column, the same rate on every row — the temptation is to collapse them into one spanning cell. That output is non-conforming.

Printed (9 separate lines):    Non-conforming output:
| 1 | 82.13% |                 | 1 | [rowspan=9]82.13%  |
| 2 | 82.13% |                 | 2 | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE  |  ← merges a value
| … | 82.13% |                 | … | ROW_SPAN_CONTINUE  |    printed 9 times
Why merging is wrong, not just different

A rowspan is a claim about the page: "these cells are one cell." When the page printed nine cells, that claim is false — the never invent failure. Anyone counting records downstream then gets one where the document has nine, and the loss is invisible because the output still looks well-formed. A span that cannot be pointed to on the page is an error even when the values under it are right.

Deciding from the geometry

The decision MUST be taken from where the value is printed, not from how the column reads:

  • one printed occurrence spanning several rows → one cell with a rowspan;
  • distinct vertical positions → separate cells, one per row.

A column of identical values is exactly where the eye stops resolving lines, so the word positions on the page, not an impression of the column, settle it (see Boxes and Granularity§3.3). For the opposite case — where the page really did merge a cell across a multi-line record — see Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells§9.5.3.

✅ Sample — star

* printed dozens of times down every column, each on its own ruled row, so each is its own cell rather than a rowspan.

✅ Sample — aao

523 repeats down a zip-to-zone column for dozens of rows, each on its own ruled row and kept separate — and the run is broken by 323 at 85922 and 423 at 85931, which a merge would bury.

✅ Sample — ymm

2025 on every row of the Year column, never collapsed. Every body cell prints blue, underlined text; the legend above the table says blue means add/change. The underline is rendered as <u>; how the colour itself is carried is governed by Text Colors§7.3.12 and is not shown here.

✅ Sample — 0p

25.0% / 12.0% / 0.0% repeat down whole columns of a headerless table, every row its own <tr>.

✅ Sample — 10k

New York Stock Exchange repeated eleven times down the third column, each a distinct cell.

✅ Sample — waiox

Long runs of 0 in a claims triangle, kept as separate cells.

  • Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 — the same never drop, never invent discipline for columns

9.5.5 Row-Label Hierarchy

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-row-label-hierarchy · tables rule hierarchy encoding

✅ Normative

Where a table's row labels are indented to show nesting, every label cell MUST carry its absolute level as a data-level attribute: <td data-level="2">iPhone</td>. Level 0 is the leftmost label position in the stub column, 1 the next indent step, and so on — counted from the left edge of the column, never from the row above.

Financial statements and rate manuals encode hierarchy by indenting the row label. Flattened, "iPhone" and "Total net sales" read as siblings.

Printed stub:                     Rendered as:
Revenue                           <td data-level="0">Revenue</td>
  Products                        <td data-level="1">Products</td>
    iPhone          205,489       <td data-level="2">iPhone</td>
Total net sales     383,285       <th data-level="0">Total net sales</th>

A table whose indented labels all come out at the same level is the failure this rule exists to prevent.

Why flattening is dangerous

The flattened output is well-formed and looks correct. Nothing signals that a parent/child relationship was dropped, so a reader summing the column double-counts: iPhone is inside Total net sales, and the flattened table gives no way to know it. The damage is silent, which is why the indentation MUST be preserved even where the choice of encoding seems secondary.

❌ Counter-sample — 3cc

Structure lost. Under KVO shareholder the page indents two children, Renewable and Nuclear. The rendering below flattens them, leaving a second Renewable with no parent, and it also records 25 for KVO shareholder where the page prints 2.5. The total row is bold across all three cells.

Reading the level
  • The level MUST be the number of indent steps between the left edge of the stub column and the start of the label as printed. The leftmost label position is 0; each further indent step adds one. A level can therefore be checked against a single row without reading any other.
  • The label text MUST stay verbatim and the rows MUST stay in printed order.
  • Where a table carries levels, every label cell in its stub that prints a label MUST carry one, level-0 rows included. A table whose stub shows no nesting — no indentation, no "of which" rows — and has no labelled total carries none.
Absolute, not relative

A level is read off the print, never inherited from the row above:

  • A row following a level-2 row is level 3 only if the page indents it further. At the same indent it is another level-2 sibling.
  • A row MAY jump back several levels at once. Total net sales returning to 0 after an iPhone at 2 is normal and needs no marker of its own.
Not from the numbers

A level MUST NOT be deepened because the arithmetic suggests a row is a component, and MUST NOT be flattened because the arithmetic does not add up. The indentation is the evidence; the values are not. A page whose sub-items do not sum to their parent is transcribed as printed.

Not as leading whitespace

The level MUST be carried as an attribute, not as leading spaces or &nbsp;: the first trim, Markdown render or CSV round-trip removes whitespace and the structure goes with it. Where an output format cannot carry a cell attribute, the level SHOULD go into a dedicated level column rather than into whitespace.

Recognising a child row

A child is indented relative to the row above it, and its value is a component of a figure elsewhere in the column rather than an independent record. Phrases such as "out of which", "of which" and "within which" state the same relationship in words; a row introduced by one MUST be rendered as a child even where its indentation is slight. The same page may present a breakdown as an indented stub or as a row that decomposes into sub-rows; both are the same phenomenon and are rendered the same way.

A total row takes a level like any other row, usually 0; how its label cell is marked is defined in Total and Subtotal Rows§9.5.6.

✅ Sample — table-with-breakdown

"- Out of which amount written off" is indented under "Amount involved in frauds": it is a component of that figure, not a peer, so it is level 1. The header labels wrap only for width.

✅ Sample — 702

Rule numbers nest into numbered and lettered sub-items: 609. Designated Business Pursuits › 3. Teachers › a. Lab, etc. / b. not otherwise classified / c. Corporal Punishment. The coverage labels sit at four printed indent positions, levels 0 to 3; the rule-number column is not part of the label hierarchy. Labels that wrap at the column edge are joined.

✅ Sample — yellow

Numbered parents (1)–(10) with indented lettered children — (A) Short / (B) Intermediate / (C) Long, (A) Dividends / (B) Capital gains — and an indented, unlettered dividends under (5) Preferred stock. The yellow fill marks input cells and carries no value, so it is not rendered.

✅ Sample — sssa

Ticket and Transactions are indented under the Same Shop Sales parent rows. The parent rows are bold in every cell, values included; the stub header Fiscal year ending December, is italic and not bold. Most percentages print a space before %, a few do not — kept as printed.

✅ Sample — dt1

Bold TAMI / Professional Services parents over italic children (TAMI, Technology, …). The page prints no indentation: every label starts at the same left edge, so every row is level 0. The parent/child distinction is carried only by weight and slant, which apply to every cell of those rows and are rendered per cell. The table closes with a TOTAL row, so its stub carries levels.

✅ Sample — P200509160137_0137_6519

細分 breakdown：批發 Wholesale and 其中 within which：航空運輸 Air transport open breakdowns of the bold category above them. The page prints no indentation; the relationship is stated in words, so each breakdown row is level 1, and the plain-weight rows that continue the same breakdown (零售 Retail, 陸上運輸 Land transport, 海運 Maritime transport) are level 1 with it.

Two more stub shapes
Two-column stubs

Where a table sets sub-labels in a second stub column to the right of the parent label, one per line, each with its own values, the output MUST render a two-column stub: the parent label in the first column, spanning its children with a rowspan where the page prints it as one cell, and each sub-label in the second column on its own row.

✅ Sample — a stub split into two columns

Unallocated interest charges sits in the first stub column, one ruled cell tall enough for both sub-labels, with – external and – intra-group in a second column to its right, each with its own values; the 6 months 2024 cell of – external is empty. Every group on the page closes with an unlabelled bold total. No label is indented, so every label — in either stub column — is level 0; the closing grand total is a labelled total, so its label cell is a <th>.

✅ Sample — values staggered inside one column

A Japanese profit-and-loss statement with one 金額 (amount) column: parent amounts right-aligned at the column edge, children set further left, and （うち…） ("of which") sub-items further left still. One value column. The stagger is styling; the hierarchy is carried only by the stub's data-level: the bold categories are 0, their items 1, and the （うち…） rows, introduced by "of which", 2.

✅ Sample — a two-column stub, ruled

Statutory turnover and Proportionate EBITDA sit in the first stub column; – NorthStar Wireless and – Other Americas in a second column beside each, one per line, each with values; an unlabelled bold subtotal closes each pair. Here the rules run across the first column between the two lines, so Proportionate EBITDA and (before exceptional items) are two cells, not one spanning cell.

9.5.6 Total and Subtotal Rows

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-total-and-subtotal-rows · tables rule semantics rows

✅ Normative

In a total or subtotal row, the label cell MUST be a <th> and the value cells MUST stay <td>. The label cell MUST carry the row's absolute level as data-level, read as for the stub hierarchy — a top-level total is data-level="0". Label and values MUST be kept exactly as printed, bold only where the page prints them bold.

| iPhone          | 205,489 |
| Mac             |  29,357 |
| **Total**       | 234,846 |   ← bold + a double rule above it
The rendering
<tr><td data-level="1">iPhone</td><td>205,489</td></tr>
<tr><td data-level="1">Mac</td><td>29,357</td></tr>
<tr><th data-level="0">Total</th><td>234,846</td></tr>
  • The <th> states that the cell labels rather than reports.
  • data-level records the printed absolute indentation of the label, counted from the left edge of the stub as in Row-Label Hierarchy§9.5.5; because a total carries a level, every label cell of its stub carries one too.
  • The level MUST be the printed one even where it contradicts the apparent grouping — a total set further right than the items it sums keeps that deeper level. Arithmetic membership MUST NOT be inferred from indentation, and indentation MUST NOT be adjusted to fit the arithmetic.
  • A total row whose label position prints nothing has no label cell to mark: it MUST be rendered with an empty <td></td> there — never an invented Total and never an empty <th>.
A <th> is a per-cell decision

A row can be part header, part data, and a total row is exactly that: a heading cell on the left and reported values to its right. Marking the whole row <th> would claim the numbers are headings; marking none of it loses the distinction between the cell that names the aggregate and the cells that report it. Both are non-conforming.

The same holds in reverse for a full-width band or divider row, where every cell is heading and none is data — see Bands Inside the Grid§9.2.1 and Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3.

Recognising one

A total or subtotal row usually carries three tells at once: a label that names an aggregate ("Total", "Total net sales", "5 YR. TOTAL"), a rule or double rule printed above it, and bold or otherwise emphasised type. Any one alone is weak evidence — bold is applied unreliably in both directions (Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2) — but together they are reliable.

✅ Sample — warn

Several bold, ruled totals in one balance sheet — Total current assets, Total assets, Total current liabilities, Total liabilities, Total … stockholders' equity, Total equity. No label is indented, so every level is 0. The italic stub heading is not bold.

✅ Sample — dt1

A bold, ruled TOTAL row closes the relocation summary (923 · 100% · 24,582,483 · 100%).

✅ Sample — 3tables2

A bold 5 YR. TOTAL row closes each class block. Each class block and the credibility grid under it are separately framed with a gap between them, so they are separate tables; the first class block is shown.

✅ Sample — en

A bold, ruled TOTAL 90 50% row closes the weightage table.

✅ Sample — 3t

A bold 1997-2017 summary row under a rule closes each cohort block; its label names the whole vintage range the rows above divide up.

Row order and table sections
  • Every row MUST stay in printed order. A total MUST NOT be moved to fit a table section.
  • <thead>, <tbody> and <tfoot> wrappers MAY be used or omitted; they do not change the cells or their values, and th versus td is still decided per cell.
  • Totals printed outside the table frame are governed by Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1.
More shapes
✅ Sample — a total row with no label at all

The taxation table closes with 834 / 752 under a rule, in bold, with an empty label cell: nothing prints where Total would go. The label cell is <td></td> — no label, so no <th> and no invented Total. The rule and the bold are the only tells. The June 30, 2003 column is bold throughout.

✅ Sample — a total set further right than its children

Each Total is centred well to the right of the items it sums, twice on the page. Total other comprehensive income (loss) starts just right of the item labels and Comprehensive income between the two. Read by where each label starts, the page has four label positions, levels 0 to 3, and every total is deeper than its children; those printed levels are kept.

✅ Sample — rows printed after the total that it does not include

Total closes the Global Sales Volume block, then USA and Australia follow at the same indent as Japan and Europe. They are memo lines — USA sits inside North America — not components of the total. They stay in the same table, in printed order, at the level their indent prints; splitting them off into a second table is non-conforming.

✅ Sample — a scanned lease table with an unlabelled total

Note 6: four years and four amounts under a lone $ header, then 130,220 under a double rule, with no label at all — so its label cell is empty. Note 5 above it is a borderless statement whose Balance, end of year total sits under a double rule, not bold. The printed rules are not rows.

✅ Sample — a total label printed in the town column

A county / municipality / count list continued from an earlier page. Each ASHFORD Total, BRANDYWINE Total label is set in bold, right-aligned inside the municipality column, with the sum in the count column. The label stays in that column as a <th>; it starts to the right of the municipality names, so its level is 1.

✅ Sample — a subtotal label in the unit column

Row A prints SUM OF ITEMS 1 THRU 4 in the description column and SUBTOTAL in the UNIT column, with the sum under TOTAL; row B prints TOTAL BID = in one cell spanning the unit, quantity and unit-cost columns. The label is split across columns the page uses for other things; each part stays in the column it is printed in, and the label cells are <th>.

9.6 Cell values

9.6.1 Accounting Number Formats

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-accounting-number-formats · tables fidelity numbers

✅ Normative

Every number in a cell MUST be transcribed exactly as printed — parentheses, currency dashes, separators and change markers included. The output MUST NOT carry a normalised twin of the value beside it, and MUST NOT replace the printed form with a normalised one.

Accounting pages print numbers in shapes that look as if they ask to be tidied up. They do not: the cell is copied character for character.

Printed:     (1,204)    $—     n/m     1.204,50 (EU)     △2.5%
Verbatim:    (1,204)    $—     n/m     1.204,50          △2.5%
Normalized:  -1204      0?     null?   1204.50           +2.5%? -2.5%?
Requirements
Printed form Requirement
Parenthesised negative — (1,204), (2.0)%, ($8.75) MUST keep its parentheses; MUST NOT be rewritten with a minus sign.
Leading minus — -50.009 MUST stay a leading minus; MUST NOT be converted into parentheses. The page's convention is the one recorded.
Currency and percent dashes — $—, — % MUST stay dashes, with their currency or percent sign.
Placeholders — n/m, NM, anything printed in place of a figure MUST be transcribed as written.
Separators — 1.074.778, 1.204,50 MUST stay as printed: thousands points stay points, a decimal comma stays a comma, and no separator is removed or swapped for the other convention.
Change markers — △2.5% MUST stay attached to the number, in the same cell.

Spacing printed inside a value — 3.8 %, $ 17,565.8 — is part of the printed form and is kept.

✅ Sample — sssa

Negative percentages as (2.0)% and (8.3)%, and elsewhere with a space before the percent sign, (2.6) %, (3.5) % — each kept as printed. The two parent rows are bold in every cell; Ticket and Transactions are indented under them.

✅ Sample — e22

Parenthesised negatives printed in red — ($8.75), ($11.99). The parentheses already carry the sign, so the red is decoration and the text is kept as printed. The column headings are bold as a row; Rx Claim Information is also underlined.

✅ Sample — entwick

German conventions: 1.074.778 with thousands points, and -50.009 with a leading minus rather than parentheses. Cells the page leaves blank stay empty. The column headings wrap inside words at printed hyphens (Kapital- / rücklagen), so each is one label; the closing row is bold.

Why no normalised twin

A cleaned-up value beside the printed one looks free to produce and saves every consumer the same work. It is refused for two reasons.

Normalisation here is not a transformation, it is a guess. A "clean" column would have to decide things the page does not say: is $— zero, or not applicable? Is n/m null, an empty string, or a string literal? Does △2.5% mean up or down — the triangle's direction is conventional and the sign is not printed at all. A twin column would carry three guesses dressed as data, and nothing downstream distinguishes a guessed value from a read one.

A second value is a second thing to be wrong. The printed form is verifiable against the page; the derived form is verifiable only against whatever rules produced it. A consumer that needs a number applies its own conventions to the printed string — and it knows its own conventions, which the producer does not.

Hence: one value per cell, and it is the one on the page. Verbatim leaves the interpretation to whoever consumes the table, the only place it can be made safely.

✅ Sample — yef

$ — for a nil value beside (626.6) parenthesised negatives, and a bare — in the rows below. The page sets a space between $ and the figure, and it is kept. The year line is a bold band across the grid, rendered as a spanning header cell.

✅ Sample — wdb

(8)%, NM and — % in one table — three different ways of writing not a number here, each kept as printed. The years sit on the second header line with an empty ruled cell beneath them, so they take no rowspan. The row labels are bold; the Total revenues and Adjusted EBITDA rows are bold in every cell.

9.6.2 Bold and Italic Inside Tables

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-bold-and-italic-inside-tables · tables formatting

✅ Normative

Inside a table, bold, italic and underline MUST be marked per cell, and only where the printed glyphs of that cell are heavier, slanted or underlined. A whole column or a whole header row MUST NOT be styled on principle. Inside an HTML table cell, bold MUST be written <strong>, italic <em> and underline <u>.

The same holds for strikeout and coloured text: they are properties of the glyphs in one cell, not of the role that cell plays.

Page bolds one column:        Over-bolded output:
| **Doc** | Status |          | **Doc** | **Status** |
| **A-1** | Filed  |          | **A-1** | **Filed**  |

The block on the right is the error this rule exists to prevent: the page bolds a single column, and every cell came back bold.

Markup inside a cell

Emphasis inside a table cell is written with HTML elements, not Markdown ** and *. Strikeout inside a cell follows Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7.

Printed Rendering in a cell
Bold <td><strong>Net sales</strong></td>
Italic <td><em>P. abyssalis</em></td>
Bold and italic <td><em><strong>All other plans</strong></em></td>
Underlined <th><u>Rx Claim Information</u></th>
Styling on part of a cell only that run: <td><em>ZRK2</em> kinase inhibitor</td>
  • **…** and *…* MUST NOT be used inside a table cell.
  • The markup MUST cover exactly the styled run. A cell that is bold throughout wraps its whole content; a cell with one bold word wraps that word.
Header rows

A <th> cell states the cell's role, not its weight. Where every cell of the header rows is printed in the same weight, that shared weight SHOULD NOT be repeated as <strong> in each header cell — that styles the header row on principle. A header cell whose glyphs differ from the rest of the header — an italic stub heading, an underlined label, one bold heading among regular ones — MUST carry that difference.

Deciding cell by cell
  1. The structure — rows, columns, header tiers — is read first, blind to weight and slant.
  2. Styling is then taken from the glyphs of each cell, one cell at a time.

Weight differences are often subtle, so a cell is judged against its neighbours rather than on its own. Where it cannot be told whether a cell is heavier, the cell SHOULD be left unstyled: an unmarked cell loses a nuance, a wrongly marked one asserts something the page does not say.

✅ Sample — 70th

Only the rate-value cells are bold; the plan-design cells beside them are not. Per cell, as printed — though the weight difference is subtle on the page, which is part of why producers over-apply it. The column headings are bold as a whole header, so they carry no <strong>; each is one wrapped label.

✅ Sample — single

Only the three Tarnwick Capital Partners index rows are bold — per row, not blanket. Their labels are printed in mixed case and end in a superscript 1. One label wraps at the column edge and is joined.

✅ Sample — spa

ZRK2 and P. abyssalis (P. abyssalis) italicised within otherwise plain cells — per run, not per cell. The phase labels printed in coloured pills are bold; the pill colour repeats what the text says and is not carried.

✅ Sample — 3r

One stub cell bold only, the next bold and italic — a genuine per-cell style distinction. The column headings share one weight and carry no <strong>.

✅ Sample — e1

Two independent sources of weight in one table: the shaded 2005 columns are bold in every row, and five whole rows (Net sales, both excluding items affecting comparability rows, Income for the period, Value creation) are bold across every cell. Each cell is marked from its own glyphs. The stub heading is italic as well as bold, so it alone among the headings carries <em>.

The same error, seen from both ends

Over-styling comes from reasoning about the category — "this is a header, headers are bold" — instead of from the glyphs. The mirror image is in Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1: a band that is not bold gets missed because a header is expected to be bold.

Both are prevented by the same discipline: detect structure blind to styling, and take styling from the glyphs.

Related
  • Bold and Italics§7.2.1 — the same rule outside tables, in Markdown syntax
  • Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 — the mirror error: structure missed because it is not bold
  • Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7 — strikeout is also a per-glyph property
  • Total and Subtotal Rows§9.5.6 — bold total rows are styled from their glyphs, cell by cell
  • Highlighted Text§7.2.5 — highlighting inside tables follows the same per-cell discipline

9.6.3 Cell Text Fidelity

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-cell-text-fidelity · tables fidelity ocr

✅ Normative

The text of a cell MUST be what the rendered page shows — not the text layer, not OCR, and not what the value ought to be. A character that cannot be read at any zoom MUST be written as [illegible], never as a plausible guess.

The text layer and the rendered image disagree at the character level far more often than expected, and the cost of a single wrong digit depends entirely on who reads the table. The text layer is a hint about roughly what is there; the image decides.

Three cells that were read wrong

In each of these the transcription and the OCR agreed with each other — and a zoomed view of the page proved both wrong:

printed 0.99        → transcribed 0.98      (Age-to-Ultimate factor)
printed 2012.5-(A)  → transcribed 2013.5-(A)
printed 1.0400^(W)  → transcribed 1.04009^(W)

A disputed cell SHOULD be settled from a zoomed crop of the cell or from the word coordinates, and MUST NOT be settled by plausibility. "Plausible" is exactly what produced all three errors above: 0.98 is a perfectly reasonable factor.

❌ Counter-sample — 3samehead

A plausible value substituted for the printed one. The page prints 32031.9% for the 2004+ % of Premium cell; the non-conforming output records 10.9%. The wrong value is the believable one — exactly the failure this rule prevents. The section lines (Issue Year, Issue Age) are bands across the grid.

What is printed is what is written
  • Typos stay. A word misspelled inside a cell MUST keep its misspelling.
  • Numbers are copied digit by digit, with thousands and decimal separators exactly as printed. See Accounting Number Formats§9.6.1.
  • Wrapped codes are not fused with their neighbours. In a narrow column a code can wrap onto two lines, or two short codes can sit in neighbouring cells and look like one. The column boundaries and the cell's span decide: fusing B-2 with VC, or TR-1 with TR-2, is an error, and it also throws off the column count of the whole row.
  • A blank cell stays empty. A cell that prints nothing MUST be rendered empty; a dash MUST NOT be supplied because the column has dashes elsewhere.
❌ Counter-sample — 3cc

The page prints 2.5 for the KVO shareholder TWh figure; the non-conforming output records 25 — a dropped decimal point, silently. Renewable and Nuclear below it are indented one step; the total row is bold.

❌ Counter-sample — entwick

The reverse error: in the Rückkauf eigener Anteile row the Eigene Anteile cell is printed blank, and the non-conforming output invents an em dash for it.

Characters the image cannot tell apart

Some characters are visually identical and no zoom separates them: µ (U+00B5) and μ (U+03BC), a non-breaking space and an ordinary space, a minus sign and a hyphen.

  • The output MUST keep the visible form and the character count exactly as printed, and SHOULD use the character normally typed for that glyph.
  • The text layer MUST NOT be used to break the tie: it is a hint about the content, never the authority on it.
  • A consumer or checker MUST treat the members of each family below as equal, so the choice among them cannot make an output non-conforming.
Family Written as
µ (U+00B5) ≡ μ (U+03BC) either
non-breaking space ≡ ordinary space an ordinary space
minus sign (U+2212) ≡ hyphen-minus -
non-breaking hyphen ≡ hyphen-minus -
figure dash, en dash ≡ hyphen, inside a numeric range either

The image outranks every other source on what is printed. Where two codepoints are indistinguishable there is no fact about the page for it to be authoritative over — µ and μ are the same ink. The visible form is fidelity and stays exact; the codepoint underneath is a serialisation detail.

A dash that is doing something is not a homoglyph question. An em dash alone in a cell is a value — see Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 — and a struck-through digit is not a character variant at all.

✅ Sample — a true minus sign

−742 and −2,710 are set with a true minus sign rather than a hyphen, beside — for nil. The minus sign is written as the hyphen-minus -; the em dashes stay em dashes. The header cells are genuinely merged across two rows and wrapped labels are joined; the Net Sales and Other Items bands are bold where the headings are not.

What else rests on the image
  • Duplicated Tables§9.2.4 — the rendered page decides whether a repeated table is really printed twice.
  • Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7 — OCR silently joins a struck value to its replacement and produces a number that appears nowhere on the page. Only the image catches it.

  • Accounting Number Formats§9.6.1 — verbatim numbers, signs and separators
  • Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7 — the image separates a struck value from its replacement
  • Duplicated Tables§9.2.4 — the image decides whether a table is printed twice
  • Borderless Whitespace Tables§9.1.1 — column boundaries without rules, where fused cells are most likely

9.6.4 Color as the Value

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-color-as-the-value · tables color marks

✅ Normative

A cell whose only content is a coloured fill MUST be rendered as an empty <mark> carrying the colour: <td><mark style="background-color: red"></mark></td>. The colour MUST be the nearest HTML colour name, never the meaning a legend assigns it, and the cell MUST NOT be left blank.

Risk matrices and heatmap tables put the meaning in the fill. The cell has no text at all:

| Likelihood ╲ Impact | Low | High |
| Rare                | 🟩  | 🟨   |   ← the fill IS the value
| Likely              | 🟨  | 🟥   |

Read straight through, the body of that table is blank, and a blank body makes the whole grid meaningless.

The rendering
<tr>
  <td>Rare</td>
  <td><mark style="background-color: green"></mark></td>
  <td><mark style="background-color: yellow"></mark></td>
</tr>
  • The <mark> MUST be empty: the cell prints no text, and adding some would be inventing content.
  • The colour rides on the style attribute — the same mechanism as highlighted text in Highlighted Text§7.2.5 and Text Formatting Conventions§7.1. One vocabulary covers both: the nearest HTML colour name in style="background-color: …".
  • The colour MUST NOT be written as the cell's text. A cell reading green is indistinguishable from a cell whose printed content is the word "green" — and heatmap legends do sometimes spell their colours out. Text is what the page printed; the attribute is how the cell was filled.

The rendering degrades correctly. A consumer that ignores attributes sees an empty cell, which is truthful — the page printed no text there. A consumer that reads them gets the value. Neither is misled.

Why not the meaning

Writing "Low risk" instead of "green" means reading a legend, and the legend is routinely elsewhere on the page or on another page entirely. A rendering that depends on material outside the region would be a guess whenever that material is out of reach. The colour name needs no legend, stays faithful to the page, and leaves the interpretation to whoever reads the table.

Colour that is not the value

The two cases MUST be kept apart:

The cell prints Rendering
A fill and text The text is the value; the fill is decoration or revision tracking. The text is transcribed and the fill is not carried.
A fill and nothing else The case of this rule: an empty <mark> with the fill's colour.
❌ Counter-sample — yellow

Cells carry a yellow fill and printed numbers — decoration layered over real content, not a colour-only cell, so only the text is rendered. The lettered rows are indented under their numbered parents, while dividends under (5) Preferred stock is printed flush left; Sum of line (1) thru (9) is the total row, indented under (10) Total; each column heading is one wrapped label.

❌ Counter-sample — 3lineperrowhili

Every body cell is filled green as revision tracking, yet each still prints its own text: colour as annotation, not as value, so only the text is rendered. The body text is bold in every cell, territory codes included, and is marked so; the column headings share one weight.

Shading that means "not applicable"

A grey fill over cells the page does not compute MUST be rendered the same way: an empty <mark> per shaded cell with the nearest colour name, e.g. <td><mark style="background-color: gray"></mark></td>. The fill is what the page printed there, and a consumer ignoring attributes still sees an empty cell. The shaded region MUST NOT be rendered as a colspan or rowspan: the page prints the cells separately.

✅ Sample — shading that means "not applicable"

The Recovery Claim % column is filled grey for the whole Distributable Proceeds block and for the Intercompany creditor row, in all three scenarios: one empty <mark> in each, darkgray being the nearest colour name to the fill. The $ typeset in its own track joins its value; each wrapped heading, Distributio over n included, is one label.

✅ Sample — shaded cells in a segment table

Under Volume, three Convenient Foods cells and three Beverages cells are filled grey with no text where a segment has no volume measure: one empty <mark> each, silver being the nearest colour name. The Revenue and Volume groups share one row stub across a blank gap, so they are one table. The group titles printed above the frame are elided here, as are the second table and the EPS row beneath it.

9.6.5 Handwriting and Stamps

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-handwriting-and-stamps · tables marks redline

✅ Normative

Handwriting over a printed value MUST keep both, the struck-through printed value first: ~~60~~ 55 — the same markup as a printed redline replacement. A stamp over a table MUST keep its text and MUST be rendered outside the table, as page-level content; it MUST NOT be assigned to a cell.

Filled-in ledgers and approved/void stamps put ink on top of a grid that was printed empty.

| Qty | Description | Amount |
| 2   | Widget      | ~60~ 55 (handwritten) |  ← replaces? joins? annotates?

     [ APPROVED ]   ← stamp overlapping three cells: which cell gets it? any?
Handwriting over a printed value

The cell MUST hold the printed value struck through, then the handwritten one:

page shows:   60 (printed, crossed out)   55 (handwritten)
rendered as:  ~~60~~ 55

This is deliberately the same markup as Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7. A printed correction and a handwritten one are the same act — a value replaced in place — and the ink used to make the change is not what a consumer needs to know. One encoding covers both, so nothing downstream has to distinguish a pen from a strikethrough font to read the cell.

The printed and the handwritten digits MUST NOT be merged into one number. OCR readily runs them together and produces a number that appears nowhere on the page and looks entirely reasonable; the image decides which glyphs are printed and which are written, and they are recorded as two values.

Handwriting that adds a value where the printed cell was empty is simply the cell's content.

Stamps

A stamp belongs to the page, not to a cell. It overlaps cells only because of where it landed, so any cell it could be assigned to is arbitrary — and putting its text inside a cell corrupts a value that is otherwise correct.

  • The stamp MUST be kept and rendered outside the table, as its [stamp: …] marker — see Stamps§7.3.11.
  • Its letters MUST NOT be distributed across the cells it crosses, and it MUST NOT be dropped for having nowhere obvious to go.

Assigning a stamp to a cell fails in both directions: it corrupts the cell's value, and it makes the stamp's own text unreadable by splitting it. Every candidate cell is equally arbitrary, which is the tell that the cell level is the wrong level.

No example page exercises either case yet; the sketches above stand in for one.

  • Watermarks§7.3.13 — the other page-level mark rendered outside the content it overlaps
  • Stamps§7.3.11 — the [stamp: …] marker
  • Seals and Round Stamps§7.3.9 — round seals and their [seal: …] marker
  • Handwritten Annotations§7.3.3 — handwriting in a margin, which replaces nothing
