9.6.6 Marks and Symbols in Cells

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-marks-and-symbols-in-cells · tables marks encoding

✅ Normative

A footnote marker MUST stay in the cell of the value it is attached to. An em-dash alone in a cell is a value and MUST be kept; a cell printed blank MUST stay blank. A cell whose content is a symbol or icon MUST be rendered as a bracketed transcription of what the mark asserts, and MUST NOT be replaced by an emoji.

A sun/water requirements table where the icons are the values — a full sun versus a partial sun, one droplet versus two. A rendering that leaves those cells empty says nothing at all.

| Subscribers¹ | 48,210³ |   ← superscripts attached to a value
| Dividend     | —       |   ← an em-dash standing alone in a cell
| Approved     | ✓       |   ← a checkmark standing in for a value
Footnote superscripts
  • A footnote marker MUST stay in the same cell as the value it is attached to, rendered with <sup>: 48,210<sup>3</sup>, New Program<sup>2</sup> — see Superscript and Subscript§7.2.11.
  • The marker MUST NOT be stripped, and MUST NOT be given a column of its own. It points at one number; separated from that number it points at nothing.
The em-dash
  • An em-dash alone in a cell is a value and MUST be rendered as —. In accounting it means zero, and we checked — a different claim from an empty cell, which means nothing here.
  • The rule holds in both directions, and the second is the one most often broken: a cell printed blank MUST be rendered as an empty cell, and a dash MUST NOT be supplied for it, however many of its neighbours carry one (never invent).

The same reasoning makes the structural blank meaningful in Triangles and Matrix Tables§9.8.2 and the coloured fill meaningful in Color as the Value§9.6.4 — a non-value that is a value.

✅ Sample — single

Em-dashes stand in for the not-yet-available 15-year figures of two private indexes, alongside ¹ footnote markers on the index names. The dashes are values; the markers stay on the names.

❌ Counter-sample — entwick

On the Rückkauf eigener Anteile row the page prints nothing in Eigene Anteile — only the Gesamtkapital column carries a value, 0. A rendering that writes an em-dash into the blank cell invents a value: the em-dash rule cuts both ways.

Checkmarks, crosses and icons
  • A mark that stands in for a value MUST be rendered as a bracketed word stating what it asserts: [yes], [no], [checked], [locked], [icon: present].
  • The nearest emoji MUST NOT be substituted. An emoji looks faithful and is not: it carries a shape rather than the claim the page makes, and no two producers pick the same one.
  • Where a symbol is glued to a value rather than standing in for one — ▲ 512.40, a bare + or - carrying a superscript — the glyph MUST stay with the value in the cell, as printed. See Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4 for marks outside tables.
| Feature | Basic | Pro |
| SSO     | 🔒    | ✓   |   → | SSO | [locked] | [yes] |
A repeated mark is a scale

Some columns grade a value by printing the mark more than once — one droplet for low water, two for high; one star, three stars.

  • A repeated mark MUST be transcribed once per printed mark: [water], [water][water]. The count is the value; collapsing the pair to one token loses the distinction the column exists to draw.
  • A count notation such as [water:2] MUST NOT be used.
  • The vocabulary MUST distinguish every distinct mark the scale prints. A sun column printing a solid, a half-filled and an outline glyph is a three-step scale; a rendering with two names for it has lost a step.
✅ Sample — wqa

X is a disclosure-control placeholder standing in for a suppressed value; the note below the table says so. It is printed text and is kept as X. The row labels and the Total row are bold.

✅ Sample — ed

Checkmark glyphs in Independent and Financial Expert (1) assert a yes; they are rendered as [yes], and an unmarked cell stays empty.

✅ Sample — du

▲ 512.40 — an up-triangle glued to the value, kept with it in the cell. The 대비 and 대비율(%) figures are set heavier than the rest of the row, so those cells are bold.

✅ Sample — lakecruise

↓ stands in the time cells of stops a service does not list a time for, and a row of small ⊛ glyphs sits under the service numbers. Both are printed characters and are kept as printed; no emoji replaces them. Station rows set in heavy type are bold; the arrows in them show no extra weight and stay plain.

✅ Sample — vap

A body made entirely of bare + / - symbols, some carrying (1), (2), (3) superscripts. The marks are printed characters and stay as printed, each superscript in the cell of the mark it is attached to. The Precision band is set in bold italic.

9.6.7 Struck and Replaced Values

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-struck-and-replaced-values · tables redline ocr failure-mode

✅ Normative

A cell holding a struck value and its replacement MUST render both, struck first — ~~1.316~~ 1.335 — and MUST NOT merge them into one figure. The ~~ MUST cover exactly the glyphs struck on the page: 1.~~316~~ 335 when only the digits are crossed out.

A cell holds an old value crossed out plus its replacement. A text layer joins them without a trace:

page shows:  1.316 (struck)  1.335
text layer:  1.316335        ← this number does not exist on the page

That is the worst outcome available on a table: not a drop and not a garble, but a fabricated number that looks entirely plausible and that nothing downstream can catch. Struck cells MUST be read from the rendered page, never from the text layer — see Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3.

Writing the cell
  • A struck value and its replacement MUST be rendered ~~old~~ new, which keeps the two readings distinct and marks which one is superseded.
  • Where the page marks the change with an underline instead of a strike, the replacement MUST be rendered <u>1.335</u>, recording what is actually drawn.
  • A handwritten correction over a printed value MUST use the same markup — see Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5. A printed strikethrough and a pen stroke are the same act, so a consumer never has to tell them apart.
  • The output MUST NOT restructure the table into "Previous" and "Current" columns. Where the page itself prints the old and new figures in separate tables or columns, each MUST be rendered where it appears rather than folded into one cell.
✅ Sample — strike

Every Current Rates figure is struck through, with its live replacement in the Proposed Rates tables alongside: 54 struck values across two tables. Each struck value is wrapped in ~~…~~, and the four blocks stay four tables.

Note what the page itself does: it splits old and new into parallel tables, so the replacement is not in the same cell. The output follows the page and does not fold them together.

The strike span mirrors the printed strike

Where the strike starts and stops is printed information, and the markup carries it: exactly the struck glyphs, no more, no less.

whole value struck:      1.316 (all struck)  335        →  ~~1.316~~ 335
only the digits struck:  1.316 (316 struck)  335        →  1.~~316~~ 335

The unstruck 1. sits outside the ~~, because that is where it sits on the page. Nothing is reconstructed and nothing is invented — the prefix is transcribed because it is printed and was never struck.

1.~~316~~ 335 gives a reader everything needed to arrive at 1.335 without the output asserting it. The 1. is printed, unstruck, and therefore still part of the value; the replacement digits follow. The reading falls out of the transcription instead of being asserted on top of it.

That is why the span must be exact. ~~1.316~~ 335 for a page that only struck 316 throws away the prefix a reader needs, and 1.~~316~~ 335 for a page that struck the whole value claims ink that is not there. Both are losses, in opposite directions.

One struck cell puts the column in play

Strikes are thin and reproduce badly at page zoom, so a struck cell is easy to miss. One struck cell means the column is a redline column: every other cell in it MUST be read for a strike before the column is rendered.

Redline in prose
  • Deleted text MUST be rendered ~~…~~ and inserted underlined text <u>…</u>, each over exactly the printed span.
  • Where colour distinguishes revisions or authors, the colour MUST be preserved as well. Insertion MUST NOT be inferred from colour alone where the page marks nothing else.
✅ Sample — an interlineated court rule

Paragraph (4): [Deleted.] struck through in red, followed by red underlined replacement text; everything above it is plain black. Strike and underline already carry the revision, so the red adds nothing a strike and an underline do not.

✅ Sample — insertions marked by colour alone


Source: Advisory Committee on Civil Rules (U.S. Courts), Proposed Amendments to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 30(b)(6) (public domain)

Proposed rule text: deletions (then, make this designation) struck through in black, insertions in red with no underline. Without the colour the insertions become indistinguishable from the settled text, so the colour is kept. The colour is written as <font color="red"> around the inserted words, as Text Colors§7.3.12 requires.

Related

  • Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5 — the handwritten equivalent uses the same markup
  • Underlined Text§7.2.12 — <u>, not <ins>, for an underline
  • Watermarks§7.3.13 — "Redline Version" is often stamped on exactly these pages

9.7 Titles and edges

9.7.1 Bottom Edge Totals and Islands

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-bottom-edge-totals-and-islands · tables drops boundaries

✅ Normative

Content printed below or beside a table MUST NOT be dropped, even when it sits outside the ruled frame. Where it continues the table's ruled grid it MUST be rendered as rows of that table; where it stands apart as its own unbordered block it MUST be rendered as its own small key-value table.

The bottom edge is where content goes missing most often, because everything here sits past the last rule of the frame — and it is usually the numbers the reader actually wanted.

| Item   | Qty | Rate | Amount |
| Widget | 2   | 30   | 60     |
└──── ruled frame ends ────────┘
               Subtotal    60      ← outside the frame:
               Shipping    10        footer rows of the table? its own KV
               Total       70        table? dropped entirely?
The frame decides

The block under the table is placed by one question: does it sit inside the ruled frame, or visually continue the table's ruled column grid?

Block under the table Rendering
Inside the frame, or continuing its ruled column grid footer rows of that table, each value in its printed column
Standing apart as a separate unbordered block — even if its columns loosely line up under the table's rightmost columns its own key-value table: one row per printed line, a label cell and a value cell

The block MUST NOT be omitted, and a block that is not part of the grid MUST NOT be padded into the main table as extra footer rows. This is the frame test of Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3, applied at the other edge of the table. Footnotes are the one exception — see Footnotes Inside the Frame§9.7.2.

✅ Sample — a totals block continuing the frame

Subtotal to TOTAL sit under the item grid inside the frame's two right-hand columns, ruled the same way, with the left three columns absent below the last item row. They are footer rows of the item table, label under Unit Price and value under Extension; the printed empty item rows are kept as empty rows.

Trailing aligned summary lines

Lines such as "Selected …" or "Reserve to Surplus Ratio:" whose values land under real columns are rows of the grid. They MUST be rendered as rows, each value in its printed column — not as prose after the table.

| Year | Reserves | Surplus |
| 2023 | 1,204    | 887     |
Selected             1,190     ← values align under real columns:
Reserve/Surplus:     1.36        rows of the table
Invoice-style totals blocks

A Subtotal / Discount / Shipping / Total block printed below the line-item table and outside its frame MUST be rendered as its own key-value table: label and value, one row per printed line.

This is a deliberate exception to the treatment of ungridded key-value regions in Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1. Trailing totals are a numeric continuation of the table's data, and a table whose totals are missing has lost the part of the page most people read first.

✅ Sample — 2cc

A Total - 175 line below the table, outside its implicit frame and not even aligned with the second column. It is kept, as its own one-row key-value table after the list. The column headers are bold and underlined.

Detached cell islands

A small offset group of cells that lines up with a table's column tracks is content. It MUST be rendered; it is not decoration.

| (1) | (2) | (3)  |
| 100 | 82  | 0.82 |

            | 0.79 |   ← "(8) Benchmark" offset box, aligned
                         with column (3)'s track

Where it goes is decided by one test: does the island line up with an existing table's column tracks?

  • Yes → it belongs to that table and MUST be appended as an extra row: the label in the stub column, the value in the column whose track it lines up with.
  • No → it MUST be rendered as its own small table.

Column-track alignment is the typesetter saying "this value belongs under that heading". A floating box that lines up with nothing makes no such claim, so it stands alone.

✅ Sample — wwa

The boxed Selected: / Trend values, the boxed trend period and the Rolling 4-Qtr / Annual Trend table sit outside the main frame and do not continue its column grid, so each is its own small table after the main one. The main table's italic footnote line follows it as footnote text.

✅ Sample — 2tab

Calibration Factors: and Highest vs Lowest: sit detached below the ruled frames, aligned to the value columns, so they are appended as rows of the table: the four boxed calibration factors under Final Area Factors and the three prior-year columns, 1.1498 under Final Area Factors. The two panels share one Region row spine and are rendered as one wide table (see Column Continuation§9.2.2).

✅ Sample — 3d

A boxed Weighted Average Lapse Rate summary detached below the main frame, its two values aligned under the Implied and "Current" lapse-rate columns. It is stitched back in as trailing rows, each value in the column it lines up with.

✅ Sample — 2tt

Boxed Percentage Change: -8.3% / +30.0% values below each frame, aligned under the Proposed Rate/Factor column, folded back in as trailing rows.

Alignment on its own is not proof

Alignment places an island once it is known to belong to the table; it cannot by itself prove that an out-of-frame line is a footer row. On a premium-tax page an underline closes a Premium Tax / Total mini-table, and the 3. DCCE to Loss Ratio line printed beneath it sits under the same columns while belonging to neither table.

The frame test MUST be applied first, and alignment used only to place what it hands over — not the other way round.

Where the frame is genuinely ambiguous

Some pages have no ruled border either way. There, both encodings — footer rows of the table, or a separate key-value table — conform, provided every printed line is kept. A document MUST use one of them throughout. See Accepted Alternatives§A.1 and Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2.

Related
  • Total and Subtotal Rows§9.5.6 — totals printed inside the grid
  • Footnotes Inside the Frame§9.7.2 — the one bottom-edge block that never becomes a row
  • Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3 — the same frame test at the top edge
  • Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1 — the key-value treatment this rule makes an exception to

9.7.2 Footnotes Inside the Frame

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-footnotes-inside-the-frame · tables captions boundaries

✅ Normative

A table footnote MUST be rendered outside the table, as footnote text placed after it — even when the page prints it inside the table's ruled border. It MUST NOT be rendered as a row of the table. It retains the Footnote class and MUST NOT be wrapped in <caption>. This is a deliberate exception to the frame test.

A footnote line printed within the table's own ruled border:

| Rate A     | 1.10¹   |
| Rate B     | 1.25    |
| ¹ Excludes riders    |   ← printed INSIDE the ruled frame
Why the frame test does not decide footnotes

The frame test — ink inside the border is a row, ink outside it is a caption — decides titles and banners in Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3 and totals blocks in Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1. It is worth having because it is mechanical.

A footnote is where it gives the wrong answer. The line names no columns and carries no values, so rendering it as a row asserts something false about the table: a consumer counting records gets one too many, and the row's single cell has no relationship to any column above it. Where the typesetter drew the border is a layout accident — the footnote is commentary on the table either way.

The carve-out costs the frame test its single-signal property, and that price is paid deliberately: the frame decides titles and banners; it does not decide footnotes.

✅ Sample — wwa

(Justify Selection and Trend Period in Filing Memorandum) is printed inside the table's grid, under the last data row — the case where the frame test and instinct disagree. It is set in italics, and it follows the table as footnote text.

Rendering the footnote
  • Wherever the border falls, the footnote MUST be footnote text placed immediately after the table. It MUST be transcribed verbatim, including its leading marker, and MUST stay attached to the table it annotates rather than drifting into the surrounding prose.
  • A line opening ¹, *, (a) or Note: that refers to a marker printed in a cell above it is a footnote, not a row.
  • Superscript markers inside cells MUST stay attached to their values — see Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6. The footnote body leaving the table does not take the reference with it, so 1.10¹ in the cell and ¹ Excludes riders after the table still point at each other.
  • The text MUST survive either way. Only its placement is decided here; dropping it is never conforming.
✅ Sample — two footnotes inside a shaded frame

Footnotes 1 and 2 sit inside the grey-bordered panel that frames the trading table, under the Total row, in a smaller face. Both follow the table as footnote text; the superscript markers stay in the header cells and the Other trading label. Only the year band and the Total row are printed bold; the hyphenated header wraps (per- / form- / ance) are joined.

Related
  • Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3 — the frame test that decides titles and banners, and does not decide footnotes
  • Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1 — the frame test applied to totals and islands at the same edge
  • Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 — the in-cell marker that points at the footnote

9.7.3 Titles Banners Captions

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-titles-banners-captions · tables captions headers

✅ Normative

For a table-only title, the frame and the fill decide. A band that shares the table's border or fill MUST be rendered as a header row inside the table; a table-only title outside the ruled frame MUST be rendered as <caption> inside the table HTML. Table and chart captions MUST be the first or last content inside <table> according to reading order and MUST appear once.

22. Consolidated Income Statement        ← title line above the table:
| Revenue | 2024 | 2023 |              ## heading? first header row? both?

| [colspan=3]LAWNS & ANNUALS |       ← band sharing the table's border/fill:
| Name | Water | Sun |                 header row inside, or heading outside?
Structural statement titles

A table-only caption is first told apart from a principal financial-statement or numbered schedule title using Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7. A principal statement title can be a document heading, and a company line printed directly above it joins that heading (see Stacked Headings§6.9); a units line cannot. A numbered schedule title printed within a grid keeps its structural role, but its text MUST stay in the table once and MUST NOT be duplicated as an outside heading. The frame test below applies to ordinary table captions and bands.

The frame test

The position of the ink relative to the ruled border, and whether the band carries the table's fill, decide:

The band… Rendering
shares the border or the fill a header row inside the table. A coloured "LAWNS & ANNUALS" band that runs to the table's own edges is a <th colspan=N> banner row. Such bands MUST NOT be omitted — they carry the heading for everything under them.
sits outside the ruled frame <caption> inside the table HTML, first or last according to reading order

Only text that belongs to the table alone counts. A page heading that happens to sit above a table, and would still make sense if the table were removed, is not a title band.

A bold caption with paragraph spacing directly above a bordered mini-table follows the same rule: it MUST be the first <caption> inside the table HTML.

✅ Sample — star

APPLICABILITY CHART as a full-width band sharing the table's own ruled border — in-frame by the frame test, so it is the first header row.

✅ Sample — 3t

A coloured colspan title bar (TIMBER IMPACT INVESTING FUNDS) sharing the table's fill and width opens each of the three tables.

✅ Sample — ylf

Years Loss Free With BMI Post Inception is a title band inside the second table's ruled frame, spanning both columns, so it is the table's first header row and is not repeated as text above it.

An in-table title is one full-width cell

A title band rendered as a row MUST be a single full-width <th colspan=N> — never the title in one column with empty cells padded beside it.

| [colspan=3]Table 13 — Scale G2 |    vs    | Table 13 — Scale G2 |  |  |
                                             ↑ padded: a spurious record

A full-width single-value row is recognised as a title and set aside; the padded form reads as a real data row with missing values, and adds a row that the table does not have.

A table-only title therefore has two forms, chosen by its printed role: a full-width header row for an in-frame band, or <caption> for a caption outside the printed frame.

A title appears once

A title MUST appear once, in the form selected by the frame test. A <caption> MUST NOT also appear as a paragraph outside the table or as a header row.

Banner colspan follows the region, not the ink

A centred band title MUST span the region it heads, not the pixels its letters happen to cover.

|      Proposed      |            ← ink covers 4 of 14 column tracks:
| c1 | c2 | … | c14 |              colspan=4 or colspan=14?

A "Proposed" banner over a 14-column table is colspan=14, even though its ink reaches only the middle four. Centred text shrinks toward the middle whatever it spans, so measuring the glyphs measures the font, not the structure.

✅ Sample — lakecruise

Coloured GROSSE SEERUNDFAHRT / KLEINE SEERUNDFAHRT banners span each timetable's full width, so each is one full-width header cell (all nine columns in the first table), carrying the duration printed at its right end. Bold stop rows (Lindenhafen, Seewinkel) are bold per cell.

Section-divider rows

A divider row that names no columns — "Part I — Financial Information" and the like — SHOULD be rendered as a bold body row (<td colspan=N>); a <th> row MAY be used instead. A document MUST use one of the two for every visually identical band — see Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2. Whichever tag is used, a divider MUST NOT be promoted into the column-name tier: it labels a region, not a column.

| Part I — Financial Information |   ← names no columns
| Item 1 | 10-Q | 45 |

Bold <td> is the preferred form because a <th> claims "this labels the cells below it", and a section divider makes no such claim.

❌ Counter-sample — wood

The region bands (AFRICA, AUSTRALIA, NORTH AMERICA) are visually identical grey bold bands. A rendering that tags one of them as a body cell and another as <th> in the same document violates the one-form-per-document requirement. The conforming rendering uses one form — here the preferred bold <td> — for every band in both tables.

How a caption is rendered

A table or chart caption MUST be rendered once as <caption>…</caption> inside the HTML table that represents its object. Reading order determines its position in the HTML source:

  • A caption read before the table or chart MUST be the first content line after the opening <table> tag, before any rows or table-section wrappers.
  • A caption read after the table or chart MUST be the last content line before </table>, after all rows and table-section wrappers.
  • A chart's table MUST still open with <table data-source="chart">.
caption before the table:
<table>
  <caption>Table 5 — Lapse Rates</caption>
  <!-- rows -->
</table>

caption after the chart:
<table data-source="chart">
  <!-- rows -->
  <caption>Figure 2 — Annual losses</caption>
</table>

The first/last requirement concerns the serialized HTML, including captions after the final row. Source notes, footnotes and nearby prose retain their own roles and MUST NOT be turned into captions. Captions of objects that are not represented by tables retain their adjacent paragraphs.

In the element list, a caption MUST be attached to the table or chart it describes wherever the association is clear from the page. It retains the Caption class and its own box even when its rendering is nested inside <table>; the table or chart box follows Block Boundaries§5.2. When the association is unclear, the output MUST NOT invent an attachment.

Caption formatting is content

Captions are rarely plain text, and their styling is printed content like any other. It MUST be preserved as printed, per run:

printed:      Figure 2. Predicted vs True Tree count on the test set.
              ^^^^^^^^^ bold          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ plain
output:       <caption><strong>Figure 2.</strong> Predicted vs True Tree count on the test set.</caption>

printed:      FIG.2.3. Electric and non-electric energy growth rate (from [1]).
              ^ all italic
output:       <caption><em>FIG.2.3. Electric and non-electric energy growth rate (from [1]).</em></caption>

Three shapes recur: fully italic, a bold label followed by plain text, and a caption set in a heading-like face. A bold run stays bold, an italic run stays italic, and a mixed caption keeps the boundary between them. Styles MUST NOT be normalised to one, and MUST NOT be dropped because the text survives without them. The per-run discipline is the one that governs styling inside tables — see Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2.

A caption MUST NOT be converted into a heading, even when it is set in a heading-like face. A ## heading above the table asserts a document section that the page did not print, and it survives into any structure derived from the headings. A caption names an object; a heading opens a section.

This is the placement rule only. Whether a given piece of text is a caption at all, or a title band inside the table, is settled by the frame test above.

✅ Sample — a title printed in the corner cell

Financial highlights, bold and underlined, sits in the top-left cell of the frame — where the stub header goes — with the period tiers to its right. It is the stub header, in the header row, and there is no caption. The SOUTHERN AND EASTERN EUROPE heading above the frame would make sense without the table, so it stays a heading; the (1) note below the frame follows the table.

9.8 Special table types

9.8.1 Rotated and Diagonal Content

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-rotated-and-diagonal-content · tables orientation headers

✅ Normative

A rotated table MUST be read in its own orientation, never in page orientation. A diagonally split corner cell MUST stay one cell holding both labels separated by a slash — Region \ Year — the label across the top first.

One printed cell carrying two labels: MONTH across the top, COUNTRY down the side, split by a diagonal rule. There is only one cell to put them in.

A landscape table on a portrait page
  • A table printed sideways MUST be rendered as a reader would read it after turning the page: rows are rows as the table reads, not as the page is filed.
  • Sideways text MUST NOT be transcribed in page order.
Vertical column headers

Labels printed at 90° over narrow columns are ordinary headers. Each MUST be rendered as normal header text, upright, in the column it heads.

| ⤴A⤴ | ⤴B⤴ | ⤴C⤴ |   ← headers printed vertically
| 1   | 2   | 3   |

Nothing about the rotation changes the structure — it is a typesetting choice made because the column is narrow.

The diagonally split corner cell
| Region ╲ Year | 2023 | 2024 |   ← one printed cell, two labels
| East          | 40   | 44   |
  • Both labels MUST survive: one names the stub column, the other names the header row, and losing either leaves an axis unnamed.
  • There is one printed cell, so it MUST stay one cell, the two labels separated by a slash — Region \ Year — in the reading order the diagonal implies: the label across the top first, then the one down the side.
  • The corner MUST NOT be split into two header cells.
✅ Sample — a landscape page in a portrait document

A paper page rendered sideways: the body text, both tables and the Table 3 caption read bottom-to-top. Upright, the two tables are ordinary tables; nothing about them is special except that a reader has to turn the page. The page is cut off after the Kestrel 33B row of the second table, so nothing below it is rendered.

What makes this the useful case is that the rotation is not marked anywhere. There is no landscape flag; the only signal is that the text runs the wrong way. A rendering in page orientation transposes headers and rows and still looks structurally plausible.

Note also the blank corner cells above both stub columns, and the en-dashes standing in for missing benchmark scores — see Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 and Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6.

✅ Sample — a vertical stub header

The leftmost column carries a label running bottom-to-top along the side of the table, spanning every body row, while all the other headers sit horizontally. It labels the whole stub, which is why the typesetter turned it — there was no width for it any other way. The coloured shapes in the second column have no legend on the page, so each is described as drawn.

The rotation is a layout constraint, not a property of the header: the label is rendered upright as a normal header cell spanning the rows it spans. The table's bilingual text and its landscape setting change nothing either.

✅ Sample — a landscape reference table on a portrait page

Table C.1. (Cont.): twenty-five chemicals with CAS numbers, formulae and properties, printed sideways. Upright it is an ordinary eleven-column table (No. plus ten property columns); the header cells carry units and subscripts (D_a, cm² s⁻¹), the formulae carry subscripts, and one melting point prints 123.5 decomposes on two lines. The page number C-6, printed beside the title in the table's own orientation, is rendered first as the page's header band.

Related
  • Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3 — the corner cell also appears there as the "$ in millions" note
  • Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 — the blank corner cell
  • Chart With a Printed Data Grid§9.1.2 — the other transposition problem

9.8.2 Triangles and Matrix Tables

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

tables-triangles-and-matrix-tables · tables encoding empty-cells

✅ Normative

Every row MUST carry the full column count. The jagged half MUST be padded with individual empty cells — one <td></td> per missing position. A colspan or rowspan over the empty region MUST NOT be used, and a 0 or any other value MUST NOT be invented.

Loss development exhibits and similar matrices are jagged on purpose. The missing half is meaningfully empty — that development period has not happened yet — not data that failed to be read.

Accident yr | 12mo | 24mo | 36mo |
| 2021      | 450  | 512  | 530  |
| 2022      | 470  | 528  |      |  ← structurally empty,
| 2023      | 465  |      |      |    not "failed to read"
Requirements
  • The shape MUST be kept. Every row has the full column count; the cells past the end of the row are present and empty. Rows MUST NOT be truncated.
  • One empty cell per missing position. Four unhappened periods are four <td></td>, not one colspan="4". The span would say "this region is one thing", and it is not — it is four distinct coordinates that each have not happened yet.
  • The empty half MUST NOT be padded with values. Filling it with 0, n/a or a repeat of the last figure destroys the only thing the triangle asserts.
  • A printed value MUST NOT be read as structural emptiness either. Some pages print 0 across the future half. A zero is a claim and a blank is an absence; the output MUST render whichever the page prints.
  • A cell that is empty because it cannot be read is a different situation — see Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3.
✅ Sample — ppy

Stacked loss-development exhibits where the empty lower-right is meaningfully empty: those development periods have not happened. Every row of the first triangle carries all eleven cells. The column headers are underlined, not bold.

❌ Counter-sample — waiox

The same shape, filled differently: the un-earned future half is printed with explicit 0s rather than left blank. A zero is a claim; a blank is an absence — here every 0 is kept.

Why a span is wrong here, when it is free elsewhere

Blank and Spacer Rows§9.5.1 leaves the encoding of an unruled empty region free: leading empty cells and one blank spanning block render identically, and neither is preferred.

A triangle is the carve-out. Every empty cell sits at a real coordinate — an accident year crossed with a development period — and "12 months has not elapsed for the 2023 year" is a separate fact from the same statement about 24 months. Collapsed into one span, those coordinates stop being addressable: a consumer can no longer ask what the 2023 row holds at 24 months, because the cell it would look in no longer exists.

Elsewhere the empty region is one undifferentiated blank. Here it is a set of individually meaningful absences that happen to be adjacent.

This is the same principle that settles blank space beside a header in Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1: a span is a claim that the page merged something. The page did not merge these.

Why the blank matters more here than elsewhere

In most tables, blank versus an explicit empty marker is cosmetic. In a loss triangle the blank carries actuarial meaning: it asserts this development period does not exist yet, which is a fact about the world, not a gap in the transcription. That is the same argument that makes the em-dash a value in Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 and the coloured fill a value in Color as the Value§9.6.4 — a non-value that is a value.

  • Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 — the em-dash and the blank as values
  • Blank and Spacer Rows§9.5.1 — where the encoding of an empty region is free
  • Header Body Column Count Mismatch§9.4.2 — padding short rows to the column count

§10 Forms

10.1 Forms and Key-Value Regions

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-forms-and-key-value-regions · forms

✅ Normative

Fill-in fields and checkbox regions are key-value content, not tables: they MUST be rendered as the key-value list of The Key-Value List§10.3.2 and MUST NOT be rendered as a table. The output MUST NOT contain a two-column key/value table that the page does not print as a ruled grid.

Form controls printed on the page — labels waiting for a value, checkbox rows, signature and date lines — look tabular because they line up in columns. They are not tables: the alignment is typesetting, not structure.

Insurer: ________        NAIC #: ________
☒ Renewal     ☐ New business

- **Insurer:** [blank]
- **NAIC #:** [blank]
- [x] Renewal
- [ ] New business

Fillable or static

A region is form content when it prints labelled fields to fill, checkboxes, or blanks — even when its layout looks like a plain grid of labels and values. Such a region MUST be rendered as a key-value list.

A static key-value reference — a legend, a specification sheet, a summary box, filing metadata — prints fixed labels and values and nothing to fill in and no checkbox. It is not a form. The test is whether anything on it was meant to be filled in.

The border test for static key-value blocks

A page that raises this question is usually half form, half grid, so the decision is made region by region. For each static block of label: value pairs:

The block Rendering
Printed inside a ruled border (a gridded key/value block) It MUST be rendered as a table, per Is This Even a Table§9.1.5; leaving it out drops a table.
Not ruled — a specification stack, a cluster of Label: value fields above a table, an address block, a prose-line legend It MUST be rendered as text in reading order and MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

A totals block printed under a table is the one exception: it belongs to the table above it, not to the surrounding fields — see Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1.

✅ Sample — ratefiling

SERFF filing metadata as ungridded Label: value fields above two genuine ruled tables on the same page. Nothing on the page is fillable, so the fields are static text lines; only the two ruled grids are tables.

✅ Sample — 10k

Yes/No lines answered with check marks (no box is drawn around the options) and address blocks around a real securities table. The ruled securities grid is a table; the check-mark questions are option groups.

✅ Sample — 2linebug

Policyholder:, Policy Number:, Signature: and ☐ Power of Attorney ☐ Conservator ☐ Other: fields outside the options grid. The grid is a table and keeps its own checkboxes; the fields around it are key-value content. The red bracket numbers are bold and printed, so they are kept.

✅ Sample — sln

Below the specification grid, a small ruled block pairs Signature of Quotation Bidder (with seal) and Name of Quotation Bidder with one shared cell holding a handwritten signature. It is a key-value block to fill in, not a data row of the grid above.

Why not a small table

A two-column key/value table built from an unruled block creates a record that exists nowhere on the page — the never invent failure of Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2. It teaches whatever learns from the output that structure can be conjured from whitespace. Rendering the block as text or as a key-value list loses nothing, because nothing there was ever printed as tabular.

  • The Key-Value List§10.3.2 — how form content is transcribed once it is recognised
  • Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 — the test a ruled static block goes through
  • Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6 — checkbox glyphs used as values inside a real table cell
  • Empty Pre-Printed Grids§9.1.3 — a fully blank ruled form, where the structure is the content

10.2 Repeated and Unlabelled Fields

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-repeated-and-unlabelled-fields · forms

✅ Normative

Field groups that repeat without a printed heading MUST be kept as anonymous groups in printed order, separated by a blank line in the Markdown. The output MUST NOT invent a heading, label or positional id — no Vehicle 1, no Child 2 — for a group or field the page does not name.

Repeating unlabelled record blocks

Insurance-application premises, vehicle and applicant blocks, and family-court residence blocks repeat the same field set several times and print no heading of their own.

  • Each repetition MUST be rendered as its own group of key-value lines, in printed order.
  • Consecutive groups MUST be separated by one blank line in the Markdown; when a sidecar is produced, each group MUST be its own nested group of items.
  • A heading, number or label that the page does not print MUST NOT be added to tell the groups apart.

Where non-field text goes

Instructions, preambles and fine print MUST be transcribed at their printed reading position, between the fields they accompany — see Fields Outside the Form§10.5.1.

Unlabelled entries with no id

An entry with neither a printed id nor a printed label MUST be rendered as its bare value, or as a bare [blank] when it is empty. A label or positional id MUST NOT be invented for it.

✅ Sample — three identical child blocks

Section 2 prints Child’s Name / Address / City, State / Dates: From … To / Lived with / Relationship to Child three times over, with no heading on any of the three blocks. Each block is an anonymous group, read row by row; the blocks are separated by blank lines.

Related

  • The Key-Value List§10.3.2 — the line format every group uses
  • Sections and Grouped Fields§10.5.3 — groups that do print a heading
  • Fields Outside the Form§10.5.1 — where non-field text is placed
  • Values Are Verbatim§10.3.3 — what goes after the label

10.3 The output format

10.3.1 Ids and Labels

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-ids-and-labels · forms

✅ Normative

A field's id is its printed designator, written exactly as printed in escaped brackets outside the bold label. Its label is the printed caption, verbatim. A label MUST NOT repeat the id, and a caption MUST NOT be written as an id.

The distinction

An id is a short printed designator that indexes into the form — 1a, e, H1, Part III. It is what a reader cites when they say "see line 12a".

A label is the caption. A caption is never an id. On a 1099, only the numbered boxes have ids; PAYER'S TIN is a label with no id.

✅  - \[1a\] **Total amount**: 4,200
❌  - **1a Total amount**: 4,200      ← id folded into the label
❌  - \[PAYER'S TIN\] **...**          ← a caption is not an id
Nothing is cleaned up

A label MUST keep its abbreviations, capitalisation and punctuation exactly as printed. A label MUST NOT be renamed, expanded or tidied: FAX (A/C, No) stays FAX (A/C, No).

Implicit numbers

When a printed id carries an implicit number, the id MUST include it.


Source: IRS Form 1040 (2020), Refund section, lines 35a–35d (public domain)

A block printed 35a then b, c, d has the ids 35a, 35b, 35c, 35d — not 35a, b, c, d. The 35 is implied by position and is part of how the field is cited; dropping it makes three of the four ids unusable for reference.

Escaping

\[x\] is a printed id "x"; [x] is a checked box. The escape is what keeps them apart — see The Key-Value List§10.3.2.

Related
  • The Key-Value List§10.3.2 — the line format ids and labels sit in
  • Fill-Ins§10.4.4 — fields with an id but no label
  • Form Reading Order§10.5.2 — ids set the order of the fields

10.3.2 The Key-Value List

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-the-key-value-list · forms

✅ Normative

Fillable form content MUST be rendered as a Markdown key-value list, not as a table. Every field MUST be one list item using the - marker.

The shape
### \[Part I\] Information About the Partnership

- \[A\] **Partnership's employer identification number**: 27-4162308
- \[D\] **Check if this is a publicly traded partnership (PTP)**: [ ]
- **CONTACT NAME:** Melinda Clayton
- **FAX (A/C, No):** [blank]
- \[G\]
  - [x] General partner or LLC member-manager
  - [ ] Limited partner or other LLC member
- **Your signature**: [signature: John Doe]
The line format
- \[id\] **Label**: value
  • The id and the label MUST each appear only when printed. A field with no printed id carries no brackets.
  • An id MUST be written in escaped square brackets — \[1a\] — outside the bold label.
  • An empty fill-in MUST be rendered as [blank]. A checkbox MUST be rendered as [x] (checked) or [ ] (unchecked).
  • An option line MUST be box-first: - [x] Single.
  • A printed section heading MUST be rendered as a Markdown heading. A box whose id covers several fields MUST be rendered as a parent list item with the fields nested beneath it.
Why the id is escaped

\[x\] is a printed field designator "x"; [x] is a checked box. Without the escape the two cannot be told apart, and a field id silently becomes a tick.

Colons
  • When the printed label ends in :, the colon MUST stay inside the bold label: - **CONTACT NAME:** Melinda Clayton.
  • When the value is not printed on the same line as its label — a caption printed under its line, an answer area below its question — the : after the label MUST be omitted: - **SIGNATURE OF DEPONENT** [blank].
Related
  • Ids and Labels§10.3.1 — what counts as an id and what as a label
  • Values Are Verbatim§10.3.3 — what goes after the label
  • Fill-Ins§10.4.4 · Checkboxes§10.4.2 · Option Groups§10.4.5 — the field shapes
  • Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1 — deciding that a region is form content at all

10.3.3 Values Are Verbatim

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-values-are-verbatim · forms fidelity

✅ Normative

Entered content MUST be transcribed exactly as it appears on the page. A value MUST NOT be rounded, reformatted, computed or summarised.

This is Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3 applied to what someone wrote into a field.

Printed Output Not
29,513 29,513 29513, 29,513.00
590.50 590.50 590.5
1.0000000000 % 1.0000000000 % 1.0%, 1
-599,459 -599,459 (599,459)
(284,791) (284,791) -284,791

A negative amount MUST keep the form the page printed: a leading minus stays a minus, parentheses stay parentheses. Converting between them is a reformat, and a reformat is how a value stops matching the document it came from.

Identifiers are not normalised either

An entered SSN, TIN, policy number or account number MUST be transcribed exactly as printed. It MUST NOT be rewritten to a canonical mask such as XXX-XX-XXXX or re-grouped to a standard shape.

This holds however the form splits the digits. A social security number printed across three boxed groups is the printed digits, in the grouping the page uses:

- \[E\] **Partner's SSN or TIN**: 27-4162256

Normalising an identifier looks harmless because the canonical form is more readable. It is the same failure as rounding a number: the output stops matching the document, and a reader verifying a value against the page finds a string that is not on it. A consumer that needs a canonical form can derive one; it cannot recover the printed one.

Split dollar and cent columns

A form that prints dollars and cents in two ruled columns holds one value. It MUST be rendered as one value — 1,234.00 — and MUST NOT be split across two fields. The rule lines are typesetting, not structure.

Related
  • Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3 — the same rule inside tables
  • Accounting Number Formats§9.6.1 — negative and zero forms kept as printed
  • The Key-Value List§10.3.2 · Fill-Ins§10.4.4 — where values sit

10.4 Fields

10.4.1 Blanks Inside Sentences

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-blanks-inside-sentences · forms

✅ Normative

A sentence with fill-in gaps MUST be kept intact, with each gap rendered as [blank] at its printed position. A hint printed with a blank MUST be kept next to that blank, once.

Affidavits, declarations and notarial blocks print their fields as prose with gaps in it:

The Enterprise is ______________% Black Owned using the flow-through principle …
Executed on the (date) ______ day of (month) ____________ (year) ________

The Enterprise is [blank]% Black Owned using the flow-through principle …
Executed on the *(date)* [blank] day of *(month)* [blank] *(year)* [blank]

Fill-Ins§10.4.4 assumes a label followed by a field. Here there is no label — the sentence is the label, and one sentence can hold three blanks. The sentence MUST NOT be broken up into key-value lines, and a key MUST NOT be made up from the words before a blank.

The sub-cases
The page prints Output
A blank inside a sentence [blank] in its printed position
A hint inside or beside the blank The hint as printed, next to its own blank, once
A caption under the line The caption kept with that blank, once, never duplicated
A currency glyph before a blank $[blank], keeping the printed spacing
✅ Sample — blanks inside bulleted sentences

Each bullet is a sentence with one percentage blank in it; the indented group prints a short label, =, then the blank. The page also carries a three-row table whose last column is an unlabelled tick box.

✅ Sample — hints printed inside the blanks

Executed on the (date) ___ day of (month) ___ (year) ___: the hints sit before each blank, in blue italic. Print Your Name: and Your Signature: are ordinary labelled fill-ins; the (If any) hint of Lawyer Signature: stays beside its blank.

✅ Sample — captions printed under the line

A notarial block where the caption is set in small capitals beneath each dotted line — NAME, DATE, SIGNATURE OF DEPONENT — and a fee line that prints $ before its blank. A standalone line takes its caption as its label, with no colon because the two sit on different lines; the NAME line inside the sentence keeps its caption right after its blank.

Related
  • Fill-Ins§10.4.4 — the labelled case this rule extends
  • Ids and Labels§10.3.1 — a label is verbatim, which is why inventing one is a failure
  • Fields Outside the Form§10.5.1 — non-field prose on a form page

10.4.2 Checkboxes

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-checkboxes · forms

✅ Normative

A checked box MUST be rendered as [x] and an unchecked box as [ ]. An unchecked box MUST be transcribed explicitly and MUST NOT be dropped.

What counts as checked

A box is checked when it holds a clear, unambiguous mark inside it — a check, a cross, a filled box.

  • Handwriting or a mark near a box MUST NOT make it checked.
  • A box whose state is in doubt MUST be rendered [ ].
  • A decorative bullet (●) printed beside a required field is not a check mark.
The rendered page decides

A check mark can exist only as drawn strokes with no text-layer glyph — common on degraded scans. The state MUST be read from the rendered page, never from the text layer: a tick the text layer never saw is still a tick. See The Page Is the Ground Truth§2.1.

A lone labelled checkbox

The box sits in the value position:

- **FATCA filing requirement**: [x]
- \[D\] **Check if this is a publicly traded partnership (PTP)**: [ ]
A checkbox with its own write-in

One line — the box first, then the entered text:

- \[3\] [x] 8888
- **Other (specify):** [x] consulting
Every box on the page

A checkbox MUST be included wherever it sits — header, margin, footer: Final K-1 / Amended K-1 at the very top of a K-1, CORRECTED (if checked) at the top of a 1099. See Fields Outside the Form§10.5.1.

Radio buttons

A radio control MUST be rendered with the same [ ] / [x] notation as a checkbox. Every option MUST be kept, with its grouping, and a printed pick-one instruction MUST be kept as text.

✅ Sample — radio buttons beside checkboxes

A motion form with [ ☐ ] bracketed boxes for the reasons and [ ○ ] bracketed circles for DENIED / GRANTED and objects / does not object. The circles are pick-one controls; the notation is [ ] or [x], preserving each printed state. A Print Form button sits at the foot.

Related
  • Option Groups§10.4.5 — several boxes answering one question
  • Checklists§10.4.3 — items each led by a box, with no question asked
  • Tables Inside Forms§10.5.4 — checkboxes inside a grid
  • Fields Outside the Form§10.5.1 — boxes in headers and footers

10.4.3 Checklists

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-checklists · forms checkboxes

✅ Normative

Each checklist item MUST be rendered box-first — the box before its printed label — and items MUST be nested under their group label. A group-level box MUST stay on its group's line. A form's group labels MUST NOT be promoted to document headings.

A list of items each led by a box, sometimes under a group label that carries a box of its own. Nothing is being answered; the page is a to-do list or a required-documents list.

☐ Division 9 rate filings
    ☐ Transmittal information
    ☐ Certification (EC-1, residential property)
    ☐ Rate filing checklist (Exhibit A)

- [ ] **Division 9 rate filings**
  - [ ] Transmittal information
  - [ ] Certification (EC-1, residential property)
  - [ ] Rate filing checklist (Exhibit A)

A checklist item has no caption above it and no label before its box, so neither shape of The Key-Value List§10.3.2 applies unchanged: it is not an option of a captioned group, and it is not a labelled field with a box in the value position. It is rendered box-first, like an option line.

✅ Sample — a filing checklist

Two bold group labels, each with a large box before it; ten and one indented items under them, each with a smaller box. Four labelled fill-ins sit in the top-right corner.

✅ Sample — boxes on section headings of a court form

PAYMENT OF CLAIM:, DENIAL OF CLAIM and COUNTERCLAIM: each carry a box before the label; the denial line then prints two more boxes inside its sentence (hearing {or} jury trial). Each label stays on its box's line, with what it governs nested beneath it; none becomes a heading.

✅ Sample — an option group laid out in two rows

Audit history … is followed by five boxed options set in three columns over two rows, with no ids. With no ids to follow, the options are read row by row, like any unnumbered grid of equal items.

Blank lines used as check marks

A short printed line that stands where a box would be, in front of a checklist item, is a checklist control: it MUST be rendered [ ] (or [x] when marked). [blank] MUST be used only when the line asks for a written value.

✅ Sample — blank lines used as check marks

Every item is led by ___ rather than a box, including the indented * SCHEDULE A … * SCHEDULE J run. A REFERENCE column of citations sits at the right margin under its own printed header, aligned to the items, so each section is a two-column table whose item cells hold the checklist.

A grid of checklists

A ruled grid whose cells each hold a checklist is a table: the cells are the table's content, and each cell's checklist is rendered as list items inside the cell.

✅ Sample — nine checklists in a grid

A three-by-three ruled grid, each cell a centred title over a list of boxed items, some with an italic qualifier. The cells are the table's content and the boxes are the cells' content.

A box printed before an id

The order of box and id. A lettered or numbered item can print its box before its id: ☐ (h) The crime of …. It MUST be rendered box first, then the escaped id — - [ ] \[h\] The crime of … — so that the box always opens the line whether or not an id follows it.

✅ Sample — a box before a lettered id

Items (h) to (k) each print a box, then the letter id, then a paragraph with blanks inside it. Each line opens with the box, then the escaped id: - [ ] \[h\].

Related
  • Checkboxes§10.4.2 — what counts as checked
  • Option Groups§10.4.5 — boxes answering one captioned question
  • The Key-Value List§10.3.2 — the two field shapes a checklist sits between
  • Form Reading Order§10.5.2 — ids decide the order; where there are none, rows do

10.4.4 Fill-Ins

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-fill-ins · forms

✅ Normative

Each printed entry field MUST be rendered as one line. An empty field MUST be rendered as [blank] and MUST NOT be omitted.

The blank is the word marker [blank], like the protocol's other markers ([signature], [seal], [stamp]). It replaces the older [___], whose underscores pair up as emphasis whenever two blanks share a line (from [___] to [___]) and vanish when the Markdown is rendered. A printed bracketed word [blank] on the page is escaped, \[blank\] — see Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4.

- \[1\] **Wages, tips, other compensation**: 29,513
- \[7\] **Social security tips**: [blank]
- \[9\]: [blank]
The shapes
The page prints Output
id + label + value - \[1\] **Label**: value
id, no label (shaded or unused boxes) - \[9\]: [blank]
neither id nor label, filled the bare value
neither id nor label, empty a bare [blank]
An empty field is content

An empty field says this was asked and not answered. Dropping it loses that, and the field count no longer matches the form — on a W-2 that is boxes 7–11, on a 1040 page 2 most of lines 17–31.

Adjacent boxes are separate fields

Two entry boxes printed side by side under one id are two fields and MUST NOT be fused into one value. W-2 box 15 prints State and Employer's state ID number side by side:

- \[15\]
  - **State**: SC
  - **Employer's state ID number**: 00-0000056

A currency glyph before a blank

A currency glyph printed before an empty field MUST be kept immediately before the blank — $[blank] — with any printed spacing preserved. The field's label MUST stay unchanged: the glyph is not folded into it.

✅ Sample — $ in empty cells

Every value cell in the Part III grids prints a $ and nothing else; two print N/A. Each $ cell is an empty field with its glyph kept: $[blank].

✅ Sample — $ before a dotted fee line

The bottom of a notarial form: $ then a dotted blank captioned FEE beneath the line. The same page is the sample for Blanks Inside Sentences§10.4.1.

A field printed as several ruled lines

One answer field MUST be rendered as one [blank], however many ruled writing lines it offers. Separate blanks MUST be emitted only for fields that are separately labelled or independently answerable.

✅ Sample — numbered answer areas of four lines each

Items 24, 25 and 26 each print four ruled lines, then three checkbox lines, the last with a blank inside its sentence (OBJECTION# ______ listed above). Each item's four lines are one field.

Values printed before anyone fills the form

A preprinted or computed value MUST be transcribed exactly as printed, including 0 % and 0.00. A visible value MUST NOT be replaced with a blank.

✅ Sample — computed zeros in an unfilled invoice

Yellow input cells sit empty; every item row prints 0 % under % Total Budget and % Spent To Date, and the total rows print 0.00. A [A] reference tag sits beside the first total.

✅ Sample — a totals block under an empty grid

Six empty item rows, then Subtotal, Sales Tax, Shipping/Handling, TOTAL continuing the frame's two right-hand columns, each printing 0.00; the last with a $. The totals stay in the table, and every empty row is kept.

A label with no blank after it

An empty entry label such as Signed: or Date: MUST be followed by [blank] when the surrounding form clearly asks for that value, even though no line, box or space is drawn. A field MUST NOT be inferred from a colon in ordinary prose.

✅ Sample — signature lines with no line

Corresponding Author: with Signed: and Date: nested beneath it, each followed by a run of dashes and no ruled line or box. Each is an empty field.

✅ Sample — dotted lines as answer areas

Six full-width dotted lines continue a statement from the previous page; Answer …… after each of three questions; Dated at …… this …… day of …… 20…… with four blanks in one sentence. The six lines are one field, and each Answer word stays beside its blank.

✅ Sample — spreadsheet errors as printed values

A rotated-header pro-forma grid whose Utility Rebate column prints #DIV/0! in every row and whose totals print $0, under a SAMPLE watermark; a [enter contract # ] placeholder in the title and a <<State Institution>> placeholder in the corner header. The error strings are printed values and are kept; the Simple Payback (Years) column has a header and no body cells.

10.4.5 Option Groups

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-option-groups · forms

✅ Normative

A question answered by ticking one or more of several printed boxes MUST be rendered as one group: the caption line, then one nested box-first line per option. Every printed option MUST be listed, ticked or not.

Pick-one
- **Filing Status**
  - [x] Single
  - [ ] Married filing jointly
  - [ ] Married filing separately (MFS)
  - [ ] Head of household (HOH)
  - [ ] Qualifying widow(er) (QW)
A group whose caption is only its id

W-2 box 13 prints three independent checkboxes. They are one printed cluster, so they are one group, captioned by the id alone:

- \[13\]
  - [x] Statutory employee
  - [ ] Retirement plan
  - [ ] Third-party sick pay
Options keep their own ids and may carry a write-in

An option MUST keep its printed id — here printed before the box, and written there — and an option with a write-in MUST carry the write-in after its box:

- \[16\] **Tax (see instructions). Check if any from Form(s):**
  - \[1\] [ ] 8814
  - \[2\] [ ] 4972
  - \[3\] [ ] [blank]
- \[16\]: 0.00

The line-16 amount is a separate unlabelled entry that shares the printed id, rendered right after the group. An id printed once per role appears once per role; that is not a duplicate.

Yes/No questions are option groups

A caption with two boxes — a virtual-currency question, K-1 items G and H1 — has the same structure as a five-option filing status and MUST be rendered the same way.


Source: IRS Form 1040 (2020), digital-asset question line (public domain)

- **At any time during 2020, did you receive, sell, send, exchange, or otherwise acquire any financial interest in any virtual currency?**
  - [x] Yes
  - [ ] No
Related
  • Checkboxes§10.4.2 — the state of each box
  • The Key-Value List§10.3.2 — the line format
  • Ids and Labels§10.3.1 — option ids and caption ids

10.4.6 Printed Buttons and Placeholders

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-printed-buttons-and-placeholders · forms furniture

✅ Normative

The text of a printed button, and the caption of a box reserved for a later stamp or seal, MUST be transcribed as text where it sits, in reading order. A reserved box is not a fill-in and MUST NOT be rendered with [blank].

Fillable PDFs export their widgets into the page: Print, Save, Clear buttons and the notice beside them. Court forms reserve empty boxes — [SEAL], File Stamp Here, COURT USE ONLY — for something to be added by hand later.

Printed thing Rendering
Buttons — Print · Save · Clear in coloured pills at the page foot their text, as text, in reading order — they are printed, so they are kept (never drop)
Reserved boxes — an empty ruled box whose caption says what will go in it the caption as text, nothing else — no blank, since nothing is filled in there (never invent)
✅ Sample — buttons and a seal placeholder

Print, Save, Clear in coloured boxes at the foot, a grey notice beside them, and an empty box captioned [SEAL] at the left of item 5. Item 5 also nests a second row of options under d. The button labels and the [SEAL] caption are plain text.

✅ Sample — an empty stamp box in a caption

File Stamp Here inside an otherwise empty ruled box on the right of the caption block. It is rendered as its caption, with no blank.

✅ Sample — a web page printed to paper

Accordion rows with chevrons, a See Less toggle, a text input printing its placeholder Enter tracking or barcode numbers, and an FAQs button, all scanned. The browser's own header and footer URL are printed too. Every visible string is kept as text.

Related
  • Fill-Ins§10.4.4 — a blank a person fills in, which these are not
  • Seals and Round Stamps§7.3.9 — what arrives in the reserved box
  • Court Caption Blocks§5.4 — where the reserved box usually sits

10.5 Structure

10.5.1 Fields Outside the Form

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-fields-outside-the-form · forms

✅ Normative

A field printed in a header, a footer or anywhere outside the main form body MUST still be rendered. A field printed above the form MUST be placed before the form content; any other such field MUST be placed after it.

CORRECTED, Final K-1, Amended K-1 sit outside the ruled form body and are easy to sweep past, but each changes what the whole document means: a K-1 marked Amended is not the same filing as one that is not.

Non-field text

Instructions, preambles and fine print on a form page MUST be transcribed at their printed reading position, between the fields they accompany. They MUST NOT be gathered at the end of the region or dropped.

✅ Sample — an instruction between two sections

"Skip this section if both parties signed Section 12 above." sits between the section 13 heading and its first field, in blue. It is not a field and is transcribed where it is printed.

Related
  • Checkboxes§10.4.2 — header and footer boxes are still checkboxes
  • Form Reading Order§10.5.2 — the order of the fields inside the form
  • The Key-Value List§10.3.2 — the line format for these fields too

10.5.2 Form Reading Order

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-form-reading-order · forms

✅ Normative

The fields of a form MUST be ordered by the form's printed indexing scheme — its ids — rather than by column-first or row-first geometry.

A form's ids are its intended order. Where lettered and numbered fields share a page, one scheme MUST be read through, then the other, rather than sweeping across the page and interleaving them.

An id sequence stays contiguous
  • Fields whose ids run in sequence MUST stay together and in order, with no un-id'd field between them.
  • Unlabelled fields MUST be placed around the sequence, not inside it. A 1099-MISC is the standard case.
Sections do not interleave

Fields from different printed sections MUST NOT be mixed, even when they sit side by side on the page.

Where this differs from block reading order

Reading Order§5.9 orders regions on a page the way a person reads them. This rule orders fields within a form, and the form's own numbering overrides visual position when the two disagree — which on a dense tax form they routinely do. Where a group of fields prints no ids, the order of Reading Order§5.9 applies.

Related
  • Sections and Grouped Fields§10.5.3 — the sections that must not interleave
  • Ids and Labels§10.3.1 — what an id is
  • Fields Outside the Form§10.5.1 — fields outside the body go before or after it
  • Reading Order§5.9 — the order of regions, and of fields with no ids

10.5.3 Sections and Grouped Fields

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-sections-and-grouped-fields · forms

✅ Normative

A printed heading that names a group of fields opens a section. Only a printed grouping MAY get a parent: fields MUST NOT be wrapped in a section or group the form does not print.

A printed grouping takes one of two shapes, depending on its size.

Form grouping and the document outline

The Markdown headings of this rule delimit local form groups. They do not make every form label a section of the document: a form's section labels are form content and MUST NOT be added to the containing page's outline — least of all inside an embedded screenshot of a form. See Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7 for form furniture and real document titles.

Band or part headings become Markdown headings

A bold or boxed caption in the margin or spanning the page — Part I, Filing Status, POLICY INFORMATION, Sign Here — MUST be rendered as a ### heading, and every field printed under or beside it MUST follow that heading.

The heading is in addition to the field labels inside it; both MUST be kept.

Where a printed designator sits beside a descriptive title, the designator is the id and the title is the heading text:

### \[Part II\] Information About the Partner

- \[E\] **Partner's SSN or TIN (Do not use TIN of a disregarded entity. See inst.)**: 38-7714902
- \[I1\] **What type of entity is this partner?**: CORPORATION

Bands with no printed ids work the same way:

### POLICY INFORMATION

- **PROPOSED EFF DATE**: 08/23/2026
- **PROPOSED EXP DATE**: 08/23/2027
- **PAYMENT PLAN**: MONTHLY
- **MINIMUM PREMIUM**: [blank]
- **POLICY PREMIUM**: 34,259.95

A section almost never holds a single field. One field under a heading usually means the heading was invented.

Small captioned boxes become nested list items

A printed box whose label groups a few entries MUST be rendered as a parent list item with its entries nested one level beneath it:

- \[e\]
  - **Employee's first name and initial**: Joan Jackson
  - **Last name**: [blank]
  - **Suff.**: [blank]
- \[12a\]
  - **Code**: D
  - 1,500.00
- \[15\]
  - **State**: SC
  - **Employer's state ID number**: 00-0000056

The 12a amount slot prints no label, so it is the bare value; an unlabelled empty entry would be a bare [blank] — see Fill-Ins§10.4.4.

Repeating groups without labels

Field groups that repeat without a printed heading are anonymous groups in printed order, separated by blank lines, with no invented Vehicle 1 heading — see Repeated and Unlabelled Fields§10.2.

Never invent a wrapper

The W-2 is almost entirely flat. It prints no Identification or Employer grouping, so neither appears in the output. Inventing one is the same failure as inventing a table header: it adds structure the page does not have.

Related
  • The Key-Value List§10.3.2 — the line format inside each section
  • Fill-Ins§10.4.4 — the entries a box groups
  • Form Reading Order§10.5.2 — sections do not interleave
  • Ids and Labels§10.3.1 — the designator beside a section title

10.5.4 Tables Inside Forms

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

forms-tables-inside-forms · forms tables

✅ Normative

Inside a form, a table MUST be used only for a genuine grid: one shared set of printed column headers over repeating rows of the same shape, or a printed row-by-column matrix. Where it is ambiguous, the fields SHOULD be rendered as individual field lines.

Numbered form lines are never table rows

A line with its own caption and one amount box is a field line, even when the amount boxes align into a ruled column. It MUST be rendered as a field line, not as a table row: the alignment is typesetting, the caption is the structure.

Dollars and cents printed in two ruled columns MUST be rendered as one value — 1,234.00 — never split.

A matrix keeps its blank corner

The empty corner header of a matrix MUST be kept. Dropping it shifts every heading one column left:

<table>
  <tr><th></th><th>Beginning</th><th>Ending</th></tr>
  <tr><td>Profit</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td></tr>
  <tr><td>Loss</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td></tr>
  <tr><td>Capital</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td></tr>
</table>

This is the rule of a blank corner cell in any table§9.3.1.

Cells carry the normal form notation
  • A checkbox cell MUST be rendered [x] or [ ]. A blank cell intended to be checked is a checkbox; a blank cell not intended to be checked stays empty.
  • Every printed row MUST be emitted, blank rows included, as full rows of empty cells. Rows MUST NOT be merged, reordered or added.
  • Each entry belongs to its own row's rule lines, never to a neighbour's. Insurance-application coverage grids are the stress test.
  • A cell containing form fields MUST use the normal form notation, as list items inside the cell.
<tr><td>Jane</td><td>Doe</td><td>987-65-4321</td><td>Daughter</td><td>[x]</td><td>[ ]</td></tr>
<tr><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td>- [ ]</td><td>- [ ]</td></tr>
A table as a field's value

Some keyed entries take a grid as their value. The key MUST stay a normal field line, and the table MUST be placed below it, indented to the list item's content column, with a blank line on each side:

- \[J\] **Partner's share of profit, loss, and capital (see instructions):**

  <table>
    <tr><th></th><th>Beginning</th><th>Ending</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Profit</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td><td>1.0000000000 %</td></tr>
  </table>

- **Check if decrease is due to sale or exchange of partnership interest.**: [ ]

The indent is load-bearing. An indented table belongs to the list item, so the list — and the depth of everything after it — survives. A flush-left table between bullets ends the list and flattens everything that follows.

Not every table on a form page is form content

A large standalone data table that is not part of the fillable form — an embedded financial schedule — is an ordinary table. See Is This Even a Table§9.1.5.

✅ Sample — a self-certification form built from grids

Part III prints two side-by-side asset grids sharing one header row (Type of Asset, (A) Cash Value*, (B) Annual Income), each rendered as its own table; Parts I, II and IV are field lines, and the description tables under Parts III and IV are empty pre-printed rows. Several empty value cells print only a $ — see Fill-Ins§10.4.4.

§11 Charts

11.1 The annotation

11.1.1 Cover Every Data Point

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-cover-every-data-point · charts basics

✅ Normative

A chart MUST be rendered as a chart table that holds every data point the chart draws: every category position × every series, plus every printed callout that belongs to a position. A data point MUST NOT be skipped because it is hard to read; it MAY be left out only when no printed text can locate it or it is genuinely unreadable.

A chart is a data display, so its conforming rendering is its content — see Images and Figures§12.1.2. A rendering that gets a few prominent points right while the rest of the chart is missing is not a rendering of the chart.

What full coverage means
Chart Data points the chart table MUST hold
Grouped or stacked bars positions × series (the sample below: 6 years × 4 groups = 24 values)
Single series one per position
Printed callouts and totals one each, where a printed label can locate them — see Legend and Overlay Values§11.2.4
Multi-panel figure every panel, without exception — see Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3

Two kinds of position MUST still be covered:

  • A labeled position with no mark is a data point whose value is 0 — the histogram's empty 1500 bin is 0 (see Bars and Histograms§11.2.1).
  • A position the axis does not label is located by its axis value: 2023 on a year axis that ticks every third year, 2500 on a bin axis that labels every other bin. The printed, regularly labeled axis is the calibration; a position that no printed calibration reaches is not locatable.
What may be left out

The default is in. A data point that can be read MAY be left out only when:

  • no printed text can uniquely locate it — see Labels§11.1.2; the unnamed companion curve in Legend and Overlay Values§11.2.4 is the standing example; or
  • it is genuinely unreadable — too blurred, too dense, or overlapping beyond judgment.

Leaving a point out MUST NOT be replaced by invented text: a made-up series name, a made-up category or a placeholder cell stands for nothing on the page (see Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2).

The page is the only reference

Values are read from the page. A value MUST NOT be shaded towards what some parser or earlier rendering produced, and a correct value stays correct however many renderings disagree with it (see The Page Is the Ground Truth§2.1).

The chart table

Every table representing a chart MUST open with <table data-source="chart">. The data-source="chart" attribute belongs on the opening <table> tag, including when the chart prints a data grid that supplies the table's content (see Chart With a Printed Data Grid§9.1.2). A table representing an ordinary printed table MUST NOT carry data-source="chart".

The layout of the chart table. A chart table MUST be laid out as follows, so that every chart table reads the same way — category down, series across:

  • one HTML <table data-source="chart"> per chart or panel, at the chart's place in reading order;
  • the chart's title, subtitle or caption in <caption> inside that table, first or last according to reading order (see Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3); its printed notes and source follow the table;
  • one row per category position (axis tick, bar, bin, slice, tile, region, named point), in the order the axis runs — left to right, top to bottom, a pie clockwise from the top;
  • a first column holding the category labels, then one column per series in legend order;
  • a header row holding the printed series names, its first cell holding the printed category-axis title or left empty; a single series with no printed name is headed by the printed value-axis title; when nothing printed names any column, the table has no header row;
  • a printed total that is not itself a category (a stack total above its bar) sits in a last column under an empty header cell;
  • printed text of the chart that is not a data point — axis titles not used as headers, unit notes, reference-line labels, event callouts, annotation boxes, legend entries of series that carry no value — follows the table as plain text in reading order.

The value in each cell is governed by Values and Tolerances§11.1.4; the labels in the first column and the header row by Labels§11.1.2.

✅ Sample — digital-services-survey-2024_p62

Six stacked bars over six labeled years, four legend series, every segment printing its value: full coverage is 6 × 4 = 24 values, all printed, so all copied as printed — count and share together.
