11.1.2 Labels

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-labels · charts labels

✅ Normative

The category labels and series names of a chart table MUST be text printed on the chart — an axis tick, a legend entry, a direct label — copied verbatim. A label MUST NOT carry unit text imported from elsewhere on the page, colour words, chart-type words or an expanded abbreviation, and two dimensions MUST NOT be merged into one label.

Each value in a chart table is located by the labels on its row and in its column, so the labels are the lookup key of the whole table: a value under the wrong label is a wrong value.

Which label goes where
Chart Row label Column label
Single series the category (Cleaners) — see Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 the series name, or the value-axis title when no name is printed
Two-dimensional (grouped, stacked, multi-line) the category (China) the series (Ride hailing)
Grouped or nested categories the category, with its printed group (axis tier) in a column of its own where the category alone repeats the series

A value MUST sit at the intersection of exactly the labels that locate it: its category's row and its series' column. Dimensions stay independent — 2024 in the row and Revenue in the column, never one label 2024 - Revenue.

Verbatim, and what "no units" means

Each label is one printed string, copied whole — SEA, > 15000, Option-Adjusted Spread (OAS), REDBIKE (Akira), first-day-of-month price. Parentheses printed inside a legend entry are part of the legend text and MUST be kept.

The no-units requirement forbids importing unit text from elsewhere on the page into a label. Where the axis corner prints (millions of euros) and the tick prints 2024, the label is 2024, not 2024 (millions of euros). Likewise Revenue, not Revenue (USD bn), when the unit prints as an axis note rather than inside the legend entry. The unit note itself is not dropped: it stays in the output as the chart's own text (see Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1).

A label MUST NOT be rewritten:

  • no colour words — Blue line - GDP Growth is GDP Growth;
  • no descriptive or chart-type suffixes — no (line), no (bars);
  • no expanded abbreviations — SEA stays SEA.
Positions the axis does not label

A position on a printed, regularly labeled axis that carries no tick label of its own is labeled by its axis value — 2023 on a year axis ticked every third year, 2500 on a bin axis labeled every other bin. That label is a reading against printed calibration, not invented text (see Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1).

Several charts with the same labels

Each chart or panel has its own chart table with its own printed title in <caption> (see Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3), so charts that reuse one label set are told apart by their captions, without altering their labels. The caption appears once inside the table, first or last according to reading order (see Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3).

  • The twin pies in Legend and Overlay Values§11.2.4 reuse every slice name; each pie's title (Month of September 2025: $346B, Fiscal Year 2025 to Date: $7,010B) is what distinguishes them.
  • The solar panels in Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3 need nothing more: China with 619 appears only in the avoided-emissions panel.

A point that no printed label can locate is not rendered in the chart table (see Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1); the unnamed companion curve in Legend and Overlay Values§11.2.4 is the standing example.

✅ Sample — mobility-survey-2024_p13

Four legend series over eight labeled regions, every value printed on its bar: 32 values, rows labeled from the axis and columns from the legend, verbatim. Region abbreviations stay as printed (SEA, ME, NEA). The values printed in heavier type are bold in the table; the red ones carry no colour mark, since colour on a data label is styling.

11.1.3 Multiple Charts and Reference Ink

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-multiple-charts-and-reference-ink · charts structure

✅ Normative

Each chart or panel on a page MUST get its own chart table, and every panel MUST be covered (see Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1). Reference ink — labeled averages, trend lines, shaded bands, event callouts — draws no data points and MUST NOT be rendered as data: it gets no row, no column and no value in any chart table. Its printed text MUST still be kept.

Several charts on one page

Every chart and every panel of a multi-panel figure is its own chart table, in reading order, with its printed title or panel heading in <caption>. The same one-row-per-position, one-column-per-series coverage applies to each. Where charts share a label set, each table's caption tells them apart (see Labels§11.1.2).

A caption shared by several panels MUST appear once: first inside the first panel's table when read before the group, or last inside the last panel's table when read after the group. A shared caption and that panel's own title are kept in printed order within the same <caption>.

Ink printed once for several panels — a shared axis title, a single legend serving every panel — MUST NOT be lost:

  • a shared legend names the series of every panel it serves, so each panel's table carries those series names as its column headers;
  • a shared axis title is printed text of the figure and is kept once, as text.
Reference ink is not data
Reference ink Why it is not data
A labeled average or trend line (10-year average, a line fitted through a scatter) it summarises the data points; it is not one of them
A shaded band or background region it marks a span of the axis, not a value
An event callout naming a year (1976: Tangshan Earthquake, China — see Log Scale Charts§11.2.6) it comments on a point; its value is the point's own

A chart table that gains a column for a trend line, or a row for a shaded band, contains values the chart never drew as data — invented content (see Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2). The printed labels of reference ink are text on the page, kept as text, after the table in reading order — see the chart table's layout in Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1.

✅ Sample — RenewablesDeploymentTracker2024_p13

Six titled panels — five bar panels (World, China, European Union, United States, India) over the same five years, and one horizontal panel (Avoided emissions) over regions — every bar printing its value: 30 values in six tables. Each single-series panel is headed by its value-axis title (GW, Mt CO₂). China appears both as a panel and as a row of the avoided-emissions panel; each table's title keeps them apart. The bar values are printed in bold. The running header and tab label are elided.

✅ Sample — two panels sharing a legend and an axis

Two bar panels stacked vertically, each with its own underlined period caption (1960–1973, 1973–1980), over one rotated axis title on the far left and one legend that serves both. Each panel is its own table, and both tables carry the three legend series as their headers: read alone, the lower panel's bars are unnamed. The axis title, printed once, is kept once. Every bar prints its value; the printed minus signs are written -. The lower panel runs negative, bars descending below a zero line that crosses the panel. In the lower panel, the value label under Marolia's second bar is covered by the bar itself and that bar is drawn both above and below the zero line, so the Marolia row is elided. The running header is elided.

✅ Sample — sixteen small panels under two captions

Figure 3a and Figure 3b hold eight stacked-bar panels each, every panel headed by its deposition type and its element's flux title, each drawing ten stacks of four fill colours. No panel prints a site name, a tick value or a legend, so no bar can be located or calibrated: the panels carry no chart table, and the output keeps their printed headings and titles, in reading order. Figure 3b and the text below it are elided.

✅ Sample — recession bands behind four lines


Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Monthly Labor Review, February 2003, Chart 5 and Table 4 (public domain)

Four line styles, each named by a direct label with a leader line, over 33 years (1970–2002, the axis labeling every second year as 1970, 72, 74 …) and five grey vertical bands that the note says are recessions. The four named series are the table's columns; the bands are reference ink and add nothing to it, while the note that explains them is kept. No value is printed, so every cell is an estimate against the 2-point grid. Only the first two labeled years are shown; the table continues through 02, and the table sharing the page is elided.

11.1.4 Values and Tolerances

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-values-and-tolerances · charts values

✅ Normative

Each cell of a chart table holds one of three values. A value printed on the chart MUST be copied character for character and in full. A value not printed MUST be estimated at the mark's visual centre against the mark's own axis. A mark drawn at the baseline, or a labeled position with no mark, MUST be 0.

Printed values — copied exactly

Whatever the chart prints at, on or beside the mark is the value, in full:

  • 25 (13.0%) stays 25 (13.0%) — not 25, not 13.0%, and never 25 countries (13.0%);
  • printed formats stay: thousands separators (11,270), decimal commas (2,08), currency and percent marks, parentheses for negatives (($60B)), footnote markers (<sup>1,2</sup>3.60);
  • printed beats geometry: where the label says 43, the value is 43 even if the bar top measures a hair lower.
Estimated values — the visual centre

Where nothing is printed, the value is read at the mark's visual centre against its own axis — a second axis where the series is scaled by one (see Dual-Axis and Combo Charts§11.2.2), the decade bands of a logarithmic axis (see Log Scale Charts§11.2.6), and a stacked segment's own two boundaries (see Stacked Bars and Waterfalls§11.2.9).

An estimate SHOULD be a value a careful reader could defend within the readability tolerance below — neither falsely precise nor coarser than the axis allows.

How an estimated value is written. An estimated value MUST be written as a bare number in the axis's own format — its unit mark (2.5% on a percent axis) and its digit grouping (17 000 on an axis ticked 18 000) — with no approximation marker, and no more precise than the reading supports: at most one decimal place beyond the axis's tick labels, and two significant figures on a logarithmic axis. Whether a value was printed or estimated is recoverable from the page and is not marked in the Markdown.

Zeros

A mark drawn at the baseline is 0. A labeled position with no mark at all is also 0 — the histogram's empty 1500 bin is 0 (see Bars and Histograms§11.2.1). A stack that simply has no segment of one series leaves that cell empty instead (see Stacked Bars and Waterfalls§11.2.9).

Bars drawn in perspective

A printed bar value is copied first. Otherwise the value-bearing edge is read against the corresponding axis plane, excluding perspective depth. Where the reference plane is ambiguous, the value is the midpoint of the plausible readings.

How a checker compares values

A checker compares each cell with the value it reads off the page:

  • Printed value — the same number, compared exactly. Formatting variants of the same number (thousands separators, decimal comma or point, currency and percent marks) MAY be treated as equal; a different number is wrong.
  • Estimated value — accepted within a relative tolerance of the checker's own reading, chosen by how readable the mark is:
How readable is the mark? Relative tolerance
Sits on a gridline 0.05
Between gridlines, judgeable 0.1
Small, dense, or unclear scale 0.15 – 0.2
Near zero, where a relative band is too narrow wider, as the reading demands (a -1 read on a 10-unit grid takes 0.3)

Most estimates fall between 0.05 and 0.15, and a tolerance above 0.2 is exceptional. The tolerance is the range a careful eye can defend: not so tight that a second careful reading fails it, not so loose that a wrong reading passes. For bars drawn in perspective it is widened to cover every plausible reading.

✅ Sample — health-workforce-2024_p46

One series, twelve bars. Three bars print their number (43, 22, 5) and are copied exactly; the other nine are estimates against the 5-unit grid, most on or near a gridline (tolerance 0.05), the small Software developers bar harder to judge (0.1). Doctors stays 5 although its bar top measures a touch lower. The red EU average bar is an ordinary row: highlighting is styling, not structure. The single series has no printed name, so its column is headed by the value-axis title.

✅ Sample — bars drawn in perspective

Two 3-D bar charts with no printed values. Each bar has a front top edge and a back top edge at different heights. The axis ticks and the baseline sit on the front plane, so the front top edge is the value-bearing edge; every value below is an estimate, read to two significant figures on the first chart and to a tenth of a percent on the second. The tick labels print 1.200 and 12.00%, but an estimate is not written to that precision. The paragraphs between and around the charts are elided.

11.2 Chart types

11.2.1 Bars and Histograms

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-bars-and-histograms · charts types

✅ Normative

A bar chart MUST be rendered as a chart table with one value per bar: one row per category, one column per series. A histogram is a bar chart whose category is the bin: a bin the axis does not label MUST still get its row, labeled by its axis value, and a labeled position with no bar MUST hold 0.

  • A single series gives a two-column table — see the full example in Values and Tolerances§11.1.4.
  • Grouped bars give one column per legend series — see the full example in Labels§11.1.2.
  • Horizontal bars change nothing: the category axis simply runs vertically, and rows follow it top to bottom.
  • A highlighted or average bar (EU average, shaded behind the rest) is an ordinary row. An average line is reference ink and adds nothing to the table (see Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3).
Histogram bins

Printed bin labels are copied verbatim, catch-alls included (> 15000). When the axis labels only every other bin, the unlabeled bins still exist: each gets a row labeled by its axis value — 2000 between the ticks 1500 and 2500 on an axis labeled every $1 000. A bin that no printed calibration reaches is not locatable (see Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1).

✅ Sample — catastrophe-review-2025_p4

Bins every $500, labels every $1 000, a printed catch-all, and one labeled position (1500) with no bar. Full coverage is 29 rows: 1500 holds 0; the unlabeled bins are labeled by their axis values (2000, 3000 …); every count is an estimate against the 20-unit grid. The catch-all keeps its printed space (> 15000). The value axis title heads the single value column; the category axis title heads the label column.

Progress and target bars

A goal statement with a single bar, its current value marked on it and the target at its right end, is a one-row bar chart, not a chart type of its own. Its chart table MUST hold the current value, the target and the axis end-points: the bar's meaning is relative to its scale, and 7 against 8 or 42% against 50% is only legible with that scale kept.

✅ Sample — goal cards with progress bars

Three goal cards separated by rules. Each bar marks its current value (40%, 7, 42%, each with the year 2024 beneath it) against a scale from its start (0%, 0) to its target (100% with 2030 Target, 8 with 2025 Target). The rows follow the axis: start, current value, target. The third card's scale end-points fall below the crop and are not shown, so its table holds only the current value.

11.2.2 Dual-Axis and Combo Charts

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-dual-axis-and-combo-charts · charts types

✅ Normative

Bars and lines on one canvas, or a second value axis, change only how values are read: each series' values MUST be copied or estimated against its own axis. The chart table is laid out as usual — one row per x position, one column per series — and a series name MUST NOT gain its mark type or axis side (no (line), no right axis).

Before a value is estimated, the axis that scales its series is identified — from the legend order, the mark type and the magnitudes of each axis's tick labels — and the value is traced to that axis. A percentage series scaled by the right-hand axis read against the level axis on the left is a wrong value, however plausible it looks.

✅ Sample — industrial-group-financial-report-2024_p15

Two bar series in euros and a percentage line share one canvas; no value axis is drawn, and every mark prints its value, so every cell is copied rather than read. Full coverage is 15 values under the legend entries, copied whole (Earnings per share (EUR) keeps the parenthesis printed inside the legend). The chart prints decimal commas (2,08, 48,1%), and the cells keep them. The earnings values are printed in bold.

11.2.3 Gantt and Sankey Charts

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-gantt-and-sankey-charts · charts types

✅ Normative

A gantt chart MUST be rendered with one row per mark, giving the mark's label, its start and its end on the time axis — for a milestone, start and end are the same period. A sankey diagram MUST be rendered with one row per flow, giving its source node, its target node and the value it carries. Each family uses its one shape throughout, whatever the chart prints.

Gantt

The time axis is the value axis. Each bar's two edges are read against the printed ticks and written as the periods the axis prints: months as month tokens (Jan), quarters under year headers as quarter tokens with their year (Q1 2025). When the page prints exact dates for each task, those printed dates are the start and end; when it prints them as a table beside the bars, that printed table is the rendering and the bars add nothing to it (see Chart With a Printed Data Grid§9.1.2).

Nothing on the page prints the words start or end, and they MUST NOT be invented as labels of a mark; the pair lives in the row's two period cells.

How a gantt row is laid out. A gantt chart MUST be one table with one row per task bar or milestone, in the chart's top-to-bottom order: the printed label, the start period, the end period. Its header row MUST be Start | End over the two period columns, with the first cell holding the printed label column's title or left empty. These header cells are protocol vocabulary, like the markers [blank] or [logo: …]: the page does not print them, and they are the one deliberate exception to never invent, so that the columns can be read without guessing. They are written exactly as given.

A bar edge on a period boundary. A bar that fills January through March has its right edge on the April tick. Its end MUST be the last period the bar visibly fills (Mar), and one reading MUST be used throughout a document (see Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2). A checker accepts a reading one boundary off.

✅ Sample (constructed) — make_gantt

Four task bars and a diamond milestone on a month axis: five rows, the milestone with start and end both Dec. Design fills January to March and its end is Mar, the last month it fills.

✅ Sample — metro_s2_p18

Four task bars, one milestone and the revenue-service window on a quarter axis under two year headers — six rows in the chart's top-to-bottom order. The Sub Comp 2026 down-triangle is a single-position mark, so start and end are the same quarter; the double-headed RSD 2026 arrow spans the Q4 2026 column, both its edges in one quarter, so it too resolves to one period. A mark whose two edges fall in one quarter still gets its row. The dashed vertical line is a status marker with no label and adds nothing. The labels are printed in bold; the report headings above the chart are elided.

✅ Sample — guideway_schedule_p100

A schedule whose left-hand table prints each activity's ID, name, duration, start and finish: that printed table is the rendering, with its printed dates as the span of each bar, and the bar area to its right — year and quarter headers, bars, bar labels — adds nothing. The table lists 26 activities under group and crew bands. Long names are clipped at the edge of the name column and are written as far as they are visible ((cre on EGCC1270; on EGCC1350 the next letter is cut mid-glyph and left out). The first five activities are shown.

Sankey

A flow's value is the number it carries. Where only node totals are printed, a node with a single inflow or a single outflow gives that one flow its value, and the flow takes the same row shape. A node that both splits and merges has no single flow its total belongs to: its total gives no flow row, and its printed total is kept as text. A sankey that prints no values has no readable flows: ribbon widths MUST NOT be estimated.

Node names in the source and target cells are copied without any printed node total. A ribbon is traced from end to end before its row is written — values often print at the ribbon's start, far from the target node, and a thin ribbon can pass under several others. A ribbon that cannot be traced unambiguously gets no row.

How a sankey flow is laid out. A sankey diagram MUST be one table with one row per flow, ordered by source from top to bottom and then by target, under the header row Source | Target | Value. Each printed node total that is not any one flow's value follows the table as text, as printed (Industry 165). These header cells are protocol vocabulary, like the markers [blank] or [logo: …]: the page does not print them, and they are the one deliberate exception to never invent, so that the columns can be read without guessing. They are written exactly as given.

✅ Sample (constructed) — make_sankey

Every ribbon prints its value: four rows. Coal 120 and Wind 30 each feed a single flow, so their totals are already the flows' values; Gas 130, Industry 165 and Buildings 115 each join or split several flows, and their printed totals follow the table. The (TWh) in the printed title stays in the title. Node labels are printed in bold.

✅ Sample — llnl_energy_2023_p1


Source: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy — Estimated U.S. Energy Consumption in 2023 (public domain)

About 45 ribbons, each printing its own value in quads: one row per ribbon. Six of them, thick and thin, are shown; the rest of the table, the node totals that are no single flow's value, and the source note are elided. All text on this chart is printed in bold.

✅ Sample — material-flows-2020_p4

Nothing prints on the ribbons — every number is a node total. Where a node has a single inflow or a single outflow, its total is that one flow's value: fourteen flows are read out this way, in the same row shape as a chart whose ribbons print values. Processed material (7.98) and Total emissions (2.60) each merge several inflows and split into several outflows, so their totals are no single flow's value: they give no row and follow the table as printed. Backfiling is copied as printed. All chart text is printed in bold.

How a checker judges spans and flows

A gantt span and a sankey flow are judged on meaning, not on a table shape: a checker accepts any output that conveys both endpoints of a span at the granularity the axis prints — a positional grid correctly aligned to the periods included — and accepts a span end one period boundary off. A flow is accepted wherever the output conveys its source, its target and its value together. A flow or span whose parts are scattered so that they can no longer be paired is not conveyed.

11.2.4 Legend and Overlay Values

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-legend-and-overlay-values · charts types

✅ Normative

When a chart's values are printed only in its legend or as data labels over its marks, those printed numbers are the data: every one of them MUST be in the chart table, copied exactly. A companion series without printed values is estimated as usual — unless no printed label can locate its points, in which case it has no column (see Labels§11.1.2).

Values print in three places, and all three are treated the same (see Values and Tolerances§11.1.4):

Where the value prints What goes in the table
On or beside each mark — bar-top numbers, slice amounts, point callouts the printed value in the mark's cell
In the legend — Solar (45%)-style entries the name part as the row or column label, the number part as the value
At a direct label — a line end stating its value (see Line Charts§11.2.5) the printed value in the cell of that end position
✅ Sample — MonthlyTreasuryStatement_202509_p8


Source: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Monthly Treasury Statement — Figure 7 (public domain)

Twin pies sharing one legend, amounts printed beside the slices. Every slice name appears in both pies with a different value, so each pie is its own table under its own printed title, and the title is what tells them apart. Rows follow each pie clockwise from the top. The amounts are copied as printed — $1,581B with its separator, and ($60B), whose parentheses mark the Other slice of September as negative. The footnote under the legend is cut off at the bottom of the page and is elided.

✅ Sample — upstream_financial_review_2024_p9

A daily price curve with no printed name or values, and a triangle-marker series whose legend entry reads first-day-of-month price, all twelve of its values printed at the markers. The named series is the table's one column: 12 printed values, copied with their $. The daily curve has no printed name that could head a column — Jan alone also locates the marker series — so it gets no column. The two bold average statements are printed text, not data points, and follow the table.

Related
  • Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 — printed values, verbatim
  • Labels§11.1.2 — the twin pies told apart by their titles; the curve no label can locate
  • Maps and Treemaps§11.2.7 — compositions that are nothing but printed values
  • Dual-Axis and Combo Charts§11.2.2 — a combo chart whose every mark prints its value

11.2.5 Line Charts

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-line-charts · charts types

✅ Normative

A line chart MUST be rendered with one value per series per x position: one row per x position, one column per series, each series named by its legend entry or by its direct label at the line's end. A value printed at a point MUST be copied; every other value is read against the axis. Wiggles between x positions are not positions.

  • A line labeled directly at its end is a named series: the printed name at the line's end heads its column (see Labels§11.1.2).
  • An x position the axis does not label is labeled by its axis value (see Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1).
  • A labeled trend, average or reference line adds no column (see Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3).
  • Scenario lines that share one drawn curve early on have identical values in those positions — correct, not a copying slip.
✅ Sample — health-workforce-2024_p45

Five lines named by their direct labels over eleven labeled years, nothing printed on the lines: 5 × 11 = 55 values, each the line's centre at the year read against the 5-unit grid (tolerance 0.05 where the vertex sits near a gridline, 0.1 where it does not). Columns follow the direct labels from top to bottom. The value-axis title follows the table. The axis also prints a stray . after 2022, at a position with no line; it is not given a row.

✅ Sample — energy-outlook-2025_p20

Three scenario lines named and valued by their end labels (High: 11 Tcf, +150% …). The name part heads each column; the rest of the label, printed at the 2040 end of the line, is that line's 2040 value, copied whole — the Low label's second line (from 2024 levels) included. The Low line ends near 8.5 on the axis, but its printed 8 Tcf wins. Every other value is an estimate on the 2-unit grid; the shared early curve gives all three series the same values in 2024 and 2026, and Mid and Low the same values in 2028 and 2030. The rows are the 9 printed ticks (2024–2040, every second year): 3 × 9 = 27 values.

Related
  • Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 — printed values beat axis readings
  • Labels§11.1.2 — direct labels as series names
  • Log Scale Charts§11.2.6 — the same reading over logarithmic bands
  • Dual-Axis and Combo Charts§11.2.2 — lines sharing a canvas with bars

11.2.6 Log Scale Charts

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-log-scale-charts · charts types

✅ Normative

A logarithmic axis changes the reading, not the chart table. Unprinted values MUST be estimated against the printed decade bands, by the mark's position inside its band, and SHOULD be given to no more than two significant figures.

On a tenfold-per-band axis the same visual gap covers ever larger ranges, so a value is interpolated by position inside the band, not linearly: a mark a third of the way from 1 000 to 10 000 is near 2 000, not near 4 000. The tolerance a checker allows is chosen by readability like any estimate (see Values and Tolerances§11.1.4).

Event callouts naming years (1976: Tangshan Earthquake, China) are commentary: they add no row or column, and their text is kept as text (see Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3).

✅ Sample — catastrophe-review-2025_p26

Two charts over the same 55-year axis ticked every third year: event counts on a linear axis (Figure 16) and victims on 1 000 → 10 000 000 decade bands (Figure 17). Each has its own table under its own title, both series across all 55 years — the ticked years by their printed labels, the years between by their axis values (1971, 2023). On the log chart, every value is a band-position estimate to two significant figures, written in the axis's digit grouping, except the two 2024 values, which the side text prints (11 000, 3 200): printed beats geometry, so they are copied. The event callouts and the side text follow the log chart's table as text. Only the first two and last two years of each table are shown.

Related
  • Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 — estimates and tolerances, whatever the axis
  • Line Charts§11.2.5 — the linear-axis version of the same coverage
  • Labels§11.1.2 — axis-value labels for unticked years
  • Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3 — event callouts as commentary

11.2.7 Maps and Treemaps

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-maps-and-treemaps · charts types

✅ Normative

A treemap MUST be rendered with one row per tile: the tile's label and its printed value. Tile area MUST NOT be turned into a value: no axis calibrates it. A map with printed values per region MUST be rendered with one row per printed region–value pair. A shading-only map with a discrete legend MUST give each region whose fill matches one swatch unambiguously that legend class, copied verbatim.

Treemaps

A tile's printed value is copied as printed. A tile that prints no value, only a comparator (<1%), or a truncated label (Re…) gets no estimated value: its printed text is kept as it is, and nothing is read from its area.

✅ Sample — threat-report-2025_p29

Every tile prints its label and share: eight rows in reading order, left to right and top to bottom. The percent sign is printed raised beside each number and is written as a superscript. All tile text is set in a heavier weight.

✅ Sample — crypto_usage_report2024_p33

Eight tiles, every label copied whole, parenthesis and all. Seven print a number and the eighth, Social, prints <1% — a comparator, not a value. Its row keeps the printed <1%; no value is estimated from the sliver it draws. The footer's logo, copyright line and page number are elided.

Maps

Two readable layers, each with its own place in the table (see also Geographic Maps§12.2.4):

  • Values printed per region or per pin — one row per printed pair: the region or callout text as the label, the printed value copied as printed. A callout on a leader line (DE 1) is read like any other.
  • Shading with a discrete legend — each region's fill is compared with the legend swatches, and the region takes the legend class verbatim. A region whose fill falls between two adjacent swatches is given no class.

Where a map's classes go. A choropleth MUST be one table with one row per region, in reading order: the region label, its printed value when it has one, and its legend class in a last column headed by the legend's printed title (no header row when the legend has none). A region with an ambiguous fill has an empty class cell. Where the region names are recognised from the outlines rather than printed, the region column's header carries data-recognised — see Geographic Maps§12.2.4.

A checker judges a class on meaning: it accepts the class string, an equivalent range, or a value inside the class's range, and treats region-name variants (CO / Colorado) as the same region.

✅ Sample — apport_p19


Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Apportionment of the U.S. House of Representatives Based on the 2020 Census (public domain)

Both layers on one page: every state prints its seat count, and the fill classes its change, so each state's row holds both — 50 states. Five states are shown, then the rest; the DE 1 callout on a leader line is read like any other. Delaware's fill is too small to compare with the swatches, so its class cell is empty. The agency footer is elided.

✅ Sample — cdc_p3


Source: U.S. CDC, Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (public domain)

No values anywhere — state abbreviations printed, six legend classes, no legend title. Each region takes its class: every state, DC and territory shown (about 53 regions). Four regions spread across the classes are shown, then the rest. The legend draws ≥35% as a > glyph over an underline bar; ≥35% is the reading, and a checker treats >35% as the same class. The source lines are cut off at the page edge and are elided.

❌ Counter-sample — regional-catastrophe-report-2023_p54

Event pins over a regional map, each callout naming an event and describing its losses (Eco: USD1.9bn / Ins: USD240mn). The map's shading has no discrete legend to class regions against, and a pin's position is not a value, so the map gives no chart table: its printed text is transcribed as text. The data of this page is the loss chart beside the map, which is a chart table like any other; its bars print no values, so they are estimates on the 20-unit grid. The map's title, callouts and place names are elided.

Related
  • Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 — printed-or-nothing is the treemap rule
  • Labels§11.1.2 — tile labels, region abbreviations and callout text as labels
  • Geographic Maps§12.2.4 — how a map is rendered when it is geography rather than data
  • Gantt and Sankey Charts§11.2.3 — the other families where bare geometry is not read

11.2.8 Scatter and Error Bars

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-scatter-and-error-bars · charts types

✅ Normative

A named scatter point MUST be rendered as one row holding its x value and its y value. Marker series over categories are ordinary series columns. An error bar's centre is an ordinary value, and its whisker span MUST be given with it: the low and high ends read at the whisker caps. A box plot MUST give its median, first and third quartiles, and its whisker ends when they are drawn. Points with no printed name have nothing to locate them and are not rendered as rows.

Scatter

Each named dot contributes its two coordinates, each read against its own axis (see Values and Tolerances§11.1.4). A fitted trend line through the cloud is reference ink (see Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3).

How scatter points, whiskers and boxes appear in the chart table.

  • A scatter chart MUST give one row per named point, a column for x and a column for y, each headed by its printed axis title.
  • An error bar's interval MUST be written in the centre's cell, after the centre, as centre (low–high) — 3.60 (3.47–3.73).
  • A box plot MUST give one row per box: its label, then the low whisker end, first quartile, median, third quartile and high whisker end in axis order, the whisker ends only where drawn, under the header row Low | Q1 | Median | Q3 | High (first cell: the printed label column's title, or empty). These header cells are protocol vocabulary, like the markers [blank] or [logo: …]: the page does not print them, and they are the one deliberate exception to never invent, so that the columns can be read without guessing. They are written exactly as given.
✅ Sample (constructed) — make_scatter

Ten named points, one row each, x and y under the two printed axis titles. The plotted values are whole numbers by construction; on a printed page they would be estimates, judged with a tolerance.

Dot and marker series over categories

Dots drawn per category — markers above bars, one marker per gender per country — are ordinary series: one column per marker series, one value per mark.

✅ Sample — health-profile-europe-2024_p105

A bar series and two marker series over thirty-three countries, nothing printed on the marks: 33 × 3 = 99 values, each an estimate on the 50-unit grid (tolerance 0.05 to 0.1 by readability). The highlighted EU27 bar is an ordinary row. The value-axis title follows the table.

Error bars

The centre is copied when printed and estimated otherwise. The whisker ends are read at the caps against the axis, like any estimate. A whisker whose ends cannot be read honestly is not given an interval.

A checker judges the interval on meaning: it accepts any output that conveys it — 3.60 ± 0.13, 3.60 (3.47–3.73), separate low and high columns, prose — within the tolerance of an ordinary estimate, and fails a centre given with no interval.

✅ Sample — db242_p2


Source: CDC/NCHS, National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2009–2012 — Figure 2 (public domain)

Six bars printing their means, with footnote markers, and 95% confidence whiskers drawn but not printed. Each cell holds the printed centre, markers included, followed by the whisker ends read against the 0.50 grid. The dashed Adequate intake lines are reference ink: their labels follow the table as text. The whisker symbol before 95% confidence interval. is not text.

✅ Sample — climate-assessment-sdm_p7

Nothing is printed on any mark: centres and whisker ends are all estimates on the 0.5 grid. A three-panel figure, each panel its own table headed by its axis unit (°C): panel (a) has a single bar with no category label; in panel (b), Solar and volcanic drivers and Internal variability are drawn on the zero line, so their centre is 0, with whiskers either side. Panel (c) shows its first three bars, then the rest; its two bracket captions follow its table as text. The page heading and the figure caption below the panels are elided.

✅ Sample — ac8b3538-en_p131

Five bars with confidence whiskers, nothing printed: five rows, negatives included, each with its interval. The whisker ends are read at the drawn caps against the printed axis. The GHG-intensive occupations bar sits almost on zero: a relative tolerance means little there, so a checker widens it (0.3) rather than tightening the reading.

Box plots

A box's median, quartiles and drawn whisker ends are read from the geometry. Statistics printed beside the plot are text on the page and are copied as printed.

✅ Sample — charpy_verification_p24

Two box plots, both over the category HH-103, each its own table under its own figure caption, which tells them apart. Each box gives five readings against its axis; the printed annotation box and the labels of the dashed outlier-limit lines follow the table as text. The individual test values (crosses) and the mean marker carry no name and are not rows.

  • Labels§11.1.2 — named points, and the tie between two boxes over one category
  • Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3 — trend lines and reference lines are not data

11.2.9 Stacked Bars and Waterfalls

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

charts-stacked-bars-and-waterfalls · charts types

✅ Normative

A stacked segment's value MUST be the segment's own span — the size it draws between its two boundaries — never the cumulative height at its top edge. A waterfall step follows the same rule on a floating segment: its value is the rise or fall the step itself draws. Each segment series is a column; a printed total is a value of its own.

Writing the running total instead of the segment is the failure this family exists to catch. An estimated segment is read at both boundaries, and its value is the difference.

  • A category whose stack has no segment of one series leaves that cell empty.
  • A printed total above a stack sits in the stack's row, in a last column under an empty header cell (see the chart table's layout in Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1).
  • A waterfall's anchor bars (start and end levels) are categories of their own; their values are levels, not changes.
✅ Sample — global-income-report-2026_p59

Eight regional stacks, four legend series, every segment printing its share: 32 values, copied with their percent marks. The running header is elided.

✅ Sample — credit-outlook-jun2025_p12

Unlabeled segments over a percent grid, with legend-named components and a printed total above each stack. Every segment is read as its own span — EUR High Yield's grey segment runs from about 2.5% to 5.7%, so its value is 3.2%, not 5.7% — and carries the axis's percent mark. Three of the five classes have no hedging segment: those cells are empty. The printed totals, in bold, sit in the last column. The source line runs off the right edge of the page and is written as far as it is visible.

✅ Sample — renewables-outlook-2025_p24

A waterfall between two anchors: 2024 prints its level (10 000), 2030 and the five steps are estimates, each step its own rise. A marker series for each share rides on the anchors against the right-hand axis, printing its values (see Dual-Axis and Combo Charts§11.2.2); the steps have no markers, so those cells are empty. The printed second axis tier (Generation, Change) groups the categories and has a column of its own; Change spans the five steps as printed. The bars have no legend entry, so their column is headed by the left-hand axis title. Estimates are written in the axis's digit grouping.

✅ Sample — a waterfall where every step prints its value

Eight steps from EBT to FCF, each printing its value above or below its bar, negatives in parentheses; Tax paid and Working Capital are drawn as a line rather than a bar and print their values the same way. Every value is copied as printed. The category labels keep their footnote superscripts, and the unit note heads the value column. The page heading above the chart, and the panels and notes below it, are elided.

✅ Sample — stacked bars with an annotation column

Four horizontal stacks, one per business area, each printing a growth figure at its end and, in a column to the right, one or two lines naming sub-businesses with their own growth. This is one table, one row per bar, with a column holding each row's annotation lines as a list, so the annotations stay attached to their bar. The two segments of each stack print no value and no axis calibrates them, so they give no column; their legend follows the table as text. The labels and growth figures in heavier type are bold.

  • Bars and Histograms§11.2.1 — the unstacked base case
  • Dual-Axis and Combo Charts§11.2.2 — the right-hand-axis marker series on the anchors

§12 Images and diagrams

12.1 Images

12.1.1 Images

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

images-images · rule images

✅ Normative

The content of an image MUST be put into the text stream as whatever the image actually is — transcribed text, a table or a diagram. The output MUST NOT contain a file reference or a bracketed placeholder in place of an image.

An image is not a thing to point at; it is content that happens to have been rasterised. Whatever a reader would take away from looking at it MUST end up in the output as text, or it is lost — the never drop failure.

Decide what the image is, then encode that
The image is really… The output MUST contain
Text rendered as a picture The text, transcribed verbatim
A data display (chart, plot) A chart table — Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1
A labelled schematic or conceptual figure A suitable diagram/<language> block; description only if none can preserve it — Slide Diagrams§12.2.5
A graph of relationships or a flow A diagram/<language> fenced block (for example diagram/mermaid or diagram/plantUml) — Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2
A photo or decorative art A prose description of what it shows

The rows are tried in order. Where any text at all is legible inside the image, that text MUST be transcribed: it is content, and describing it instead ("a chart showing quarterly revenue") drops every number on the page.

When the type is not obvious

Some figures resist the table above: maps, chemical structures, electrical schematics, blueprints, printed staves. Each has its own rule — Geographic Maps§12.2.4, Chemical Molecules§13.1, Electrical Schematics§12.2.3, Blueprints§12.2.1, Music Notation§13.2, Slide Diagrams§12.2.5. Where that rule has no settled encoding yet, the fallback is the same: every label and every legible string MUST be preserved, and the output MUST use the encoding that loses no content.

Related
  • Images and Figures§12.1.2 — the same rule with equations and multi-column pages
  • Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4 — the small, semantically loaded end of the same spectrum
  • Logos§12.1.3 — what a brand mark becomes in the text stream
  • Output Options§3.5 — when a saved image may be referenced instead of described

12.1.2 Images and Figures

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

images-images-and-figures · rule diagrams images

✅ Normative

The output MUST NOT contain an image reference ![caption](path) or a bracketed placeholder such as [The image shows…]. A figure's content MUST be rendered as text, a table or a diagram — whichever the figure actually is.

An output is consumed by a model or an extraction step. An image reference is a dead end to both; the content has to be in the text stream.

Choosing the form
The figure is really… Rendering
A data display (chart, plot) A chart table — Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1
A graph of relationships A diagram/<language> fenced block (for example diagram/mermaid or diagram/plantUml) — Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2
A labelled schematic A suitable diagram/<language> block; description only if none can preserve it — Slide Diagrams§12.2.5
A photo or decorative art A prose description of what it shows
Text rendered as an image The text, transcribed
Equations

Equations MUST be LaTeX in $$ … $$, inline ones included — see Inline Equations§7.2.6. Using $$ uniformly keeps a stray currency symbol elsewhere on the page from opening an unterminated math span.

Multi-column pages

Multi-column text MUST be unrolled into a single column in reading order. The physical column split is a typesetting artefact, not structure, and MUST NOT be preserved — see Reading Order§5.9.

Related
  • Images§12.1.1 — the general rule, with the order in which the forms are tried
  • Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2 — when a figure is a graph
  • Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1 — what a chart becomes
  • Layout Regions§5.7 — separating the figure's region from the text around it

12.1.3 Logos

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

images-logos · images furniture

✅ Normative

A logo MUST be rendered as a marker carrying its printed words, [logo: OSTREVANE], at the logo's place in reading order. A logo that prints no legible text MUST be rendered as [logo]. The artwork MUST NOT be described.

Almost every slide and letterhead carries one: a wordmark in the corner, a symbol beside it, sometimes a faint version behind the content. The marker keeps the printed words (never drop) and tells a reader that they are a brand mark rather than a word of the body text.

Requirements
  • The words a logo prints MUST appear inside the marker exactly as printed, case included: [logo: VELTRAND LIFE]. A wordmark set on two lines is one marker, its lines joined with a space.
  • The marker sits at the logo's place in reading order. A logo inside a header or footer band stays inside that band — see Recurring Page Furniture§4.6.
  • A logo with no legible text — a symbol on its own — is the bare [logo].
  • A symbol printed beside its own wordmark is part of that logo; it does not get a second marker.
  • A faint copy of a mark repeated behind the content is not a second logo and adds nothing; it MUST NOT break into the table or paragraph it lies behind. A faint background mark that carries words is a watermark — see Watermarks§7.3.13.
  • The artwork — colours, shapes, the apple — MUST NOT be described.
✅ Sample — a corner wordmark and a background mark

The wordmark OSTREVANE with a yellow apple symbol sits in the bottom-right corner of the footer band, and a large faint version of the same apple sits behind the lower (CAPEX) table. The background apple is a faint repeat of the mark and adds nothing to the table; the wordmark becomes [logo: OSTREVANE] in the footer band. Expected boxes: the CAPEX table as one Table box; the footer band as page furniture, with the wordmark inside it.

✅ Sample — two stacked wordmarks on a slide

VELTRAND PROVIDENCE (set on two lines) and VELTRAND LIFE, each a red box with a white diamond symbol, top-right. Each wordmark is one marker; the two-line one joins its lines with a space. The slide's map is a real map with a two-entry legend — see Geographic Maps§12.2.4; it is elided here. Expected boxes: one box per wordmark.

Related
  • Images§12.1.1 — the general rule this point extends
  • Margin Banners§7.3.5 — brand text printed along the page edge
  • Watermarks§7.3.13 — a faint background mark that carries words
  • Output Options§3.5 — the option under which a logo may be referenced as a saved image

12.2 Diagrams

12.2.1 Blueprints

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

diagrams-blueprints · images diagrams

✅ Normative

A floor plan or architectural drawing MUST use a faithful diagram/<language> encoding, preferring diagram/tikz then diagram/svg. If no suitable language can represent it faithfully, it MUST use a fenced description block. The output MUST preserve visible geometry, labels and printed measurements without inferred relationships or computed values. It MUST NOT be a table.

Floor plans and architectural drawings.

How the element is recognised

A drawing whose content is spatial: walls, rooms, dimensions, door swings, labels placed where the thing they name sits. There are no rows and no columns — only positions.

Why a table is the wrong answer

A floor plan forced into a grid becomes a table of spatially adjacent labels that reads as data downstream. That is worse than a description, because it is confidently wrong: nothing in the output signals that the rows and columns were invented — the never invent failure. A floor plan MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

The same trap appears in Geographic Maps§12.2.4 (map coerced into a table) and Electrical Schematics§12.2.3 (circuit coerced into a graph): a spatial artefact flattened into a linear structure that cannot carry position.

Encode the spatial content

Language selection follows Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2. The encoding MUST preserve visible walls, openings, door swings, relative positions, dimensions, labels, scale bars, legends and notes. Drawing coordinates MAY follow the visible geometry; they MUST NOT assert unprinted real-world measurements. Inconsistent printed dimensions MUST be copied without correction. A room graph that drops geometry is not a faithful encoding of a floor plan.

Description fallback

Only when no suitable language can faithfully encode the drawing, use a fenced description block in this shape:

  1. What it is — one line describing the drawing.
  2. Areas and visible structure — one item per labelled area in reading order, its printed label and size verbatim, followed by visible walls, openings and spatial relationships.
  3. Dimensions and notes — every dimension line, scale bar, legend entry, north arrow label and note, verbatim.

Unshown adjacency, hidden openings, computed areas and corrected dimensions MUST NOT be added. A visible doorway or shared wall may be described as drawn; proximity alone does not establish a connection. The description MUST distinguish what is visible from what cannot be determined.

✅ Sample — a single-storey plan

Twelve labelled areas, eight of them with a printed size, and dimension lines on all four sides. The printed dimensions do not add up (32'-0", 40'-0" and 44'-0" under a 62'-0" span) and are copied as printed.

12.2.2 Diagrams and Flowcharts

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

diagrams-diagrams-and-flowcharts · rule diagrams

✅ Normative

A diagram or blueprint MUST use a fenced diagram/<language> block when a suitable language can faithfully represent its content. If no suitable language can do so, the output MUST use a fenced description block. A diagram that is really tabular SHOULD be rendered as an HTML table. A diagram MUST NOT be left out of the output.

Fence and language selection

The opening fence MUST identify the language actually used: diagram/mermaid, diagram/plantUml, diagram/dot, diagram/tikz, diagram/svg, diagram/circuitikz, or another suitable diagram/<language> tag. The suffix is case-sensitive; plantUml is the canonical PlantUML spelling. diagram/<language> is a pattern, not a literal tag. Bare mermaid, plantuml, diagram and diagram/text MUST NOT be used for diagram output.

The producer SHOULD use the following priority order, considering only languages that preserve all the figure's content. A higher-ranked language MUST NOT be used if doing so loses information. Different figures in one document MAY use different languages. An unlisted language MAY be used when it preserves content the listed choices cannot. The order is a protocol preference, not a claim that every language supports every figure in that row.

Figure type Preferred languages, in order Content that decides suitability
Flowchart, process, organisation chart Mermaid → PlantUML → Graphviz DOT → TikZ → SVG Labels, branches, arrow directions, grouping
UML, sequence, class, state, ER diagram PlantUML → Mermaid → Graphviz DOT → TikZ → SVG Diagram-specific symbols, relations, multiplicity, message order
Functional block, system or network diagram Mermaid → PlantUML → Graphviz DOT → TikZ → SVG Blocks, ports, signal paths, nesting; positions when meaningful
Dense dependency graph or tree Graphviz DOT → Mermaid → PlantUML → TikZ → SVG Complete nodes, edges, directions and clusters
Blueprint, floor plan, geometric or spatial schematic TikZ → SVG Walls, openings, geometry, orientation, dimensions and label placement
Component-level electrical circuit CircuiTikZ → TikZ circuit libraries → SVG Component symbols, pins, junctions, wire crossings, topology and orientation

Mermaid and PlantUML MAY represent a conceptual room-relationship diagram when its content is only nodes and connections. They MUST NOT replace a spatial floor plan with an automatically arranged graph that loses walls, openings, geometry or dimensions. A language being called “architecture” does not make it a floor-plan encoding.

The block body MUST be valid in its named language. Every printed label, connector, direction, meaningful grouping and spatial feature MUST be preserved, without adding inferred content. Internal identifiers and drawing coordinates are encoding, not additional printed measurements; coordinates MAY follow visible geometry but MUST NOT be presented as measured real-world values. Printed measurements MUST be copied verbatim even when inconsistent.

Description fallback

When no suitable language can faithfully encode the figure, the output MUST use a fence whose entire tag is description, not diagram/description or diagram/text. The body follows the fixed shape in Slide Diagrams§12.2.5, Blueprints§12.2.1 or Electrical Schematics§12.2.3: printed title if present, what is visibly shown, labels and their visible features, then values and notes. It MUST preserve all legible text and describe visible structure without guessing hidden connections, measurements or domain meanings. Difficulty alone does not justify replacing an encodable diagram with a description. The fallback examples below and in the specialised notes illustrate this case; they do not require descriptions when a faithful encoding is available.

Charts, geographic maps, chemical formulae and music retain their specialised content rules.

```diagram/mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Application received] --> B{Complete?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Underwriting]
  B -->|No| D[Return to applicant]
```
Preserve spatial and domain meaning

Automatic graph layout is suitable when connections carry the meaning. Where positions, orientations or physical topology matter, the chosen language MUST preserve them. Floor plans follow Blueprints§12.2.1, circuits follow Electrical Schematics§12.2.3, maps follow Geographic Maps§12.2.4, and structural formulae follow Chemical Molecules§13.1. A successful render alone does not show that an encoding preserved the source.

Labelled conceptual diagrams

When no suitable language can faithfully encode a labelled conceptual figure, it is rendered as a fenced description block that names each element and what is visibly drawn there, so a chunker keeps the labels together — see Slide Diagrams§12.2.5:

```description
## Detector cross-section
- **Anode**: top grid
- **S2**: secondary scintillation, produced in the gas phase
- **e<sup>-</sup>**: electrons drifting upward through the liquid
```
Examples
✅ Sample — an organisation chart

A staffing chart: boxed roles connected by rules into a strict hierarchy, five departments across the top and two separate contracted-services blocks below.

This is the case Mermaid is for. The content is entirely nodes and edges — who reports to whom — and none of the meaning lives in where a box sits on the page. Redrawn by a layout engine it would still say the same thing, which is exactly the test that a circuit or a floor plan fails.

Two things are easy to lose and MUST be carried across: the numbered suffixes distinguishing repeated roles (事務員①, 事務員②), and the annotations inside or beside the boxes (週29H, 週1×4H) — those are hours, not decoration, and they belong to the node they sit with. Each bracketed department label (＜管理課＞) names the group above it and becomes a subgraph title. Edges follow the printed rules: each department head connects by a rule to the stack of roles beneath it. The two lower blocks print no connecting rules, so their roles are grouped without edges. Expected boxes: the title line, and the chart as one Picture box.

12.2.3 Electrical Schematics

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

diagrams-electrical-schematics · images diagrams

✅ Normative

A component-level circuit schematic MUST use a faithful diagram/<language> encoding, preferring diagram/circuitikz, then diagram/tikz, then diagram/svg. If no suitable language can faithfully represent it, it MUST use a fenced description block. Every component symbol, designator, value, pin, terminal, net label and visibly drawn connection MUST be preserved.

Circuit diagrams.

The figure above is an IC functional block diagram rather than a component-level circuit; it follows Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2, using diagram/plantUml, diagram/mermaid or another suitable language that preserves the printed blocks and signal connections. The component-level requirements below do not apply to a functional block diagram.

How the element is recognised

Component symbols joined by wires, usually with a reference designator and a value beside each one (R1 1Ω, C3 10μF). The way the components are oriented, and whether they sit in series or in parallel, is part of the content.

Preserve circuit meaning

The encoding MUST preserve component orientation, pins, junctions, crossings and series/parallel connections as drawn. An automatic graph layout that changes circuit meaning MUST NOT be used. Functional block diagrams use the block-diagram priorities in Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2.

The fixed shape

When no suitable language can faithfully encode the circuit, the fallback uses a fenced description block (see Slide Diagrams§12.2.5).

  1. What it is — one line: Buck regulator input stage.
  2. Components — a list, one item per component in reading order (top to bottom, left to right): designator then value, both exactly as printed (R1 1Ω, C3 10μF). A component with no printed value is listed by its designator.
  3. Pins, terminals and nets — every printed pin, terminal and net label, verbatim.
  4. Connections — describe wires and junctions visibly drawn between identified parts. A crossing MUST NOT be treated as a junction unless the drawing marks it as one. Hidden or ambiguous connections MUST NOT be guessed.

Every printed designator, value and label is printed content and MUST be transcribed (never drop). Values MUST NOT be computed, normalised or corrected.

Related
  • Chemical Molecules§13.1 — the settled case of a domain notation preferred over a graph
  • Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2 — language priorities and the description fallback
  • Blueprints§12.2.1 — another spatial drawing that a linear structure cannot carry
  • Slide Diagrams§12.2.5 — labelled figures that are not circuits

12.2.4 Geographic Maps

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

diagrams-geographic-maps · images diagrams

✅ Normative

How a map is rendered depends on what it is for. A data map whose values sit in drawn regions MUST be rendered as a Region | Value table — the region names MAY be recognised from the drawn outlines when the page does not print them, and the key column is then marked data-recognised. A map of values placed only by position MUST be described, with its legend transcribed, and no table. A map whose content is geography MUST be described. Every printed label MUST be kept.

A map appearing as a figure — typically a choropleth, or a labelled regional map.

The test

What the figure is carrying decides the rendering:

The map is… Rendering
A data display wearing a costume — a shaded rate map is a Region \| Value table drawn on an outline; the geography is decoration, the numbers are the content An HTML <table data-source="chart">, region in one column and value in another, with the legend's units kept in the caption
Data placed only by position — readings plotted at points, identified by nothing but where they sit A description with the legend transcribed; no table
A real map — routes, adjacency, borders, position relative to other features; flattening it to a table destroys the only information it carried A description, with every printed label, legend entry and scale transcribed
Both — shaded values and meaningful geography, or it cannot be told which The description and the table: two encodings lose nothing, picking one loses half the figure
The key column

A table needs a key. When the regions carry no printed names, the key MAY be supplied by recognising the drawn regions — Italian regions from their outlines, US states from theirs — but only when every value sits inside one drawn, bounded region and the region is unambiguous to a reader of the page. A recognised key is not printed text, so the table MUST say so: the header cell of the key column carries the attribute data-recognised, and a header the page does not print is worded after the map's own caption or legend.

<tr> <th data-recognised>Regione</th> <th>Prevalenza (%) …</th> </tr>

Values positioned only by coordinates — a scatter of point readings with no names — have no region to recognise. They MUST NOT be tabulated by coordinate; the map is described and its legend transcribed.

Whatever the rendering, the printed text of a map — title, caption, legend, labels, scale — MUST be kept (never drop).

Examples
✅ Sample — a shaded rate map

A regional map of Italy shaded in three bands, one value printed in each region, a four-entry legend and a caption. The geography is decoration; the values are the content, so the map is a table. The map prints only values: each region is recognised from its outline, so the key column is marked data-recognised, and its header follows the caption's wording. Basilicata is printed white (n.d.) with no value, so it has no row; the caption states the gap. The table as it renders:

✅ Sample — a map that is entirely data, with no printed key


Source: U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrometeorological Prediction Center — Observed 24-Hour Precipitation map, 21 Jul 2012 (public domain)

An observed-precipitation map: state outlines, and on top of them a dense scatter of numeric readings, colour-coded by value.


Source: U.S. National Weather Service, Hydrometeorological Prediction Center — Observed 24-Hour Precipitation map (public domain)

This is a data display wearing a map, so the test says table. But it is also the case where that answer stops being practical: the readings are positioned by latitude and longitude with no station names printed, so there is no key column to put them in. The readings sit at points, not in drawn regions, so there is nothing to recognise as a key: the legend text is transcribed, the map is described, and no table is built.

The legend block in the top-left — title, valid time, sources and a red "Data not fully quality controlled" caveat — is printed text and MUST survive whatever is done with the plotted values. The red colour is emphasis, not a value, and is not carried. The plotted readings are too small to transcribe reliably at this resolution and are not listed.

✅ Sample — a real map with a printed legend

An aerial map of well locations, colour-coded by concentration band, with a six-entry legend, a scale bar, a callout (610 ng/l), a state inset and a photograph. The positions are the content, so the map is described as an image with every legend entry and label transcribed. Expected boxes: the title, the subtitle, the map with its caption, the legend, the inset with its caption and the photograph with its caption.

Related

  • Blueprints§12.2.1 — the same "coerced into a table" trap
  • Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1 — what a data display becomes when it is a chart
  • Slide Diagrams§12.2.5 — labelled figures that are neither maps nor charts

12.2.5 Slide Diagrams

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

diagrams-slide-diagrams · images diagrams

✅ Normative

A labelled figure MUST use a suitable diagram/<language> encoding when one can preserve its content faithfully, following the language priorities in Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2. A labelled figure that no suitable diagram language can faithfully express MUST be rendered as a fenced description block in the fixed shape: one line saying what the figure is, then one bullet per printed label, verbatim, followed only by what is visibly drawn there, then printed values and notes. The block MUST NOT explain what a label means.

A slide diagram or scientific figure is a picture whose meaning lives in its labels: names of parts, signal names, arrows showing direction. The labels are content and MUST NOT be lost. A plain prose description SHOULD be used only when the figure carries no labels at all.

A slide: its title, a detector cross-section with labels, two small charts (Summary, Scintillation) and two bullets. The cross-section is transcribed by the description block below; the title, charts and bullets are separate elements.

Choose a language that fits the figure

Where the figure's content is labelled parts joined by drawn lines or arrows, it is a graph, and Mermaid, PlantUML or another suitable language can carry it: preserve each labelled part, drawn connector, direction and meaningful position. Where no suitable language preserves the content of a cross-section, apparatus or anatomy drawing, use the description fallback block.

The description block

The block is a fenced code block tagged description, in the same fixed shape used for every described figure (see Blueprints§12.2.1 and Electrical Schematics§12.2.3):

  1. The figure's printed title as a ## heading, if it prints one; then one line saying what the figure is, in plain visual terms.
  2. One bullet per printed label, in reading order, the label in bold and verbatim, followed only by what is visibly drawn at it — "arrow pointing down", "row of squares at the top". A label printed several times is listed once with its count.
  3. Printed values, scales and notes, verbatim.

What a label means — "secondary scintillation signal produced in the gaseous phase" — is domain knowledge, not printed, and MUST NOT appear (never invent). Text around the figure — a slide title, bullets, small charts beside the drawing — is rendered as its own elements outside the block; a chart becomes a chart table.

```description
Cross-section of a two-layer detector.
- **Gaseous Xenon**: upper layer
- **Anode**: line to the row of squares at the top
- **S2**: in the upper layer
- **Extraction**: arrow pointing down at the boundary between the layers
- **e<sup>-</sup>** (four times): beside an arrow pointing up
- **Drift-field**: dotted arrow pointing down
- **S1**: beside a star
- **DM**: arrow pointing to the star
- **Cathode**: row of squares at the bottom
- **Liquid Xenon**: lower layer
```

Superscripts and subscripts inside the block stay inline as <sup> / <sub>, the same as anywhere else — see Superscript and Subscript§7.2.11. Equations inside the block stay in $$ … $$ — see Inline Equations§7.2.6.

Why the fenced block

The fence gives the region a boundary, so a chunker keeps the diagram's labels together rather than scattering them into surrounding prose — and a consumer that does not want diagrams can strip the block wholesale.

✅ Sample — an electrochemical cell with an equation in it

Two electrodes in a solution, Δφ(…) labels with arrows, boxed text (The cell is Pt/M′/S/M/Pt, ε can be measured) and a full equation along the bottom edge. Every string belongs to the figure. Six arrows point at the electrodes, but only five Δφ(…) labels are legible: the sixth, at the right, is hidden behind the ε can be measured box, and only its leading Δ shows — so only the Δ is transcribed. Expected boxes: the whole framed figure as one Picture box.

  • Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2 — language selection and fences for diagrams
  • Electrical Schematics§12.2.3 — a labelled figure whose topology a label list cannot carry
