§13 Other

13.1 Chemical Molecules

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

other-chemical-molecules · other rule images diagrams math

✅ Normative

Linear formulae, ions and reactions MUST be written with \ce{...}, and drawn structures, rings and branches with \chemfig{...}. Standalone chemical markup MUST be placed in a fenced latex block. Legible structure MUST be preserved; an unreadable portion MUST be described rather than guessed.

Structural formulae and reaction equations printed as figures.

A structural formula printed as a figure — exactly the case a prose description cannot reconstruct.

Which markup

The markup follows what is printed:

Printed Markup Examples
A formula, ion or reaction written on a line mhchem — \ce{...} \ce{SO4^2-}, \ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}
A 2D molecular structure: rings, branches, drawn bonds chemfig — \chemfig{...} a ring with its substituents

Why a code representation rather than a description

A structural formula is exactly reconstructable — unlike a photograph, it has a canonical textual encoding that a chemist or a downstream tool can render back to the same picture. A prose description ("a benzene ring with a hydroxyl group") is lossy and unverifiable, and it silently discards stereochemistry, charges and substituent positions. A legible structure therefore MUST NOT be rendered as prose.

The same reasoning governs Electrical Schematics§12.2.3 and Blueprints§12.2.1: a domain-specific code block is preferred wherever a faithful one exists.

Placement and unreadable structures

  • A formula standing on its own — a displayed structure or reaction — MUST be in a fenced latex block.
  • Every legible atom, bond, charge and substituent MUST be kept (never drop).
  • Where part of a structure cannot be read, that part MUST be described in words, and the output MUST NOT fill it in with a plausible guess (never invent).

Related

  • Electrical Schematics§12.2.3 — the same preference for a domain notation, still open for circuits
  • Inline Equations§7.2.6 — the $$ delimiters used for mathematics
  • Music Notation§13.2 — the notation that would follow this pattern if settled

13.2 Music Notation

✅ Normative · 📄 page rule

other-music-notation · other images diagrams

✅ Normative

Every string printed on a music page MUST be transcribed as ordinary text. The staves themselves MUST be described, not encoded: each staff region is a fenced description block in the shared fixed shape, and no notes are read into note names, ABC, LilyPond or MusicXML.

A page of printed staves. The notes on the staff have no agreed textual form yet, but a music page is rarely only staves: it carries a great deal of ordinary printed text, and none of that may be lost while the staff question is open.

Requirements

  1. Every printed string MUST be transcribed. Titles, composer and arranger credits, instrument names, tempo and expression markings, dynamics, lyrics under the staff, bar numbers, rehearsal letters, chord symbols, footnotes and copyright lines are text and follow the ordinary text rules.
  2. Notes MUST NOT be encoded. Reading a staff into pitches is error-prone and cannot be checked by reading the page; a wrong transcription is worse than an honest description (never invent). No note names and no music notation (ABC, LilyPond, MusicXML) appear in the output.
  3. Each staff region MUST be described as a fenced description block in the fixed shape shared by every described figure (see Slide Diagrams§12.2.5):
    • one line saying what it is — how many staves, for what instruments where printed, the clef, key and time signature as drawn, the number of bars;
    • one bullet per text symbol printed on the staff — chord symbols, rehearsal letters, bar numbers, dynamics — verbatim, followed only by where it is drawn;
    • lyrics printed under a staff are text and follow the block.
✅ Sample — a four-bar lead sheet

A title, an arrangement line, one treble-clef staff of four bars in common time with a boxed chord symbol over each bar, and two paragraphs of prose below. The staff is described; its four chord symbols are its labels; no notes are encoded.

Related

  • Images§12.1.1 — the general rule for what an image becomes
  • Slide Diagrams§12.2.5 — the shared shape of every described figure
  • Electrical Schematics§12.2.3 — another figure described rather than encoded

§A Equivalent forms

A.1 Accepted Alternatives

Situations where a page genuinely admits two renderings. Both conform. The middle column is the canonical form a producer SHOULD emit; the right column is also conforming, and a checker MUST treat the two as equal. Within one document, a producer MUST use one of them throughout — see Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2.

Situation Canonical rendering Also conforming
Continuation blocks separate tables, headers copied stacked as a single table; the source-printed wide grid is also accepted when blocks share one enclosing frame
Blank space beside a header label unmerged blank cells rowspan/colspan onto the label
Empty region inside a body either leading empty <td>s ≡ one blank colspan/rowspan block
Purely blank spacer rows the real ones rendered presence ≡ absence
Currency glyph one cell, $ 277.09 $-gutter colspan pair
Marker gutters (i)/(ii) own column merged "(i) text" cell
Section-divider rows bold body row <th>
Bullet list in a cell <ul><li> <br/>•
Line break inside a label <br/> if deliberate, flat if incidental either, when the page cannot settle it
Label and value in one cell — split across two existing columns
Totals block with no framing signal either way — footer rows ≡ its own key-value table

Visually identical characters

These pairs never count as a difference in text:

  • µ (U+00B5) ≡ μ (U+03BC)
  • non-breaking hyphen (U+2011) ≡ hyphen-minus (U+002D)
  • minus sign (U+2212) ≡ hyphen-minus (U+002D) — hyphen-minus is canonical
  • figure and en dashes ≡ hyphen in numeric ranges
  • non-breaking space ≡ space

The equivalence governs comparison only. A producer SHOULD transcribe the character the page prints and MUST NOT substitute a "cleaner" code point.

The costly one

Blank space beside a header label matters most, because the two renderings claim different things about the page. The canonical rendering is unmerged blank cells; a span SHOULD be extended only where the page shows a genuinely merged cell — see Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1.

HTML table sections

thead, tbody and tfoot wrappers, or their absence, are equivalent. Rows MUST stay in printed order and th/td MUST be decided per cell; a total MUST NOT move to fit a wrapper. See Total and Subtotal Rows§9.5.6.

Related

  • Conformance§1.2 — how equivalent forms are judged
  • Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2 — one form per document

§C Producing ground truth

C.1 Producing Ground Truth

This appendix is for the people who produce ground truth: the reference output a parser is scored against. It is procedure, not protocol — it says how to arrive at a conforming output, and every step points at the rule it serves.

Ground truth for a page is a conforming output of it (see Conformance§1.2): its Markdown, and, where boxes are evaluated, its boxes at the evaluated granularity (see Boxes and Granularity§3.3). Chart pages additionally carry the rules of The Ground-Truth File§C.13.

Before you start

  • Read The Page Is the Ground Truth§2.1 and Never Drop, Never Invent§2.2.
  • Settle the document-level decisions once: Document Rules§4.1.

While you work

  • When a page forces an ⚖️ choice for the first time, make it, record it with the page, and keep it for the rest of the document — see Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2.
  • When a page meets a ❓ open point, follow the working default and record the page, so the case is easy to find when the point is settled.

Before you call a page done

  • The annotation QA checklist§C.12

Related

  • About the Examples§C.2 — where the example pages come from and how their expected Markdown is derived
  • Ambiguity List — the open points and their proposed resolutions

C.2 About the Examples

Every rule in the protocol carries worked examples — a page next to the rule it demonstrates, with the Expected Markdown for the region it shows. The expected Markdown is conforming output: it is what a producer should emit, and what ground truth is built from.

Meaning
✅ Sample The rule applies; the Expected Markdown shows what conforming output looks like.
❌ Counter-sample Either it looks like the rule and isn't — the contrast case — or a rendering of it got it wrong (shown as Non-conforming output).

Why counter-samples matter as much as samples

Several rules here exist because two situations look identical on the page and resolve opposite ways. Side-by-side blocks that continue one series are a continuation; side-by-side blocks with their own titles and schemas are separate tables. A wrapped header label looks exactly like a two-row tier. You cannot teach either case with a sample alone — the pair is the lesson.

The most instructive examples are the ones that disagree

Many examples pair a page with an earlier rendering of it. That makes it possible to find pages where the two contradict each other, and those teach a rule far better than a clean case does:

Example What went wrong
3samehead The page prints 32031.9%; the rendering records a plausible-looking 10.9%
3cc The page prints 2.5; the rendering records 25 — a silently dropped decimal
entwick The page prints blank cells; the rendering invents em-dash values for them
3in1 The rendering fabricates a header tier that was never printed
w A rowspan=2 header tier with an empty second row, where one line is printed
wood Visually identical bands tagged as a header in one place and a body cell in another

Each of these is a live illustration of the two failures the whole protocol is built around: never drop, and never invent.

What the examples do not cover

One situation has no worked example, because no example page exercises it yet — Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5. That note keeps its schematic sketch until a real page turns up.

A few rules have exactly one example rather than several, for the same reason: only one page carries a struck-through value, only one carries a units row, only one shows a header and body disagreeing on column count.

Where the example pages come from

Every image in the protocol is either a synthetic page or a public-domain document.

  • Synthetic pages re-create a situation first found on a real document, with fictional companies, people and figures. Each is an HTML page under tools/synthetic/pages/, rendered by tools/synthetic/render.py; the page is the source, so the Expected Markdown beside the image is correct by construction. Where an example demonstrates an annotation error, the page prints the true value and the extract keeps the documented mistake.
  • Public-domain documents are U.S. federal government works (statistical tables, statutes, court opinions, agency guides, blank federal forms). They are reproduced as published; the credit for each lives in tools/provenance/manifest.json.
  • A few chart families — gantt, sankey, and a clean labeled scatter — carry constructed examples, marked Sample (constructed) and rendered by tools/constructed_charts/.

Each example names its page in backticks, like `3samehead`; that name is the page's stem. tools/provenance/manifest.json records where every image comes from, and the public build (tools/build_site.py --public) refuses to run while any embedded image lacks a cleared entry.

Chart values beyond those printed on the page were measured from the page's vector or pixel geometry (axis calibration by least squares over the axis-label positions, bars from fill rectangles, lines by vertex-snapping at the ticks) — they are not eyeballed.

Adding a new example is covered in SKILL.md — including the rule that you must look at the rendered image before writing a caption about it.

Pages without a paired annotation

Images named bag-<slug>.png show a situation without a full expected annotation beside them; their captions describe only what is printed and never what the annotation should be.

Related

  • The Page Is the Ground Truth§2.1 · Document Representation Protocol · The annotation QA checklist§C.12

C.3 Ground Truth — Charts

How chart ground truth is produced against the chart chapter. The file format itself is in The Ground-Truth File§C.13; the checks before a chart is done are in The annotation QA checklist§C.12.

Encoding the chart table as rules

  • Every cell of the chart table becomes one chart_data_point rule; every gantt span, sankey flow, whisker interval, box and map class becomes one chart_judge_point rule — see The Ground-Truth File§C.13. → Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1
  • A rule's labels are the smallest set of printed strings that locates one point: the category alone for a single series, category + series for two dimensions, a third label only when two are not unique. Too few labels match several points; extra labels only add ways to fail. Order inside labels does not matter. → Labels§11.1.2
  • A printed title (or a distinctive fragment of it) joins the labels only to break a tie between charts on one page that share a label set — the twin pies add September 2025 / Fiscal Year 2025, the two box plots add Figure 16 / Figure 17. All rules of a page sit in one flat list; nothing marks which chart a rule belongs to. → Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3
  • Where long labels blur and a short identifier prints crisply beside them (Activity IDs in a schedule), the identifier is the label. A label that cannot be read at zoom is not a label. → Gantt and Sankey Charts§11.2.3
  • Printed values keep their printed spelling; normalize_numbers absorbs formatting differences. Keep one number style per file. → Values and Tolerances§11.1.4
  • Estimated values carry relative_tolerance from the readability buckets and "tags": ["need_estimate"]; printed values carry no tolerance. → Values and Tolerances§11.1.4

Working a chart

  1. Census the points — positions × series, plus printed callouts, plus every panel — before judging any value. A skipped series, tail or panel is the most common coverage failure. → Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1
  2. Sweep for printed values first — on the marks, beside slices, in the legend, at line ends, in side text. A printed value missed becomes a wrong estimate. → Legend and Overlay Values§11.2.4
  3. Measure the estimates — chart values beyond those printed are measured from the page's vector or pixel geometry (axis calibration by least squares over the tick labels, bars from fill rectangles, lines by snapping vertices at the ticks), not eyeballed. Where the draft and the measurement disagree, the measurement wins; re-check the tolerance while there. → Values and Tolerances§11.1.4
  4. Flag the doubtful points rather than tightening them artificially: a 3-D bar whose reference plane is ambiguous, a near-zero estimate needing a wide tolerance, a whisker whose ends cannot be read (no judge rule), a comparator-only treemap tile (<1%, no rule), a sankey that prints no values, a ribbon that cannot be traced, a map region between two swatches (no rule — pick another region). → Scatter and Error Bars§11.2.8 · Maps and Treemaps§11.2.7 · Gantt and Sankey Charts§11.2.3
  5. Gantt boundaries — record the last period a bar visibly fills and move on; the judge accepts one boundary off. → Gantt and Sankey Charts§11.2.3
  6. Hunt invented content — no rules for reference ink or event callouts, no invented label text, no computed values, no expanded abbreviations. → Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3

Authority

  • The PDF is the only source of truth. Parse results are reference material, never truth.
  • A value is never adjusted to make a parser pass, and a correct rule is never deleted because a parse fails it — that failure is the benchmark doing its job. → Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1
  • A chart where most points cannot be located or read fails as a test case and is deleted whole.

C.4 Ground Truth — Headings and Page Structure

What to do, when producing ground truth, in the cases the heading and page-structure rules leave to review. Each step serves the rule it links to; the rule decides the output.

Situation Step Rule
A page has a multi-line block (masthead, address, banner) Keep it as one block with plain newlines and flag the page, so it can be revisited when the open point closes Line Breaks Inside a Block§6.2
It is unclear which paragraph a marginal note annotates Keep the note as its own block near its printed position and flag the page Marginal Notes§6.4
A numbered line reads plausibly both as a heading and as a list item Apply the working default and flag the page Numbered Section Headings§6.5
A page is a table of contents or index Choose the form the litmus test gives, record the choice for the document, and flag the page so both encodings stay visible Table of Contents§6.10
A page is a transcript with numbered Q/A lines Apply the working default and flag the page Transcript Pages§6.11
Whether a page-top label is a running header depends on repetition on pages not in hand Check the surrounding pages; if they are unavailable, keep the label where the page prints it and flag the page Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7 · Recurring Page Furniture§4.6
Only one page is available and a heading's absolute depth depends on pages not in hand Keep the page's relative hierarchy and flag the page rather than guessing the level Recognising Ambiguous Headings§6.7 · Heading Depth Across Pages§4.5

Related

  • Producing Ground Truth§C.1 — the general procedure these steps belong to
  • The annotation QA checklist§C.12 — the checks run before a page is called done

C.5 Ground Truth — Images, Diagrams and Other

Workflow for pages carrying figures: images, logos, diagrams, maps, schematics, floor plans, chemical structures and printed music. The rules themselves live in the protocol; this page only says what to do around them.

  1. Classify the figure before transcribing it. Decide what it really is — text, chart, graph, labelled schematic, photo — and pick the encoding from Images§12.1.1.
  2. Flag every page that falls under an open point, so the page can be revisited when the point closes:
    • a logo that carries no legible text — Logos§12.1.3;
    • a floor plan or architectural drawing — Blueprints§12.2.1;
    • a circuit schematic — Electrical Schematics§12.2.3;
    • a map, and always a data map whose values have no printed key or one that needs both a description and a table — Geographic Maps§12.2.4;
    • a labelled conceptual diagram — Slide Diagrams§12.2.5;
    • a page of printed staves — Music Notation§13.2.
  3. Flag an unreadable part of a chemical structure alongside the words that describe it, so a reviewer can check the source rather than the guess — Chemical Molecules§13.1.
  4. Check an organisation chart's edges against the printed rules, one box at a time; do not add an edge the page does not draw — Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2.
  5. Before publishing a figure page, compare every printed string on the figure with the output — labels, legend entries, scale bars, callouts, captions. A missing string is the most common defect on these pages.

C.6 Ground Truth — Inline Formatting

What to do, when producing ground truth, in the cases the inline-formatting rules leave to review. Each step serves the rule it links to; the rule decides the output.

Situation Step Rule
A drop-cap initial is genuinely unreadable Flag the page for review; do not guess the letter Drop Caps§7.2.3
A line-end hyphen cannot be classed as a break or part of the word Keep the hyphen, join the parts, and flag the word Line-End Hyphenation§7.2.7
Link anchor text differs from its target, and the target looks like it carries real meaning Keep the printed words and flag the page Links§7.2.8
An inset block is a real quotation and its quotation status looks load-bearing Flatten it as usual and flag the page Quote Blocks§7.2.9
A page carries verse or other text whose line breaks are content Apply the working default and flag the page, so it can be revisited when the open point closes Verse and Hard Line Breaks§7.2.13

C.7 Ground Truth — Layout

How ground truth is produced for the document-level and layout rules. Each step names the rule it serves; the rule, not this note, says what the result must be.

Order of work for a document

  1. Open the file and settle the document type and the cover from several sheets, including the last → Document Type§4.4.
  2. Sweep a few pages for recurring margin bands and settle them for the whole file → Recurring Page Furniture§4.6.
  3. Annotate page by page. When a page forces an either-way choice for the first time, make it, flag that page with the rendering chosen, and hold it from then on → Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2.
  4. Before publishing, run the multi-page checks in The annotation QA checklist§C.12.

With only one page available, apply what the page supports and flag the page, so the document decision can be made once the rest of the file arrives → Document Rules§4.1.

Order of work for a page

  1. Confirm the page is clear, correctly cropped and correctly oriented → Ignoring and Rejecting§5.6.
  2. Review every existing box — boundary, class, rotation, reading order. Imported and generated boxes are proposals, not answers: verify each one, and delete duplicates and spurious ones → Block Annotation§5.1, Block Classes§5.3.
  3. Add every missing box → Block Annotation§5.1.
  4. Hide the boxes and sweep the full page for unannotated content. With the boxes visible the eye fills in what it expects to see; with them hidden, gaps and clipping become obvious.
  5. Recheck the reading-order sequence after every addition, deletion or exclusion: each shifts everything after it, and a gap or duplicate introduced late is easy to miss → Reading Order§5.9.
  6. Mark the block layer Checked, tick I swept the entire page, save the draft, then Validate page. Resolve every blocker and read every warning before publishing.

Page furniture in attribution references

In a markdown_attribution sidecar, every Page-header and Page-footer reference, folios included, carries "optional": true. The bands are still annotated and their text still follows Recurring Page Furniture§4.6 and Printed Page Numbers§6.6; the flag only says that a Markdown output may leave furniture out (a consumer may drop the bands, see Markdown Rendering§3.2), so a band that no Markdown element matches is not counted as missed. A band the output does write is scored like any other block.

Decorative pictures in attribution references

In a markdown_attribution sidecar (scorer version 2), a Picture reference with no text carries "decorative": true when the page prints nothing there that the Markdown must write: purely decorative background art, shapes and ornaments that print no label or value (they MUST NOT be described, see Slide Furniture§5.10), a faint background repeat of a mark, or a scan speck. A decorative picture that no image element stands for is out of coverage; one the output does write is paired and scored like any other picture. Logos (Logos§12.1.3), icons that carry a meaning or label a field (Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4), photos and illustrations are content and never decorative.

Regions written as several blocks

When a region is naturally written as several Markdown blocks (a grid of fields, a form, a stacked label/value list, a heading printed on two lines), annotate it in a markdown_attribution sidecar as one parent reference with spans for the blocks. The existing span credit then scores an output that writes the blocks; the scorer's many-to-one group match (version 2) is only a fallback for outputs that split the region where the ground truth has no span.

When a class is unclear

Add a review note and request a second review; never pick a class merely to finish the page → Block Classes§5.3.

Excluding a region, rejecting a page

  • Ignore this visible region takes a reason from the allowed list and a short review note → Ignoring and Rejecting§5.6.
  • Page rejection takes an explanation, and the annotation lead is notified. A rejected page is never published.
  • A page with no ink at all is neither: keep it, record that it is blank, and flag it.

Pages to flag for open points

Flag the page so the pair or the case can be found once the point is settled:

  • a court caption block → Court Caption Blocks§5.4;
  • pleading paper or a line-numbered manuscript; record once, out of the reading flow, that the page carries line numbers → Pleading Line Numbers§5.8.

C.8 Ground Truth — Lists and Forms

What to do, when producing ground truth, in the cases the list and form rules leave to review. Each step serves the rule it links to; the rule decides the output.

Situation Step Rule
A form and a real ruled grid cannot be cleanly separated — they share rulings, or the fields sit inside the grid's own borders Reject the page rather than guess a boundary between form and table Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1, Ignoring and Rejecting§5.6
A page prints buttons (Print, Save, Clear), an input placeholder, or a box reserved for a stamp or seal Apply the working default and record the page, so it can be revisited when the open point closes Printed Buttons and Placeholders§10.4.6
A checklist item prints its box before its id Write the box first, per the working default, and record the page Checklists§10.4.3
A box's state cannot be read with confidence, even zoomed in Enter [ ], as the rule requires; do not guess a tick from the text layer Checkboxes§10.4.2

C.9 Ground Truth — Marks on the Page

Steps for producing ground truth on pages that carry marks, stamps and symbols. Each step serves the rule it links to; the rule, not this list, says what the output is.

  1. Clipped text — flag a page whose text runs off the edge, and record the clipping in the page's review notes, never in the transcription. Serves Clipped Text§7.3.1.
  2. Unreadable handwriting — flag the page when part of a handwritten note cannot be read, so the left-out words are visible to review. Serves Handwritten Annotations§7.3.3.
  3. Obscured characters — flag a page where an overprint hides characters, noting which string lost them. Serves Overlapping Text§7.3.6.
  4. Seals with no legible text — flag the page whenever the bare [seal] is used. Serves Seals and Round Stamps§7.3.9.
  5. Codes that do not decode — still draw the code's own box, then flag the page. Serves QR Codes and Bar Codes§7.3.7.
  6. Open encodings — flag every page where a value-bearing icon, a meaningful text colour or a watermark was encoded, so the page can be revisited when the open point closes. Serves Iconography and Symbols§7.3.4, Text Colors§7.3.12 and Watermarks§7.3.13.

C.10 Ground Truth — Tables 1-3

What to do, when producing ground truth, in the cases the table rules on detection, boundaries and headers leave to review. Each step serves the rule it links to; the rule decides the output.

Situation Step Rule
A page mixes form fields with a ruled grid Render the grid as a table and the fields as key-value lines, then flag the page Is This Even a Table§9.1.5 · Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1
A region is a form, a trailing total outside a frame, a data grid under a chart, or detached aligned cells Decide it by that case's own rule, not by the relation test alone Is This Even a Table§9.1.5
A value in a whitespace-aligned block straddles two column tracks Place it in the track its left edge is closest to and flag the page Borderless Whitespace Tables§9.1.1
A printed form grid has no values entered Keep every empty row and flag the page, so a reviewer can see the grid was empty rather than missed Empty Pre-Printed Grids§9.1.3
A form prints dozens of identical empty rows Transcribe them all rather than a few, and flag the page Empty Pre-Printed Grids§9.1.3
A header row cannot be joined to a body (gap, mismatched columns, something in between) Write the header line as text and flag the page; when the gap makes the join doubtful, do not merge Header-Only Tables§9.1.4
A fragment's title carries (cont'd), (continued) or similar Keep the marker and note in the review record that the fragment continues an earlier table Continued in the Title§9.2.3
A table continues across a page break Keep each fragment on its own page as printed, and set the continuation flags on both fragments after looking at both pages Cross-Page Tables§4.3
Column headers are printed again at the foot of a page's block Keep the repeat as a row and flag the page Cross-Page Tables§4.3
A paragraph, caption or heading sits between two fragments sharing one header Merge while the second fragment depends on the header; flag the page when the material in the gap could read as a new section Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9
A row-label column is printed once beside several value blocks Place the blocks as further columns of the labelled table and flag the page so the choice is visible Split Tables Sharing a Header§9.2.9
Stacked header lines could be a wrap or a tier Run the rule / self-standing-leaves / span test deliberately, not by eye Header Wrap vs Real Tier§9.3.2
A header stack is finished Count the leaf tracks and check that every header row adds up to that count before moving on Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3
A units line could go either way Take the second header row and keep that choice for the whole document Units Row§9.3.5 · Choices Made Once Per Document§4.2
A table may be printed twice Decide from the rendered page image, not the text layer Duplicated Tables§9.2.4

C.11 Ground Truth — Tables 4-8

Working steps for annotators producing ground truth for tables: columns, rows and cells, cell values, titles and edges, and special table types. Each step serves the rule it links to; the rule decides what the output is.

Structure before styling

  1. Read the table's structure first — rows, columns, header tiers — ignoring weight and slant. Then go cell by cell and mark bold, italic and underline only where the glyphs show it. → Bold and Italic Inside Tables§9.6.2
  2. Read each row's level from where its label starts in the stub, never from the numbers. → Row-Label Hierarchy§9.5.5
  3. Where a total's printed indent contradicts the grouping it sums, keep the printed level and add a review note describing the conflict. → Total and Subtotal Rows§9.5.6

Evidence, not eyeballing

  1. For a column of identical values, extract the word boxes and read their coordinates: one occurrence means a rowspan, distinct positions mean separate cells. → Repeated Identical Values§9.5.4
  2. Settle a disputed digit from a zoomed crop or the word coordinates, never from the text layer. → Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3
  3. Decide from the image which glyphs are printed and which are handwritten or stamped. → Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5
  4. After finding one struck-through cell, re-check the whole column at zoom. Flagging a redline table is done in addition to that check, never instead of it. → Struck and Replaced Values§9.6.7

Flag for review

  1. Flag any page where a header/body column-count mismatch was repaired by padding with empty cells. → Header Body Column Count Mismatch§9.4.2
  2. Flag pages whose icon vocabulary needed a judgement call. → Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6
  3. Where a table's frame is ambiguous (what belongs at its bottom edge), flag the page and record the encoding chosen for the document. → Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1
  4. Record once per document whether section-divider bands are bold <td> or <th>, and apply it on every page. → Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3
  5. Place a footnote by its marker, not by where the frame happens to be drawn. → Footnotes Inside the Frame§9.7.2

Older annotations

  1. A $ kept in its own column track as a spanned pair in an existing annotation is not wrong and need not be redone; new work puts the symbol in the value's cell. → Gutter Columns§9.4.1

Related

  • About the Examples§C.2 — how the worked examples in these rules were produced

C.12 The annotation QA checklist

Procedure

Work a table in this order, and run the same eight checks again before you call the page done.

1. Frame test first

Decide what belongs to the table by border and fill, then deal with the bands. → Titles Banners Captions§9.7.3

2. Count N from the leaf tracks

Take a body row and count the leaf columns — that is N. Then verify every header row's colspans sum to N, and that no group colspan covers the stub. → Multi-Row Header Tiers§9.3.3

3. Prove every rowspan

A repeated value printed once is a rowspan. Printed k times at distinct y-coordinates, it is k separate cells. When you cannot tell by eye, extract the word boxes. → Repeated Identical Values§9.5.4

4. Walk parallel blocks independently

Where the page repeats a structure — one block per year, one per topic — check each block has all of its sub-sections. It is easy to complete the first block carefully and skim the rest.

5. End-of-table check

The bottom edge is where content is most often lost. Check for:

  • the last printed row
  • trailing summary lines → Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1
  • detached islands → Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1
  • sparse trailing columns → Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1
6. Record equivalences — don't resolve them silently

When a page genuinely admits two encodings, write the canonical form and record that the other reading is also defensible. → Accepted Alternatives§A.1

7. Keep claim types separate

Never blend these into one verdict. Say which one you mean:

what you can see on the page · what an existing annotation says · a choice you made between two defensible encodings · a settled convention · an open question

This is what stops you writing "the annotation is wrong" when what you actually observed is "the annotation differs from what I would have written".

8. Escalate conflicts

Do not silently choose among open options.

Where two conventions are both live, record both and flag the page. A silent pick becomes precedent.

The completion record

Before you call a page done, you should be able to answer:

  • Which image and which crop did you inspect?
  • Which case does this fall under?
  • What is directly visible on the page?
  • What is an encoding choice you made?
  • What settled convention, if any, makes that choice the canonical one?

One page can carry several independent issues — a phantom header row, a repeated value wrongly spanned, and an out-of-frame title can all sit in a single crop. Record them separately rather than giving the page one verdict.

Working a chart

Seven checks, in order, before a chart's rules are done:

1. Census the points

Count positions × series — plus printed callouts, plus every panel — before judging any value: that is the rule count full coverage owes. A skipped series, tail, or panel is the number-one coverage failure. On the judge families the census includes the judged facts — every whisker span, box, gantt mark, and unambiguous choropleth region owes its chart_judge_point (The Ground-Truth File§C.13). → Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1 · Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3

2. Check every label

Printed text only, copied whole, the minimal set that uniquely locates the point; unlabeled positions by their axis value; a title fragment only to break a tie between charts. No colors, no chart-type words, no appended units, no merged dimensions. → Labels§11.1.2

3. Sweep for printed values first

On the marks, beside slices, in the legend, at line ends, in the side text — before estimating anything. A printed value you missed becomes a wrong estimate; every printed value is exact and tolerance-free. → Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 · Legend and Overlay Values§11.2.4

4. Verify the estimated values

Visual center, read against the mark's own axis (watch second axes and log bands), stacks and steps as their own spans, tolerance from the readability buckets. → Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 · Dual-Axis and Combo Charts§11.2.2 · Stacked Bars and Waterfalls§11.2.9 · Log Scale Charts§11.2.6

5. Audit the zeros and the gaps

A baseline mark or an empty labeled position is 0; a point no label set can locate, or a whisker end, carries no rule — deliberately, not by omission. → Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 · Scatter and Error Bars§11.2.8

6. Hunt invented content

No rules for reference ink or event callouts, no invented label text, no computed values, no expanded abbreviations, no tolerance on printed values. → Multiple Charts and Reference Ink§11.1.3 · Labels§11.1.2

7. Check the file

The envelope (expected_markdown null, test_rules, doc tags), one flat rule list, need_estimate tags on estimates, tool-managed fields untouched, ids appearing on save — not from you. → The Ground-Truth File§C.13

Before publishing a multi-page document

Checks that only fail when you look across pages, not at one — see Document Rules§4.1:

  • [ ] The document type and its cover were decided once, and every page follows them
  • [ ] Every recurring margin band is filed the same way on every page it appears on
  • [ ] No heading repeats on more than half the pages — one that does is furniture filed as structure
  • [ ] No page after the first opens at a top-level heading unless that page actually prints one
  • [ ] Every ⚖️ choice is encoded the same way on every page, and the page that made it is flagged
  • [ ] Every table that runs across a page break is one fragment per page, none is joined, and both fragments carry matching continuation flags

Before publishing a Block layout

A page-level layout pass has its own gate. Every line must be true:

  • [ ] Every meaningful visible region has one correct Block and class, or is explicitly ignored with a valid reason
  • [ ] Each Block's layout class matches the corresponding Markdown element's class in Elements§3.1; any disagreement was resolved against the printed page
  • [ ] Table and chart captions use <caption> inside their table HTML, first if read before the object and last if read after it; each retains its Caption class and its own box
  • [ ] Separate paragraphs, columns, list items, captions and notes are not merged together
  • [ ] Table and Picture boundaries contain the complete object without absorbing captions or nearby prose
  • [ ] Reading order is complete, contiguous and correct — starts at 0, no gaps, no duplicates
  • [ ] Imported and generated Block suggestions were reviewed individually
  • [ ] Hide boxes was used to sweep for gaps, clipping, duplicates and wrong classes
  • [ ] The Block annotation is marked Checked
  • [ ] I swept the entire page is ticked
  • [ ] Validate page reports no blockers, and every warning was read
  • [ ] The draft is saved before Publish page

The hide-boxes sweep is the step that finds real errors. With the boxes drawn, the eye fills in what it expects; with them hidden, a missed paragraph is obvious.

→ Block Annotation§5.1 · Block Classes§5.3 · Block Boundaries§5.2 · Reading Order§5.9

C.13 The Ground-Truth File

Procedure

The deliverable for a chart page is its {name}.test.json: chart_data_point rules, one per data point, covering every data point in the chart (Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1) — plus a chart_judge_point rule for each fact no printed text locates or no single table shape carries: whisker spans, choropleth classes, gantt spans, sankey flows.

The files on disk

File What it is
{name}.pdf the single page holding the chart — the only source of truth
{name}.test.json the ground truth — the file you deliver
{name}_llama_agentic.md a reference parse, roughly 70–80% right — reference only, never authority

The JSON envelope has three keys: expected_markdown (stays null), test_rules, and tags. The top-level tags carry document provenance from the fixed sector vocabulary (domain:government, domain:energy, …); the loader copies them onto every rule.

The rule

One rule = one data point:

{
  "type": "chart_data_point",
  "labels": ["Very high DSI", "2014"],
  "value": "25 (13.0%)",
  "max_diffs": 0,
  "normalize_numbers": true,
  "verified": true,
  "id": "4d47b974398b0306"
}

You author three things: labels (the printed text that locates the point — Labels§11.1.2), value (printed or estimated — Values and Tolerances§11.1.4), and relative_tolerance on estimated values only. The other fields (type, max_diffs, normalize_numbers, verified) are handled by the annotation tool, and id is stamped on save — never authored. Estimated rules also carry "tags": ["need_estimate"].

The judge rule

A few chart families carry facts no printed text locates — an error bar's whisker span, a choropleth's region-to-class pairing, a gantt bar's span on the time axis. Those get a second rule shape, scored by an LLM judge that accepts any output faithfully conveying the fact:

{
  "type": "chart_judge_point",
  "chart_type": "map_class",
  "labels": ["CO"],
  "expected": {"region": "CO", "class": "20%-<25%"},
  "verified": true
}

You author chart_type (error_bar, box_plot, map_class, gantt_span, or sankey_flow), the same labels, the family's expected payload, and a tolerance on estimated payloads. Where each applies, with worked pages: Scatter and Error Bars§11.2.8 (whiskers and box plots), Gantt and Sankey Charts§11.2.3 (task spans in one gantt_span shape, ribbon flows in one sankey_flow shape), Maps and Treemaps§11.2.7 (choropleth classes). Everything printed or axis-readable stays a chart_data_point.

The complete file

The file for the page in Cover Every Data Point§11.1.1: 6 years × 4 series, every value printed — 24 exact rules:

{
  "expected_markdown": null,
  "test_rules": [
    {"type": "chart_data_point", "labels": ["Low DSI", "2014"], "value": "32 (16.6%)", "max_diffs": 0, "normalize_numbers": true, "verified": true},
    {"type": "chart_data_point", "labels": ["Middle DSI", "2014"], "value": "74 (38.3%)", "max_diffs": 0, "normalize_numbers": true, "verified": true},

  ],
  "tags": ["domain:government"]
}

The checker looks each rule up independently — it finds the value in the parsed tables and verifies the labels sit on that cell's row and column. No order matters, no orientation matters, and no rule says which chart on the page it belongs to; the labels do the locating.

In the examples across these notes, rules are shown in the short authored form — labels / value / relative_tolerance / tags — since the tool supplies the rest.

  • Values and Tolerances§11.1.4 — printed, estimated, and zero values
